bio_edx.5.0.summary: Plants and algae are **producers**: they use **light energy** to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water by **photosynthesis**, so they are the main producers of food and therefore **biomass** for almost every food chain. Photosynthesis is an **endothermic reaction** because energy is transferred from the environment (as light) to the chloroplasts and stored as chemical energy in glucose. That stored energy and biomass then pass along food chains to consumers.

core.h: Producers: the start of every food chain
core.p: A **producer** is an organism that makes its own food (organic molecules) from simple inorganic substances using an energy source. On land the main producers are **green plants**; in water they are mainly **algae** (including phytoplankton). Because they make the food that all other organisms eat, they are the main producers of food and therefore of **biomass**.
bullets: Producers are at **trophic level 1** in every food chain.
Consumers (herbivores, carnivores) cannot photosynthesise, so they rely on eating producers or other consumers.
Algae in oceans, lakes and rivers produce a huge share of the Earth's biomass and oxygen.
Without producers, energy from the Sun could not enter food chains, so the whole community would collapse.

callouts.p: An organism that makes its own food by photosynthesis; the first trophic level in a food chain.

core.p: **Biomass** is the mass of living material in an organism or at a trophic level. The glucose made in photosynthesis is turned into all the other molecules (starch, cellulose, proteins, lipids) that make up a plant's body, so photosynthesis is how new biomass is built.
bullets: Biomass is often measured as **dry mass** because water content varies.
Biomass contains stored **chemical energy**, which is passed on when a consumer eats the producer.
Only part of the biomass is passed on at each level (some is lost in respiration, waste and parts not eaten), so producers always have the **largest biomass** in a pyramid of biomass.
This is why producers are said to be the main producers of food and therefore biomass for life on Earth.

callouts.p: The total mass of living material (organisms) in a given area or trophic level.

fig.cap: A pyramid of biomass. The producer level (grass) is the widest because photosynthesis builds all the biomass that the consumers above it depend on. Light energy from the Sun enters the chain only through the producers.

core.p: Photosynthesis is the process in which plants and algae use **light energy** to react **carbon dioxide** and **water** to produce **glucose** and **oxygen**. It happens in the **chloroplasts**, which contain the green pigment **chlorophyll** that absorbs the light.
bullets: Word equation: carbon dioxide + water -> glucose + oxygen (light energy and chlorophyll written over the arrow).
Balanced symbol equation: 6CO2 + 6H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2.
Light is **not** a reactant; it is the **energy source**, so it goes above the arrow.
Chlorophyll is not used up; it absorbs light and transfers the energy to the reaction.

callouts.p: carbon dioxide + water -> glucose + oxygen, and 6CO2 + 6H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2. Both sides have 6 C, 12 H and 18 O atoms.

head: Substance
Formula
Role
Where from / where to
rows: Soil, absorbed by root hair cells, carried in xylem
Used in the plant or converted to other molecules
Diffuses out through stomata or used in respiration

core.p: Photosynthesis takes place inside **chloroplasts**, found mainly in the **palisade mesophyll** cells of leaves (and in algal cells). Leaves are broad and thin so they capture a lot of light and gases only have a short distance to diffuse.
bullets: Chloroplasts contain **chlorophyll**, which absorbs mainly red and blue light and reflects green light (why plants look green).
Carbon dioxide enters the leaf by **diffusion** through **stomata**.
Water reaches the leaf from the roots through **xylem** vessels.
Oxygen leaves through the stomata by diffusion.
Root cells and other cells with no chloroplasts cannot photosynthesise.

fig.cap: Inputs and outputs of photosynthesis in a leaf. Light energy is absorbed by chlorophyll in chloroplasts, carbon dioxide diffuses in through stomata, water arrives in the xylem, glucose is made and oxygen diffuses out.

core.p: An **endothermic reaction** is one that takes in energy from the surroundings. Photosynthesis is endothermic because **energy is transferred from the environment to the chloroplasts by light**. The products (glucose and oxygen) store more chemical energy than the reactants (carbon dioxide and water).
bullets: The energy input is **light energy**, absorbed by chlorophyll.
This energy is used to build large, energy-rich glucose molecules from small, low-energy molecules.
The energy stored in glucose is the **chemical energy** that later powers respiration in the plant and in every consumer.
Respiration is the reverse overall: it is **exothermic**, releasing the energy stored in glucose.

callouts.p: A reaction in which energy is transferred from the surroundings to the reacting substances (energy is taken in).
Say that energy (light) is transferred from the environment to the chloroplasts. Just writing it needs light is often not enough for the mark.

fig.cap: Reaction profile for photosynthesis. The products are higher in energy than the reactants because light energy has been taken in from the surroundings, so the reaction is endothermic.

core.h: Energy transfers: from Sun to food chain
core.p: Photosynthesis is the route by which energy from the Sun enters living things. Light energy is transferred to chemical energy stored in glucose and then in all the biomass made from it.
bullets: Sun -> light energy -> chlorophyll -> chemical energy in glucose.
Plants respire some of that glucose to release energy for their own life processes.
The rest is stored in biomass, which is eaten by primary consumers.
Only a small fraction (around 1 to 3 per cent) of the light falling on a leaf ends up stored in biomass; the rest is reflected, passes through, or misses chlorophyll.

core.p: The spec names both **plants and algae**. Algae are simple photosynthetic organisms (many are single-celled) that live in water and carry out exactly the same overall reaction.
bullets: Algae contain chloroplasts with chlorophyll, like plant cells.
Phytoplankton (microscopic algae) are the producers in most marine food chains.
Aquatic producers use carbon dioxide dissolved in the water and release oxygen into the water.
This oxygen production is what you measure in the core practical using pondweed or algal balls.

core.h: What the plant does with glucose
core.p: Glucose made in photosynthesis is used straight away or converted into other substances. This is how photosynthesis produces biomass: glucose is the raw material for all the plant's large molecules.
bullets: **Respiration**: releases energy for active transport, growth and making new molecules.
**Starch**: insoluble storage in leaves, seeds and tubers, so it does not affect water movement by osmosis.
**Cellulose**: to build and strengthen cell walls.
**Sucrose**: the soluble sugar transported in the **phloem** to other parts of the plant.
**Lipids (fats and oils)**: energy storage, for example in seeds.
**Amino acids and proteins**: made by combining glucose with **nitrate ions** absorbed from the soil.

callouts.p: Plants store glucose as starch because it is insoluble. They transport sugar as sucrose, not starch or glucose.

core.p: Because glucose is quickly converted to starch, the presence of starch in a leaf shows that photosynthesis has taken place.
bullets: Boil the leaf in water to kill it and break down cell membranes.
Warm it in ethanol (in a water bath, not over a flame) to remove the chlorophyll.
Rinse in warm water to soften it.
Add **iodine solution**: blue-black shows starch is present; orange-brown means no starch.
Variegated leaves show starch only in the green parts, proving chlorophyll is needed.

core.p: Plants carry out **both** processes. Photosynthesis only happens in the light; respiration happens all the time in every living cell.
bullets: In bright light the rate of photosynthesis is greater than respiration, so plants take in carbon dioxide and give out oxygen overall.
In the dark there is only respiration, so plants give out carbon dioxide.
At the compensation point the two rates are equal and there is no net gas exchange.

core.h: Why photosynthesis matters for life on Earth
core.p: Photosynthesis links the non-living environment to living organisms. It provides food, stores energy, and keeps the atmosphere suitable for life.
bullets: Supplies the **food and biomass** for nearly all food chains.
Releases **oxygen** needed for aerobic respiration by most organisms.
Removes **carbon dioxide** from the atmosphere, a key step in the carbon cycle.
Fossil fuels are made from the biomass of ancient producers, so their energy also came from photosynthesis.

callouts.p: Producers make food and therefore biomass; consumers depend on that biomass for both energy and materials.

analogy.p: A leaf is like a bakery powered by solar panels. The raw ingredients are cheap and plentiful (carbon dioxide and water), the solar panels are the chlorophyll, and the power they collect is used to bake energy-rich loaves (glucose). Because the bakery has to take in power from outside to make the loaves, the process is endothermic. Some loaves are eaten by the bakers themselves (respiration), some are stored in the freezer (starch), and some are used to build the bakery walls (cellulose); customers (consumers) buy what is left, which is why every customer depends on the bakery. Where it breaks down: a real bakery uses electricity, not light directly, and oxygen being released as a by-product has no clear bakery equivalent; also, plants do not sell food on purpose, consumers simply eat them.

terms.d: The process in which plants and algae use light energy to react carbon dioxide and water to make glucose and oxygen.
An organism that makes its own food by photosynthesis; first trophic level in a food chain.
The mass of living material in an organism, trophic level or area.
A reaction that takes in energy from the surroundings.
A reaction that releases energy to the surroundings, such as respiration.
Organelle in plant and algal cells where photosynthesis takes place; contains chlorophyll.
Green pigment in chloroplasts that absorbs light energy for photosynthesis.
Simple sugar, C6H12O6, made in photosynthesis; stores chemical energy.
Insoluble storage carbohydrate made from glucose in plants.
Carbohydrate made from glucose that forms plant cell walls.
Soluble sugar made from glucose and transported in the phloem.
Pores, mainly on the underside of a leaf, through which carbon dioxide diffuses in and oxygen diffuses out.
Simple photosynthetic organisms, many single-celled, that are the main producers in aquatic ecosystems.
The feeding position of an organism in a food chain.
Mineral ions absorbed from soil and combined with glucose to make amino acids and proteins.

mistakes.w: Photosynthesis is endothermic because it needs heat.
mistakes.r: It is endothermic because energy is transferred from the environment to the chloroplasts by light.

mistakes.w: Light is a reactant in photosynthesis.
mistakes.r: Light is the energy source; it is written above the arrow, not as a reactant.

mistakes.w: Plants get their food from the soil.
mistakes.r: Plants make their own food (glucose) by photosynthesis; the soil supplies water and mineral ions.

mistakes.w: Plants only photosynthesise and animals only respire.
mistakes.r: Plants respire all the time as well as photosynthesising in the light.
6CO2 + 6H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2 (six oxygen molecules).

mistakes.w: Glucose is stored in plants as glycogen.
mistakes.r: Plants store glucose as starch; glycogen is the store in animals and fungi.

mistakes.w: Plants transport starch in the phloem.
mistakes.r: Sugar is transported in the phloem as sucrose.

mistakes.w: Chlorophyll makes energy.
mistakes.r: Chlorophyll absorbs light energy; energy cannot be made, only transferred.

mistakes.w: Producers are always plants.
mistakes.r: Plants and algae are both photosynthetic producers; algae are the main producers in water.

exam.q: Write the word equation for photosynthesis.
model: carbon dioxide + water as reactants
-> glucose + oxygen as products (light energy above arrow)
exam.tip: Do not put light or chlorophyll on the left as reactants.

exam.q: Give the balanced symbol equation for photosynthesis.
model: 6CO2 + 6H2O
exam.tip: Check the atoms balance: 6 C, 12 H, 18 O each side.

exam.q: Explain why photosynthesis is described as an endothermic reaction.
model: energy is taken in / transferred from the surroundings
light energy is transferred to the chloroplasts (and stored in glucose)
exam.tip: Mention light and where the energy goes.

exam.q: Name the part of a plant cell where photosynthesis takes place.
model: chloroplast
exam.tip: Not chlorophyll, which is the pigment, not the organelle.

exam.q: Explain why plants are described as producers.
model: they make their own food / glucose
by photosynthesis, using light energy (so they are the source of biomass for food chains)
exam.tip: Link making food to providing biomass for consumers.

exam.q: Explain why the biomass of producers is larger than the biomass of primary consumers.
model: not all of the producer is eaten (e.g. roots)
some biomass is lost / used in respiration by producers
some is lost in waste / not digested, so less is transferred to the next level
exam.tip: Refer to losses at each trophic level.

exam.q: Describe how carbon dioxide and water reach the chloroplasts in a leaf.
model: carbon dioxide diffuses in through stomata
water absorbed by root hair cells (osmosis)
water carried to the leaf in xylem
exam.tip: Use the words diffusion, stomata and xylem.

exam.q: Describe four ways a plant uses the glucose made in photosynthesis.
model: respiration to release energy
converted to starch for storage
converted to cellulose for cell walls
converted to sucrose for transport in phloem / combined with nitrates to make amino acids / made into lipids
exam.tip: One use per mark; say what each product is for.

exam.q: A student tested a variegated leaf for starch with iodine. Only the green areas turned blue-black. Explain this result.
model: green areas contain chlorophyll / chloroplasts
photosynthesis occurred only there, making glucose
glucose converted to starch, which iodine stains blue-black; white areas had no chlorophyll so no starch
exam.tip: Chain the logic: chlorophyll -> photosynthesis -> glucose -> starch.

exam.q: Explain why photosynthetic organisms are essential for almost all life on Earth.
model: plants and algae are producers at the start of food chains
they use light energy to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water
light energy is transferred to chemical energy stored in glucose (endothermic)
glucose is used to make biomass (starch, cellulose, proteins, lipids)
consumers get energy and materials by eating this biomass
photosynthesis releases oxygen needed for aerobic respiration and removes carbon dioxide from the air
exam.tip: A 6-mark answer needs a logical chain: energy in, biomass made, passed to consumers, plus oxygen.

worked.q: Show that the symbol equation 6CO2 + 6H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2 is balanced.
steps: Left: carbon = 6 x 1 = 6; hydrogen = 6 x 2 = 12; oxygen = (6 x 2) + (6 x 1) = 18.
Right: carbon = 6; hydrogen = 12; oxygen in glucose = 6, oxygen in 6O2 = 12, total 18.
All three elements have equal numbers of atoms on both sides.
worked.ans: 6 C, 12 H and 18 O on each side, so the equation is balanced.

worked.q: A pond has 5000 g of algae (dry mass) and 600 g of water fleas that eat them. Calculate the percentage of producer biomass found in the primary consumers and suggest why it is so low.
steps: Percentage = (600 / 5000) x 100.
= 12 per cent.
Biomass is lost between levels: not all algae are eaten, some biomass is used in the algae's respiration, and water fleas lose some as waste and in their own respiration.
worked.ans: 12 per cent; most producer biomass is not passed on because of respiration, waste and parts not eaten.

worked.q: Model answer: Explain how energy from the Sun ends up in a rabbit.
steps: Light energy from the Sun is absorbed by chlorophyll in the chloroplasts of grass.
Energy is transferred from the environment to the chloroplasts, so photosynthesis is endothermic.
The energy is stored as chemical energy in glucose, made from carbon dioxide and water.
Glucose is converted into biomass such as starch, cellulose and proteins.
The rabbit eats the grass and digests and absorbs these molecules, gaining their stored chemical energy.
worked.ans: Light energy is transferred to chemical energy in glucose by photosynthesis in the grass, stored in biomass, and passed to the rabbit when it eats the grass.

bio_edx.5.1.summary: The rate of photosynthesis is controlled by **limiting factors**: **light intensity**, **carbon dioxide concentration** and **temperature**. A limiting factor is the one in shortest supply, so increasing it increases the rate until something else becomes limiting and the graph levels off. Temperature is different because photosynthesis is controlled by **enzymes**, so too high a temperature makes the rate fall sharply. At Higher tier you must explain how these factors **interact**, reading graphs with several curves to work out which factor is limiting at each point.

core.p: Photosynthesis needs light energy, carbon dioxide, water, chlorophyll and a suitable temperature. At any moment, the rate is held back by whichever factor is in **shortest supply**: this is the **limiting factor**. Improving any other factor makes no difference until the limiting one is increased.
bullets: The three limiting factors on the spec are **light intensity**, **carbon dioxide concentration** and **temperature**.
Only **one** factor is limiting at a time.
When the limiting factor is increased, the rate rises; when the rate levels off, a **different** factor has become limiting.
Water is rarely limiting in practice because a plant short of water closes its stomata first, which limits carbon dioxide.

callouts.p: The factor that is in shortest supply and so stops the rate of a process (here photosynthesis) from increasing.

core.p: Light provides the **energy** for photosynthesis. As light intensity increases, more light energy is absorbed by chlorophyll, so the rate increases. On the graph, the rate rises in a straight line at first, then levels off.
bullets: Steep, straight part of the line: **light intensity is the limiting factor**.
The rate is directly proportional to light intensity in this region.
The line levels off (plateau) because **another factor**, usually carbon dioxide concentration or temperature, is now limiting.
At the plateau, increasing light further has no effect on rate.
In very low light (e.g. at night) photosynthesis stops; respiration still continues.

fig.cap: Rate against light intensity. On the rising part light is the limiting factor; on the plateau another factor (carbon dioxide or temperature) limits the rate.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="a" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0 L10 5 L0 10 z" fill="#1b2540"/></marker></defs><rect x="0" y="0" width="400" height="240" fill="#f8fafc"/><line x1="60" y1="200" x2="60" y2="35" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#a)"/><line x1="60" y1="200" x2="385" y2="200" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#a)"/><text x="30" y="120" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540" text-anchor="middle" transform="rotate(-90 30 120)">Rate of photosynthesis</text><text x="220" y="225" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540" text-anchor="middle">Light intensity</text><text x="200" y="20" font-size="13" fill="#1b2540" text-anchor="middle">Effect of light intensity</text><path d="M60 200 L190 90 Q215 72 250 70 L370 70" fill="none" stroke="#166534" stroke-width="3"/><rect x="80" y="150" width="110" height="20" rx="4" fill="#fde68a" stroke="#b45309"/><text x="135" y="164" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">Light is limiting</text><rect x="250" y="85" width="125" height="34" rx="4" fill="#dbeafe" stroke="#1d4ed8"/><text x="312" y="99" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">Plateau: another</text><text x="312" y="113" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">factor is limiting</text></svg>

core.p: Carbon dioxide is a **reactant** in photosynthesis. Increasing its concentration means more carbon dioxide molecules diffuse into the leaf and are available to be built into glucose, so the rate increases until another factor limits it.
bullets: The graph has the same shape as for light: a rise, then a plateau.
While rising, **carbon dioxide concentration is limiting**.
On the plateau, light intensity or temperature is limiting.
Atmospheric carbon dioxide is only about 0.04 per cent, so on a warm, bright day carbon dioxide is often the limiting factor.
Line starts slightly above zero CO2 only if the plant is supplying CO2 from its own respiration; you can ignore this detail in most questions.

fig.cap: Rate against carbon dioxide concentration. The rate rises while carbon dioxide is limiting, then levels off when light intensity or temperature becomes the limiting factor.

core.p: Photosynthesis is a series of reactions **controlled by enzymes**. Temperature affects the rate in the same way it affects any enzyme-controlled reaction, so the graph rises to an **optimum** and then falls steeply.
bullets: Below the optimum: increasing temperature gives molecules more **kinetic energy**, so enzyme and substrate molecules collide more often and with more energy, increasing the rate.
At the **optimum temperature** (often around 25 to 35 C for many plants) the rate is highest.
Above the optimum: the enzymes **denature**; the shape of the **active site** changes so the substrate no longer fits, and the rate falls sharply.
Low temperature is often the limiting factor in winter, even in bright light.

callouts.t: Temperature is not like light or CO2
callouts.p: Light and carbon dioxide graphs level off. The temperature graph has a peak and then drops because enzymes denature. Do not say enzymes are killed: enzymes are not alive.

fig.cap: Rate against temperature. The rate increases as kinetic energy and collisions increase, peaks at the optimum, then falls rapidly as enzymes denature.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="a" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0 L10 5 L0 10 z" fill="#1b2540"/></marker></defs><rect x="0" y="0" width="400" height="240" fill="#f8fafc"/><line x1="60" y1="200" x2="60" y2="35" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#a)"/><line x1="60" y1="200" x2="385" y2="200" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#a)"/><text x="30" y="120" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540" text-anchor="middle" transform="rotate(-90 30 120)">Rate of photosynthesis</text><text x="220" y="225" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540" text-anchor="middle">Temperature</text><text x="200" y="20" font-size="13" fill="#1b2540" text-anchor="middle">Effect of temperature</text><path d="M60 195 Q180 160 230 60 Q255 40 275 80 L310 195" fill="none" stroke="#be123c" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="250" y1="52" x2="250" y2="200" stroke="#6b7280" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><text x="255" y="45" font-size="11" fill="#be123c">Optimum</text><rect x="75" y="80" width="130" height="34" rx="4" fill="#fde68a" stroke="#b45309"/><text x="140" y="94" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">More kinetic energy,</text><text x="140" y="108" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">more collisions</text><rect x="305" y="110" width="88" height="34" rx="4" fill="#fecaca" stroke="#991b1b"/><text x="349" y="124" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">Enzymes</text><text x="349" y="138" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">denature</text></svg>

core.p: Exams often give a graph and ask which factor is limiting at a particular point. Use a simple rule.
bullets: If the line is **rising** as the x-axis factor increases, the **x-axis factor** is limiting.
If the line is **flat**, the x-axis factor is **not** limiting; something else is.
To identify that something else, look at what differs between curves on the same graph (Higher).
Always quote values from the graph with units when describing a trend.

callouts.p: When asked to describe a graph, say what happens, give values, and say where the pattern changes (e.g. rate increases until 40 units of light, then stays constant at 12 bubbles per minute).

core.p: In real conditions the factors **interact**: the maximum rate a plant can reach depends on all three at once. A graph with several curves, each at a different carbon dioxide concentration or temperature, shows this.
bullets: All curves rise together at low light because **light is limiting** for all of them.
Each curve levels off at a different height: the lower curve has levelled off because its carbon dioxide concentration or temperature is limiting.
Raising carbon dioxide (or temperature, up to the optimum) raises the plateau, so light can continue to increase the rate up to a higher level.
Comparing two curves that differ in only one factor tells you that factor was limiting on the lower plateau.
The factor that limits the rate can change during a day: light at dawn, carbon dioxide or temperature at midday.

fig.cap: Higher tier interaction graph. At low light, light limits all three curves. The bottom curve plateaus because carbon dioxide is limiting; the middle curve (high carbon dioxide) plateaus because temperature is limiting; the top curve has both raised.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="a" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0 L10 5 L0 10 z" fill="#1b2540"/></marker></defs><rect x="0" y="0" width="400" height="240" fill="#f8fafc"/><line x1="60" y1="200" x2="60" y2="35" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#a)"/><line x1="60" y1="200" x2="385" y2="200" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#a)"/><text x="30" y="120" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540" text-anchor="middle" transform="rotate(-90 30 120)">Rate of photosynthesis</text><text x="220" y="225" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540" text-anchor="middle">Light intensity</text><text x="200" y="20" font-size="13" fill="#1b2540" text-anchor="middle">Interaction of factors (Higher)</text><path d="M60 200 L170 60 Q185 45 215 45 L300 45" fill="none" stroke="#166534" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M60 200 L150 110 Q165 98 190 98 L300 98" fill="none" stroke="#1d4ed8" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M60 200 L120 155 Q132 147 150 147 L300 147" fill="none" stroke="#b45309" stroke-width="3"/><text x="305" y="49" font-size="11" fill="#166534">High CO2, 25 C</text><text x="305" y="102" font-size="11" fill="#1d4ed8">High CO2, 15 C</text><text x="305" y="151" font-size="11" fill="#b45309">Low CO2, 15 C</text></svg>

core.p: Follow a fixed method so you never confuse which factor is limiting.
bullets: Step 1: find the part of the curve you are asked about.
Step 2: if it is rising, the x-axis variable is limiting.
Step 3: if it is flat, compare with a higher curve; the condition that is different between them is the limiting factor on the lower curve.
Step 4: if two conditions differ, you cannot be sure which is limiting from those two curves alone.

head: Comparison
Difference
Conclusion about lower curve plateau
rows: Low CO2, 15 C vs high CO2, 15 C
High CO2, 15 C vs high CO2, 25 C
Low CO2, 15 C vs high CO2, 25 C
Cannot tell which one from these two curves

core.h: Why the factors matter: linking to the equation
core.p: Each factor links to part of the reaction carbon dioxide + water -> glucose + oxygen.
bullets: **Light intensity**: supplies the energy for this endothermic reaction.
**Carbon dioxide**: a raw material (reactant); more substrate means more reactions per second.
**Temperature**: controls how fast the enzymes catalyse each step.
Chlorophyll amount can also limit rate (e.g. in yellowing leaves lacking magnesium), but the spec focuses on the three named factors.

head: Factor
Why it affects rate
Graph shape
rows: Rises to optimum then falls sharply

core.p: Commercial growers control limiting factors in greenhouses to grow crops faster and increase yield.
bullets: **Paraffin heaters** raise temperature and also release carbon dioxide as they burn.
**Artificial lights** increase light intensity and allow photosynthesis to continue at night.
**Carbon dioxide** can be pumped in to raise its concentration.
Growers only add a factor while it is limiting; once the rate plateaus, adding more wastes money.
Growers must balance extra cost (fuel, electricity) against the value of the extra crop.

callouts.p: Increasing a factor that is not limiting costs money but gives no increase in rate or yield.

core.p: The same ideas explain how fast plants grow in different habitats and seasons.
bullets: Woodland floor plants are limited by **light** because the tree canopy shades them.
In winter, **temperature** and low light limit photosynthesis.
On a hot bright summer day, **carbon dioxide** is often limiting.
In deep water, light is limiting for algae, so producers are concentrated near the surface.

core.p: The effect of light intensity is investigated in the core practical using pondweed or algal balls. Other limiting factors must be **controlled** so that light intensity is the only independent variable.
bullets: Keep temperature constant, e.g. with a water bath or a heat shield between lamp and plant.
Keep carbon dioxide constant by adding the same amount of sodium hydrogencarbonate to the water.
If the rate stops increasing at high light, carbon dioxide or temperature has become limiting.

analogy.p: Imagine a café making sandwiches that needs bread, filling and staff. If there is only enough bread for 10 sandwiches an hour, ordering more filling or hiring more staff does nothing: bread is the limiting factor. Order more bread and output rises, until staff numbers become the new limit. Temperature is like the speed the staff work: a warm kitchen speeds them up, but if it gets far too hot they stop working properly altogether (like enzymes denaturing). Where it breaks down: staff recover when the kitchen cools, but denatured enzymes do not regain their shape, and in a plant light is an energy supply, not an ingredient like bread.

terms.d: The factor in shortest supply that prevents the rate of photosynthesis from increasing.
How fast glucose is made or oxygen produced, e.g. volume of oxygen or bubbles per minute.
The amount of light energy reaching a given area per unit time.
The amount of carbon dioxide in a given volume of air or water; a reactant in photosynthesis.
The temperature at which an enzyme-controlled process works fastest.
A biological catalyst, made of protein, that speeds up reactions such as those of photosynthesis.
A permanent change in the shape of an enzyme's active site so that the substrate no longer fits.
The part of an enzyme where the substrate binds.
Energy of movement; higher temperature gives molecules more kinetic energy so they collide more often.
The flat part of a graph showing the rate is no longer increasing.
The way the maximum rate depends on the levels of light, carbon dioxide and temperature together.
The amount of crop produced; increased by removing limiting factors in greenhouses.
The factor deliberately changed in an investigation, such as light intensity.
A factor kept the same so it does not affect the results, such as temperature and carbon dioxide concentration.

mistakes.w: The graph levels off because the plant has reached its maximum rate.
mistakes.r: It levels off because another factor (e.g. carbon dioxide concentration or temperature) has become limiting.

mistakes.w: At high temperatures the enzymes are killed.
mistakes.r: At high temperatures the enzymes denature: the active site changes shape so the substrate no longer fits.

mistakes.w: Light intensity is the limiting factor on the flat part of the light graph.
mistakes.r: On the plateau light is not limiting; another factor is.

mistakes.w: More light always means more photosynthesis.
mistakes.r: More light only increases the rate while light is the limiting factor.

mistakes.w: Temperature graph levels off like the light graph.
mistakes.r: Temperature graph rises to an optimum then falls sharply because of denaturation.

mistakes.w: Heat makes the reaction happen faster because it gives energy for photosynthesis.
mistakes.r: Light supplies the energy; temperature increases kinetic energy and collisions of enzyme and substrate molecules.

mistakes.w: Several factors can be limiting at the same time.
mistakes.r: Only one factor is the limiting factor at any one time.

mistakes.w: Greenhouse owners should increase all factors as much as possible.
mistakes.r: Only increase a factor while it is limiting; beyond that it costs money with no extra yield.

exam.q: State what is meant by a limiting factor.
model: the factor in shortest supply that stops the rate of photosynthesis increasing
exam.tip: Shortest supply is the key phrase.

exam.q: Name two factors, other than light intensity, that can limit the rate of photosynthesis.
model: carbon dioxide concentration
temperature
exam.tip: Say carbon dioxide concentration, not just carbon dioxide.

exam.q: Explain the shape of a graph of rate of photosynthesis against light intensity.
model: rate increases as light intensity increases
because light is the limiting factor / more energy available
rate levels off because another factor such as CO2 or temperature becomes limiting
exam.tip: Describe then explain each part of the line.

exam.q: Explain why the rate of photosynthesis decreases above 40 C.
model: enzymes control photosynthesis
enzymes denature at high temperature
active site changes shape so substrate cannot bind / fewer enzyme-substrate complexes
exam.tip: Use denature and active site.

exam.q: Explain why increasing temperature from 10 C to 25 C increases the rate of photosynthesis.
model: molecules gain more kinetic energy
more frequent successful collisions between enzymes and substrates
exam.tip: Link temperature to collisions, not to energy for photosynthesis.

exam.q: A farmer increases light intensity in a greenhouse but the yield does not change. Suggest why.
model: light was not the limiting factor
carbon dioxide concentration or temperature was limiting
exam.tip: Always name the alternative factor.

exam.q: (Higher) Look at a graph with curves for high CO2 at 25 C and high CO2 at 15 C. Explain which factor limits the lower curve on its plateau.
model: temperature is limiting
because the only difference between the curves is temperature and raising it raises the plateau
exam.tip: Identify the one condition that differs.

exam.q: (Higher) Explain why the rate on all curves is the same at very low light intensity.
model: light intensity is the limiting factor for all curves
so changing CO2 or temperature has no effect
exam.tip: Curves overlapping means they share a limiting factor.

exam.q: Describe how a greenhouse owner could increase crop yield and explain why each method works.
model: paraffin heaters to raise temperature towards the optimum, increasing enzyme activity
heaters also release CO2, increasing a reactant
artificial lighting increases light intensity / allows photosynthesis at night
only worth doing while that factor is limiting, balance cost against increased yield
exam.tip: Method plus reason for each mark pair.

exam.q: (Higher) Explain how light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature interact to determine the rate of photosynthesis in a crop over a summer day.
model: at dawn light intensity is low and is the limiting factor
as light increases the rate increases
around midday light is high so carbon dioxide concentration (about 0.04 per cent) becomes limiting
temperature may also limit; increasing it towards the optimum increases enzyme activity
if temperature becomes too high, enzymes denature and stomata may close, reducing rate
only one factor is limiting at a time and increasing it raises the rate until another factor limits
exam.tip: Structure your answer through the day and name the limiting factor at each stage.

worked.q: A plant produced 6 bubbles per minute at a light intensity of 20 units and 12 bubbles per minute at 40 units. At 60 and 80 units the rate stayed at 12 bubbles per minute. Calculate the percentage increase in rate from 20 to 40 units and identify the limiting factor between 40 and 80 units.
steps: Change = 12 - 6 = 6 bubbles per minute.
Percentage increase = (6 / 6) x 100 = 100 per cent.
Between 40 and 80 units the rate does not change, so light is not limiting.
Another factor, carbon dioxide concentration or temperature, must be limiting.
worked.ans: 100 per cent increase; between 40 and 80 units carbon dioxide concentration or temperature is limiting.

worked.q: (Higher) Curve A: 0.04 per cent CO2 at 20 C plateaus at 10 units. Curve B: 0.1 per cent CO2 at 20 C plateaus at 18 units. Curve C: 0.1 per cent CO2 at 30 C plateaus at 25 units. What limits A and B on their plateaus?
steps: A and B differ only in CO2, and B is higher, so CO2 concentration limits A.
B and C differ only in temperature, and C is higher, so temperature limits B.
C's plateau could be limited by CO2, temperature or something else; the data do not show which.
worked.ans: Carbon dioxide concentration limits curve A; temperature limits curve B.

worked.q: Model answer: Explain why a greenhouse grower stops adding extra carbon dioxide above a certain concentration.
steps: Increasing carbon dioxide increases the rate of photosynthesis while CO2 is the limiting factor.
Beyond a certain concentration the rate levels off because light intensity or temperature becomes limiting.
Adding more CO2 then gives no extra growth or yield.
The extra CO2 costs money, so it would reduce profit.
worked.ans: Above that concentration CO2 is no longer limiting, so more CO2 does not increase yield but does increase cost.

bio_edx.5.10.summary: Plants in extreme environments such as hot deserts and windy sand dunes face high rates of transpiration but very little water. They survive through adaptations of their leaves, stomata and roots that reduce water loss, store water or increase water uptake, such as spines, thick waxy cuticles, sunken stomata, rolled leaves, and shallow widespread or deep tap roots. Each adaptation must be explained using surface area, concentration gradients and evaporation.

core.h: What the spec wants (6.14B, triple only)
core.p: You must **explain how plants are adapted to survive in extreme environments**, focusing on adaptations of **leaves, stomata and roots** that help plants survive where water is scarce, such as hot deserts and windy sand dunes.
bullets: This is **triple (separate) biology only**, Paper 2.
Main extreme environment: **hot, dry deserts** (e.g. **cacti**).
Also: **windy, dry sand dunes** (e.g. **marram grass**), where water drains away quickly.
Key idea: most adaptations **reduce water loss by transpiration** or **increase water uptake and storage**.
Every adaptation must be linked to **why** it helps the plant survive.

callouts.p: A plant adapted to survive in a dry environment where water is scarce.

core.h: Why extreme environments are a problem
core.p: Plants need water for **photosynthesis**, for **support (turgor)** and to transport **mineral ions**. In hot, dry, windy places the conditions that speed up transpiration are all present, but there is little water to replace what is lost.
bullets: **High temperature**: water molecules have more kinetic energy, so faster evaporation and diffusion.
**Strong wind**: water vapour is blown away, keeping a steep concentration gradient.
**Low humidity**: dry air also gives a steep concentration gradient.
**High light intensity**: stomata tend to open, increasing water loss.
**Little rainfall** and soil that drains quickly mean little water to absorb.
If water lost is greater than water taken up, cells lose turgor and the plant **wilts** and may die.

callouts.p: Stomata must open to let carbon dioxide in for photosynthesis, but every time they open, water vapour escapes. Desert plants reduce water loss without stopping photosynthesis completely.

core.p: Water vapour is lost from the leaf surface, so a **smaller surface area** means less water lost by transpiration.
bullets: **Cacti**: leaves are reduced to **spines**, giving a very small surface area for water loss.
Spines also **protect** the plant from animals that would eat it for its stored water.
Spines can trap a layer of still air near the stem, reducing water loss.
Because leaves are tiny, the **green stem** carries out photosynthesis instead.
Some desert plants have small, **needle-like** or narrow leaves for the same reason.
Trade-off: a smaller leaf area also means **less light absorbed**, so slower photosynthesis and growth.

fig.cap: Cactus adaptations: spines instead of leaves, a thick waxy cuticle, a swollen green stem that stores water and photosynthesises, shallow widespread roots and a deep tap root.

core.p: The **waxy cuticle** is waterproof. A **thicker cuticle** reduces the amount of water that evaporates directly through the epidermis.
bullets: Wax is **waterproof**, so water cannot pass through it easily.
Reduces water loss by **evaporation** from the surface.
Also reflects some light, which helps keep the plant cooler.
Found on cacti, marram grass and many plants of dry or cold environments.
Shiny surfaces reflect heat and reduce temperature, lowering evaporation.

core.p: Most water vapour leaves through the stomata, so having **fewer stomata** means fewer routes for water to escape.
bullets: Desert plants have a **reduced number of stomata** per mm2.
Stomata are often found mainly on the side of the leaf away from the sun or wind.
Fewer stomata also means less carbon dioxide uptake, so slower photosynthesis: a trade-off.
Some cacti **open their stomata at night** when it is cooler and more humid, and **close them during the hot day**, reducing water loss.
They store carbon dioxide taken in at night to use in photosynthesis during the day.

callouts.p: If asked why stomata open at night: cooler temperature and higher humidity at night mean less water is lost by evaporation and diffusion.

core.p: **Sunken stomata** sit in pits below the leaf surface. Moist air is **trapped in the pit**, so the concentration of water vapour just outside the stoma stays high.
bullets: Humid air trapped in the pit is not blown away by wind.
This gives a **shallower concentration gradient** of water vapour between the leaf air spaces and the air outside.
So water vapour **diffuses out more slowly**.
Found in marram grass, pine needles and many desert plants.

callouts.p: Sunken stomata still open and close. They reduce water loss because of the trapped humid air, not because they are blocked.

fig.cap: A normal stoma loses water quickly because wind removes water vapour. A sunken stoma sits in a pit that traps humid air, so the gradient is shallower and water loss is slower.

core.h: Leaf adaptations: hairs and rolled leaves
core.p: **Hairs** on the leaf surface and **rolled leaves** both trap a layer of **moist, still air** around the stomata, reducing the concentration gradient.
bullets: **Hairs** reduce air movement next to the leaf surface, so water vapour is not blown away.
**Marram grass** rolls its leaves inwards, with the **stomata on the inside** of the roll.
Humid air is trapped inside the rolled leaf, so diffusion of water vapour slows.
The outer surface of a marram grass leaf has a thick waxy cuticle and few or no stomata.
Rolling also reduces the surface area exposed to wind and sun.

fig.cap: Cross-section of a rolled marram grass leaf. Stomata sit in pits on the inner surface, surrounded by hairs that trap humid air; the outer surface has a thick waxy cuticle.

core.p: Desert plants have roots that make the most of any water available, either by spreading wide near the surface or growing very deep.
bullets: **Shallow, widespread roots** quickly absorb water from brief rain showers before it evaporates or drains away.
**Long, deep tap roots** reach water deep underground (near the water table).
Many desert plants (including some cacti) have **both** types.
Marram grass has very long roots that spread through sand to find water.
A large root system gives a **large surface area** for absorbing water by osmosis.

fig.cap: Shallow widespread roots absorb rainwater quickly near the surface, while a deep tap root reaches groundwater far below.

core.p: Many desert plants store water so they can survive long periods with no rain.
bullets: **Cacti** have a **swollen, fleshy stem** that stores water in its tissues.
Some plants store water in **thick, fleshy leaves** (succulents).
Stored water keeps cells turgid and allows photosynthesis to continue during drought.
A large, rounded stem has a **small surface area to volume ratio**, so less water is lost relative to the amount stored.

callouts.p: A rounded, swollen shape has a smaller surface area compared with its volume, so less surface is available for water loss.

core.p: Very cold places can also be physiologically dry because water in the soil is **frozen** and cannot be absorbed. Plants such as **conifers** show similar adaptations to desert plants.
bullets: **Needle-shaped leaves** give a small surface area for water loss.
**Thick waxy cuticle** reduces evaporation.
**Sunken stomata** trap humid air.
Many arctic plants grow **low to the ground** to avoid strong, cold winds.

core.p: In exams, always pair each **adaptation** with its **explanation**; the explanation is where most marks are.
bullets: Use the words **surface area**, **concentration gradient**, **humid air** and **water loss by transpiration**.

head: Adaptation
How it helps
rows: Smaller surface area, so less water lost by transpiration; protection from animals
Waterproof layer reduces evaporation from the surface
Fewer pores for water vapour to diffuse out
Trap humid air, so shallower concentration gradient and slower diffusion
Trap still, moist air, reducing the concentration gradient
Trap humid air around stomata; less surface exposed
Cooler, more humid air at night so less water lost
Stores water; small surface area to volume ratio
Absorb surface water quickly after rain

core.h: Applying it: the trade-off and unfamiliar plants
core.p: Exam questions often give an **unfamiliar plant** and ask you to suggest how its features help it survive. Use the same principles: reduce water loss, increase uptake, store water.
bullets: Spot any feature that **reduces surface area**, **traps moist air** or **waterproofs** the plant.
Spot any feature that **increases root surface area** or **depth**.
Explain the cost: reducing stomata or leaf area also reduces **carbon dioxide uptake** and **light absorption**, so these plants usually **grow slowly**.
Link back to the factors in 6.12: the adaptations work against the effects of high temperature, wind and low humidity.

callouts.p: Feature, then what it does, then why that reduces water loss or increases water uptake. For example: sunken stomata, trap humid air, shallower concentration gradient so less water vapour diffuses out.

analogy.p: A desert plant is like a hiker crossing a desert with one water bottle. Spines and a waxy cuticle are like wearing a long-sleeved cover so less sweat evaporates; sunken stomata and rolled leaves are like breathing through a scarf, which traps moist air; the swollen stem is the water bottle; shallow roots are like collecting rain in a wide sheet and the tap root is like digging a deep well. Where it breaks down: the hiker can drink whenever they want, but the plant cannot move to find water and must balance water loss against taking in carbon dioxide for photosynthesis through the same stomata.

terms.d: A plant adapted to survive in dry conditions where water is scarce.
A habitat with conditions that make survival difficult, such as very high temperatures, little water or strong winds.
Loss of water vapour from the leaves of a plant, mainly through the stomata.
Pores in the leaf epidermis that allow gas exchange and water vapour loss; opened and closed by guard cells.
Stomata located in pits below the leaf surface, which trap humid air and reduce water loss.
Waterproof waxy layer on the outer surface of the leaf epidermis that reduces evaporation.
Leaves of cacti reduced to sharp points, giving a small surface area and protection from animals.
A long main root that grows deep into the ground to reach water far below the surface.
Roots spread over a large area just below the soil surface to absorb rainwater quickly.
A sand dune grass with rolled leaves, sunken stomata, hairs and long roots.
A desert plant with spines, a swollen water-storing green stem and a thick waxy cuticle.
The difference in concentration between two areas; a shallower gradient gives slower diffusion.
The amount of water vapour in the air.
Surface area divided by volume; a lower value means less surface for water loss relative to size.
Pressure of the cell contents pushing on the cell wall, which keeps plant cells firm and supports the plant.
Drooping of a plant when cells lose water and turgor.

mistakes.w: Cacti have spines so they do not lose water.
mistakes.r: Spines give a smaller surface area, so less water is lost by transpiration (water loss is reduced, not stopped).

mistakes.w: Sunken stomata are closed so no water escapes.
mistakes.r: Sunken stomata trap humid air, giving a shallower concentration gradient so water vapour diffuses out more slowly.

mistakes.w: The waxy cuticle stops sunlight getting in.
mistakes.r: The waxy cuticle is waterproof and reduces evaporation; it is transparent enough for light to pass through.

mistakes.w: Desert plants have no stomata.
mistakes.r: They have fewer stomata; they still need stomata to take in carbon dioxide for photosynthesis.

mistakes.w: Deep roots absorb more rain.
mistakes.r: Deep tap roots reach groundwater deep below; shallow widespread roots absorb rainfall.

mistakes.w: Marram grass rolls its leaves to catch water.
mistakes.r: Rolling traps humid air around the stomata on the inner surface, reducing water loss.

mistakes.w: Cacti photosynthesise in their spines.
mistakes.r: The green stem photosynthesises because the leaves are reduced to spines.

mistakes.w: Hairs absorb water from the air.
mistakes.r: Hairs trap a layer of still, moist air next to the leaf, reducing the concentration gradient.

mistakes.w: Stomata open at night because it is dark.
mistakes.r: Stomata open at night because it is cooler and more humid, so less water is lost.

exam.q: State what is meant by an extreme environment.
model: A habitat with conditions that make survival difficult, e.g. very hot, very dry or very windy.
exam.tip: Give an example condition.

exam.q: Give one way the leaves of a cactus are adapted to reduce water loss.
model: Leaves reduced to spines / small surface area / thick waxy cuticle.
exam.tip: Name a clear feature.

exam.q: Explain how the spines of a cactus help it to survive in a desert.
model: Small surface area so less water lost by transpiration.
Protect the plant from being eaten by animals.
exam.tip: One mark for water loss, one for protection.

exam.q: Explain how a thick waxy cuticle helps a plant survive in a hot, dry environment.
model: Wax is waterproof.
Reduces water loss by evaporation from the leaf surface.
exam.tip: Say what the wax does and the result.

exam.q: Explain how sunken stomata reduce water loss.
model: Humid / moist air is trapped in the pit.
Not blown away by wind.
Shallower concentration gradient so less water vapour diffuses out.
exam.tip: Concentration gradient is the key phrase.

exam.q: Describe two adaptations of roots of desert plants and explain how each helps the plant survive.
model: Shallow, widespread roots.
Absorb water quickly after rainfall before it evaporates / drains.
Long, deep tap roots.
Reach water deep underground.
exam.tip: Two adaptations, each with its explanation.

exam.q: Marram grass grows on sand dunes. Its leaves roll up in dry, windy conditions. Explain how this helps it survive.
model: Stomata are on the inner surface.
Humid air is trapped inside the rolled leaf.
Reduces the concentration gradient so less water is lost by transpiration.
exam.tip: Mention where the stomata are.

exam.q: Some cacti open their stomata at night and close them during the day. Explain the advantage of this.
model: Temperature is lower at night / humidity higher.
So less evaporation / diffusion of water vapour.
Closing during the day reduces water loss when it is hottest; carbon dioxide still taken in at night for photosynthesis.
exam.tip: Link to the factors that affect transpiration rate.

exam.q: Suggest why plants with adaptations to reduce water loss often grow more slowly than plants in wetter habitats.
model: Fewer stomata / stomata closed so less carbon dioxide taken in.
Smaller leaf area so less light absorbed, so less photosynthesis / less glucose for growth.
exam.tip: Think about the inputs of photosynthesis.

exam.q: Explain how cacti are adapted to survive in hot deserts. Refer to leaves, stems, stomata and roots.
model: Leaves reduced to spines: small surface area so less transpiration.
Spines protect from animals.
Thick waxy cuticle: waterproof, reduces evaporation.
Swollen stem stores water; green stem carries out photosynthesis.
Few / sunken stomata, or stomata open at night: reduces water vapour loss.
Shallow widespread roots absorb rainwater quickly; deep tap roots reach groundwater.
exam.tip: Cover each named structure and always explain how it helps.

exam.q: A plant from a cold mountain has small needle-shaped leaves and sunken stomata. Suggest why it needs these adaptations even though it is not hot.
model: Water in the soil is frozen / unavailable for absorption.
Strong winds increase transpiration, so reducing water loss is needed.
exam.tip: Cold places can be physiologically dry.

worked.q: A student counted stomata on the underside of two leaves in a 0.25 mm2 field of view. Leaf A (desert plant): 8 stomata. Leaf B (woodland plant): 50 stomata. Calculate the stomatal density of each and explain the difference.
steps: Density = number / area.
Leaf A: 8 / 0.25 = 32 stomata per mm2.
Leaf B: 50 / 0.25 = 200 stomata per mm2.
Leaf A has fewer stomata per mm2, so fewer pores for water vapour to diffuse out.
This reduces water loss by transpiration, an adaptation to a dry environment where water is scarce.
worked.ans: A = 32 per mm2, B = 200 per mm2; the desert plant has fewer stomata to reduce water loss.

worked.q: Model answer: explain how marram grass is adapted to survive on dry, windy sand dunes.
steps: Leaves roll inwards in dry conditions, with stomata on the inner surface.
Stomata are sunken in pits and surrounded by hairs.
Rolled leaf, pits and hairs trap humid air, so the water vapour concentration gradient is shallower and less water diffuses out.
The outer surface has a thick waxy cuticle which is waterproof and reduces evaporation.
Long, widespread roots absorb water from deep in the sand, where it drains quickly.
worked.ans: Rolled leaves, sunken stomata and hairs trap humid air; waxy cuticle reduces evaporation; long roots find water.

worked.q: Two cube-shaped models of plant stems: Model X has sides of 1 cm, Model Y has sides of 4 cm. Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of each and explain why a large swollen cactus stem helps it survive.
steps: X: surface area = 6 x 1 x 1 = 6 cm2; volume = 1 cm3; ratio = 6 : 1.
Y: surface area = 6 x 4 x 4 = 96 cm2; volume = 64 cm3; ratio = 96 / 64 = 1.5 : 1.
The larger stem has a smaller surface area to volume ratio.
So less surface is available for water loss compared with the volume of water stored.
worked.ans: X = 6 : 1, Y = 1.5 : 1; a large swollen stem stores lots of water but loses relatively little.

bio_edx.5.11.summary: Plants use hormones to control and coordinate their growth, and auxin is the hormone behind tropisms. Auxin is made in shoot and root tips and is redistributed by light (to the shaded side) and gravity (to the lower side). In shoots auxin stimulates cell elongation, but in roots it inhibits it, so shoots show positive phototropism and negative gravitropism while roots show negative phototropism and positive gravitropism.

core.h: What the spec wants (6.15B, triple only)
core.p: You must **explain how plant hormones control and coordinate plant growth and development**, including the **role of auxin in phototropism and gravitropism**.
bullets: Triple (separate) biology only, Paper 2.
Plant hormones are chemicals that **control and coordinate** growth and responses to the environment.
**Auxin** is the main hormone in tropisms.
**Phototropism**: growth in response to **light**.
**Gravitropism** (also called geotropism): growth in response to **gravity**.
You need to explain responses in **both shoots and roots**, because auxin has opposite effects in each.

callouts.p: A directional growth response of a plant to a stimulus, either towards it (positive) or away from it (negative).

core.p: Plants have no nervous system, so they respond to their environment using **hormones**. These chemicals are made in certain parts of the plant and **move to other parts**, where they affect growth.
bullets: Plant hormones are made in growing regions, such as the **tips** of shoots and roots.
They move by **diffusion** (and active transport) through cells, and in the transport tissues.
Responses are **slow** because they involve growth.
Examples: **auxins**, **gibberellins** and **ethene** (uses of these are in 6.16B).
Tropisms help shoots get **light** for photosynthesis and roots get **water and mineral ions** and **anchorage**.

core.h: Auxin: where it is made and what it does
core.p: Auxin is made in the **tips of shoots and roots** and diffuses back to the region just behind the tip, where it controls **cell elongation** (cells getting longer).
bullets: Made in the **shoot tip** and **root tip**.
In **shoots**, auxin **stimulates** cell elongation, so cells with more auxin grow longer.
In **roots**, a high concentration of auxin **inhibits** cell elongation, so cells with more auxin grow less.
Auxin is **redistributed unevenly** in response to light or gravity.
Uneven auxin causes uneven growth on the two sides, so the shoot or root **bends**.

callouts.p: Shoots: more auxin means more elongation. Roots: more auxin means less elongation. This is why shoots and roots respond in opposite directions.

fig.cap: In shoots, cells with high auxin elongate more. In roots, cells with high auxin elongate less, because auxin inhibits root cell elongation.

core.p: When light comes from one side, auxin **moves to the shaded side** of the shoot. Cells on the shaded side **elongate faster** than cells on the lit side, so the shoot **bends towards the light**.
bullets: Light hits the shoot from one side.
Auxin made in the tip moves to the **shaded side**.
Higher auxin concentration on the shaded side.
Cells on the shaded side **elongate more**.
Shoot bends **towards the light**: **positive phototropism**.
Advantage: leaves receive more light for **photosynthesis**.
If light is from directly above, auxin is spread evenly and the shoot grows straight up.

callouts.t: Auxin is not destroyed by light
callouts.p: Mark schemes reward 'auxin moves to (accumulates on) the shaded side'. Do not say the shoot bends because light kills cells or stops growth on the lit side.

fig.cap: Light from one side causes auxin to move to the shaded side of the shoot tip. Shaded cells elongate more, so the shoot bends towards the light (positive phototropism).

core.p: Roots show **negative phototropism**: they grow **away from light**. Auxin builds up on the shaded side, but in roots it **inhibits** elongation, so the lit side grows more.
bullets: Auxin accumulates on the **shaded side** of the root.
High auxin **inhibits** cell elongation in roots.
Cells on the lit side elongate **more** than those on the shaded side.
Root bends **away from the light**.
Advantage: roots grow down into the soil, towards water and minerals and for anchorage.

core.p: If a shoot is placed on its side, gravity causes auxin to collect on the **lower side**. In shoots this **stimulates** elongation, so the lower side grows faster and the shoot **curves upwards**.
bullets: Auxin accumulates on the **lower side** due to gravity.
Cells on the lower side **elongate more**.
Shoot grows **upwards, against gravity**: **negative gravitropism**.
Advantage: the shoot grows up out of the soil towards light, even before it is exposed to light.

core.p: In a root lying on its side, auxin also collects on the **lower side**, but here it **inhibits** elongation. The upper side grows faster, so the root **curves downwards**.
bullets: Auxin accumulates on the **lower side**.
High auxin **inhibits** elongation of root cells.
**Upper side** elongates more.
Root grows **downwards, with gravity**: **positive gravitropism**.
Advantage: roots grow into the soil to absorb **water and mineral ions** and **anchor** the plant.

callouts.p: Always say which side has more auxin (lower or shaded) AND which side elongates more. These are usually separate marks.

fig.cap: A seedling placed on its side. Auxin collects on the lower side of both shoot and root. The shoot's lower side elongates so it grows up; the root's lower side is inhibited so it grows down.

core.p: Learn this table: it combines the stimulus, where auxin goes, its effect, and the direction of growth.
bullets: Positive = towards the stimulus; negative = away from it.
Shoots: positive phototropism, negative gravitropism.
Roots: negative phototropism, positive gravitropism.

core.p: Classic experiments on young shoots (coleoptiles) showed that the **tip detects light** and produces a chemical (auxin) that travels down and causes bending.
bullets: **Intact tip**, light from one side: shoot bends towards light.
**Tip removed**: no bending (and little growth), so the tip is needed.
**Tip covered with an opaque (foil) cap**: no bending, so the **tip detects the light**.
**Base covered, tip exposed**: shoot still bends, so the region below the tip does not detect light.
**Tip placed on an agar block, block placed on the cut shoot**: growth occurs, so a **chemical** diffuses from the tip.
**Agar block placed on one side** of a cut shoot in the dark: shoot bends **away from the block side**, showing the chemical stimulates growth on that side.
**Impermeable barrier (mica)** inserted on the shaded side below the tip: no bending, showing the chemical moves down the shaded side.

fig.cap: Shoot tip experiments with light from the left. A intact shoot bends; B with tip cut off does not bend; C with a foil cap over the tip stays straight; D with only the base covered still bends, so the tip detects light.
