core.p: Tropisms can be investigated with seedlings such as cress or bean seedlings, using controlled conditions.
bullets: **Phototropism**: grow cress seedlings in a box with a slit letting light in from one side; compare with seedlings in the dark or with light from above.
Measure the **angle of bending** or the length of shoots.
**Gravitropism**: place germinating bean seeds on damp cotton wool in a dish pinned at different orientations; observe roots and shoots.
A **clinostat** slowly rotates seedlings so gravity (or light) acts evenly on all sides; the shoot and root then grow straight, acting as a **control**.
Control variables: same type and age of seedling, temperature, water, light intensity.

core.p: Tropisms coordinate the plant's growth so that each part is positioned for its job, improving **survival**.
bullets: Shoots towards light gives more light absorbed by **chlorophyll**, so more **photosynthesis** and more glucose for growth.
Roots downwards gives more **water** for photosynthesis and support, more **mineral ions** (e.g. nitrate for proteins, magnesium for chlorophyll), and **anchorage**.
A seed buried upside down still produces a shoot that grows up and a root that grows down, thanks to gravitropism.
Auxin also promotes growth in the tip region; removing the shoot tip reduces auxin so side shoots grow (used by gardeners).

callouts.p: Stimulus, then unequal distribution of auxin, then unequal cell elongation, then bending.

analogy.p: When a marching band turns a corner, the people on the outside of the curve take longer strides than those on the inside, so the whole line bends. In a shoot, auxin is the instruction to 'take longer strides': the side with more auxin elongates more, so the shoot bends away from that side, towards the light. In roots the instruction is reversed: more auxin means shorter strides. Where it breaks down: band members can change direction instantly, but a plant bends only by slowly growing, and its cells cannot shrink back.

terms.d: A chemical made in one part of a plant that moves to other parts and controls growth and development.
A plant hormone made in shoot and root tips that controls cell elongation; involved in phototropism and gravitropism.
A directional growth response of a plant to a stimulus.
Growth response of a plant to light.
Growth response of a plant to gravity; also called geotropism.
Another name for gravitropism.
Growth towards the stimulus.
Growth away from the stimulus.
Growth towards light, shown by shoots.
Growth away from light, shown by roots.
Growth in the direction of gravity (downwards), shown by roots.
Growth against gravity (upwards), shown by shoots.
Increase in the length of plant cells, which causes growth just behind the tip.
A change in the environment that an organism detects and responds to.
A protective sheath around the young shoot of a grass seedling, used in classic tropism experiments.
A device that slowly rotates a plant so that a stimulus such as gravity acts equally on all sides.

mistakes.w: Light destroys auxin on the lit side so the shoot bends.
mistakes.r: Auxin moves to (accumulates on) the shaded side, where cells elongate more.

mistakes.w: The shoot bends because cells on the light side grow faster.
mistakes.r: Cells on the shaded side elongate faster, so the shoot bends towards the light.

mistakes.w: Auxin makes root cells grow faster.
mistakes.r: In roots, a high concentration of auxin inhibits cell elongation.

mistakes.w: Roots show positive phototropism.
mistakes.r: Roots show negative phototropism and positive gravitropism.

mistakes.w: Auxin causes cells to divide more.
mistakes.r: Auxin causes cell elongation (cells get longer).

mistakes.w: In gravitropism auxin collects on the top side.
mistakes.r: Gravity causes auxin to collect on the lower side of both shoots and roots.

mistakes.w: The plant bends towards light because it wants more light.
mistakes.r: Give the mechanism: unequal auxin distribution causing unequal cell elongation; the advantage is more light for photosynthesis.

mistakes.w: Plant hormones travel in the blood / nerves.
mistakes.r: Plants have no blood or nerves; auxin moves by diffusion through cells.

mistakes.w: Tropism means any movement of a plant.
mistakes.r: A tropism is a directional growth response to a stimulus.

exam.q: Name the plant hormone responsible for phototropism.
model: Auxin.
exam.tip: Spelling: auxin.

exam.q: State what is meant by positive phototropism.
model: Growth (of a plant part) towards light.
exam.tip: Mention growth and direction.

exam.q: State where auxin is produced in a plant.
model: Tips of shoots / roots.
exam.tip: Either tip is accepted.

exam.q: State the type of tropism shown by roots in response to gravity and give one advantage of this.
model: Positive gravitropism.
Roots grow into soil to absorb water / mineral ions / for anchorage.
exam.tip: Give the name and one benefit.

exam.q: Explain how auxin causes a shoot to bend towards light coming from one side.
model: Auxin moves to the shaded side.
Auxin stimulates cell elongation.
Cells on the shaded side elongate more, so shoot bends towards light.
exam.tip: Three clear steps: where auxin goes, what it does, the result.

exam.q: A bean seedling is placed horizontally. Explain why its root grows downwards.
model: Auxin accumulates on the lower side (due to gravity).
Auxin inhibits cell elongation in roots.
Upper side elongates more, so root bends downwards.
exam.tip: Remember auxin inhibits in roots.

exam.q: Explain why roots and shoots respond differently to the same distribution of auxin.
model: In shoots auxin stimulates cell elongation.
In roots (high concentration of) auxin inhibits cell elongation.
exam.tip: Compare the two directly.

exam.q: A student removed the tip of a shoot and shone light on it from one side. The shoot did not bend. Explain this result.
model: The tip produces auxin / detects light.
No auxin produced / redistributed, so no unequal elongation.
exam.tip: Link the tip to auxin.

exam.q: Shoot tips were covered with foil caps and light was shone from one side. Explain why these shoots grew straight.
model: Tip cannot detect light / light cannot reach tip.
Auxin is distributed evenly, so equal elongation on both sides.
exam.tip: The tip is the light-detecting region.

exam.q: Describe how you could investigate the effect of light direction on the growth of cress seedlings.
model: Grow seedlings in three groups: light from one side (box with slit), light from above, darkness.
Keep temperature, water, type and age of seedlings the same.
Leave for a set time, e.g. several days.
Measure angle of bending / direction of growth / shoot length; repeat and compare.
exam.tip: Include independent, dependent and control variables.

exam.q: Explain how auxin controls the growth of shoots and roots in a seedling to help it survive. Refer to both light and gravity.
model: Auxin made in tips and moves to region of elongation.
Light from one side: auxin moves to shaded side; in shoot it stimulates elongation so shoot bends towards light (positive phototropism).
More light for photosynthesis.
In root, auxin inhibits elongation so root bends away from light (negative phototropism).
Gravity: auxin collects on lower side; shoot lower side elongates so shoot grows up (negative gravitropism).
Root lower side inhibited so root grows down (positive gravitropism) for water, minerals and anchorage.
exam.tip: Cover all four responses with mechanisms and advantages.

worked.q: Predict and explain the result: a shoot tip is cut off, placed on an agar block for an hour, then the agar block is placed on the left side of the cut stump, in the dark.
steps: Auxin diffuses from the tip into the agar block.
Auxin then diffuses from the block into the left side of the stump.
Left side has more auxin, so cells there elongate more.
There is no light, so the response is only due to the block's position.
worked.ans: The shoot bends to the right (away from the side with the block), because the left side elongates more.

worked.q: Cress seedlings were lit from one side. Mean shoot angle from vertical: 0 hours 0 degrees, 6 hours 18 degrees, 12 hours 42 degrees. Calculate the mean rate of bending between 6 and 12 hours.
steps: Change in angle = 42 - 18 = 24 degrees.
Time = 12 - 6 = 6 hours.
Rate = 24 / 6 = 4 degrees per hour.
Explanation: auxin moving to the shaded side causes faster elongation there, so the angle increases over time.
worked.ans: 4 degrees per hour

worked.q: Model answer: a seed germinates upside down in the soil. Explain how the shoot ends up growing upwards and the root downwards.
steps: Gravity causes auxin to accumulate on the lower side of the shoot and root.
In the shoot, auxin stimulates elongation, so the lower side grows faster and the shoot curves upward (negative gravitropism).
In the root, auxin inhibits elongation, so the upper side grows faster and the root curves downward (positive gravitropism).
The shoot reaches light for photosynthesis; the root reaches water and mineral ions and anchors the plant.
worked.ans: Unequal auxin on the lower sides causes opposite responses, so the shoot turns up and the root turns down.

bio_edx.5.2.summary: In this **core practical** you investigate how **light intensity** affects the **rate of photosynthesis** by moving a lamp to different distances from a photosynthesising organism. The Edexcel method uses **algal balls** in **hydrogencarbonate indicator** and times how long the indicator takes to change colour as carbon dioxide is used up; pondweed counting oxygen bubbles is a common alternative. Closer lamp means higher light intensity and a faster rate, until another factor becomes limiting. You must be able to plan the method, control variables, process the data (rate = 1/time) and evaluate the results.

core.p: The aim is to find out how **light intensity** affects the **rate of photosynthesis**. Light is the energy source for photosynthesis, so we predict that as light intensity increases (lamp moved closer), the rate increases, until another factor limits it.
bullets: **Independent variable**: light intensity, changed by changing the **distance** between lamp and organism.
**Dependent variable**: rate of photosynthesis, measured as time for indicator colour change (algal balls) or bubbles / volume of oxygen per minute (pondweed).
**Control variables**: temperature, carbon dioxide concentration, number of algal balls / same piece of pondweed, volume of indicator, type and power of lamp.
Hypothesis: the closer the lamp, the faster the rate of photosynthesis.

callouts.p: Light intensity is varied by moving the lamp. Shorter distance = higher light intensity.

core.p: You need a light source, a way to measure distance, the photosynthesising organism and a way to detect the rate.
bullets: Bench lamp (ideally an LED, which gives out less heat).
Metre rule to measure distance from lamp to organism.
Algal balls (algae immobilised in sodium alginate) in bijou bottles or tubes.
Hydrogencarbonate indicator solution.
Glass tank or beaker of water as a **heat shield**.
Stopwatch; colour chart or colorimeter to judge the end point.
Alternative: pondweed (e.g. Elodea or Cabomba), boiling tube, sodium hydrogencarbonate solution.

core.p: Hydrogencarbonate indicator changes colour depending on the **carbon dioxide concentration** of the solution. As algae photosynthesise they remove carbon dioxide, so the indicator changes colour from orange-red towards **purple**.
bullets: **Yellow**: high carbon dioxide concentration (more respiration than photosynthesis).
**Red / orange**: carbon dioxide at atmospheric level (starting colour).
**Purple**: low carbon dioxide concentration (photosynthesis faster than respiration).
The faster the colour reaches purple, the faster the rate of photosynthesis.

fig.cap: Hydrogencarbonate indicator colours. Photosynthesis removes carbon dioxide so the indicator turns purple; respiration adds carbon dioxide so it turns yellow.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="a" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0 L10 5 L0 10 z" fill="#1b2540"/></marker></defs><rect x="0" y="0" width="400" height="240" fill="#f8fafc"/><text x="200" y="20" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">Hydrogencarbonate indicator colours</text><rect x="30" y="50" width="100" height="70" rx="8" fill="#fde68a" stroke="#b45309"/><text x="80" y="90" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">Yellow</text><rect x="150" y="50" width="100" height="70" rx="8" fill="#fca5a5" stroke="#b91c1c"/><text x="200" y="85" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">Red / orange</text><rect x="270" y="50" width="100" height="70" rx="8" fill="#e9d5ff" stroke="#6b21a8"/><text x="320" y="90" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">Purple</text><text x="80" y="140" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">High CO2</text><text x="200" y="140" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">Atmospheric CO2</text><text x="320" y="140" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">Low CO2</text><line x1="40" y1="170" x2="360" y2="170" stroke="#166534" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#a)"/><text x="200" y="190" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#166534">Photosynthesis removes CO2</text><line x1="360" y1="210" x2="40" y2="210" stroke="#be123c" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#a)"/><text x="200" y="230" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#be123c">Respiration adds CO2</text></svg>

core.p: This is the method in the Edexcel core practical. Follow it step by step and keep everything except distance the same.
bullets: Put the same number of algal balls (e.g. 10) into each bottle with the **same volume** of hydrogencarbonate indicator.
Note the starting colour, which should be orange-red.
Place a bottle at a measured distance (e.g. 10 cm) from the lamp, with a water heat shield in between.
Switch on the lamp and start the stopwatch.
Record the time for the indicator to reach a set colour (e.g. purple, matched against a colour chart).
Repeat at other distances, e.g. 20, 30, 40 and 50 cm.
Set up a control bottle covered in foil (no light) to show any change is due to light.
Repeat each distance at least three times and calculate a mean.

fig.cap: Set-up for the algal ball practical. The lamp is placed a measured distance from the bottle, with a beaker of water acting as a heat shield. The time for the indicator to change colour is recorded at each distance.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="a" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0 L10 5 L0 10 z" fill="#1b2540"/></marker></defs><rect x="0" y="0" width="400" height="240" fill="#f8fafc"/><text x="200" y="20" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">Algal balls core practical</text><rect x="20" y="70" width="50" height="40" fill="#e5e7eb" stroke="#1b2540"/><polygon points="70,75 95,60 95,120 70,105" fill="#fde68a" stroke="#b45309"/><text x="20" y="60" font-size="11" fill="#1b2540">Lamp</text><rect x="135" y="55" width="22" height="70" fill="#dbeafe" stroke="#1d4ed8"/><text x="122" y="145" font-size="11" fill="#1d4ed8">Water</text><text x="122" y="159" font-size="11" fill="#1d4ed8">heat shield</text><rect x="230" y="40" width="40" height="100" rx="6" fill="#fecaca" stroke="#991b1b"/><circle cx="242" cy="125" r="6" fill="#4ade80" stroke="#166534"/><circle cx="257" cy="125" r="6" fill="#4ade80" stroke="#166534"/><circle cx="250" cy="113" r="6" fill="#4ade80" stroke="#166534"/><text x="280" y="70" font-size="11" fill="#991b1b">Hydrogencarbonate</text><text x="280" y="84" font-size="11" fill="#991b1b">indicator</text><text x="280" y="120" font-size="11" fill="#166534">Algal balls</text><line x1="278" y1="117" x2="264" y2="120" stroke="#166534"/><line x1="95" y1="175" x2="230" y2="175" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="1.5" marker-end="url(#a)"/><line x1="230" y1="175" x2="95" y2="175" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="1.5" marker-end="url(#a)"/><text x="172" y="195" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">Distance d (metre rule)</text><text x="20" y="225" font-size="11" fill="#1b2540">Time colour change at each distance</text></svg>

core.p: Pondweed releases **oxygen** bubbles when it photosynthesises. Counting bubbles, or measuring gas volume, gives the rate directly.
bullets: Place a piece of pondweed in a boiling tube of water containing **sodium hydrogencarbonate** to supply plenty of carbon dioxide.
Leave it for a few minutes at each distance to acclimatise.
Count the bubbles produced in one minute, or collect gas in a gas syringe or measuring cylinder for a better measure of volume.
Repeat at each distance and calculate the mean.
Measuring volume is more accurate than counting bubbles because bubbles can be different sizes.

fig.cap: Pondweed method. Oxygen bubbles released from the cut stem are counted or collected; sodium hydrogencarbonate in the water keeps carbon dioxide from becoming limiting.

core.p: For a valid test, light intensity must be the **only** factor changed. The other limiting factors, temperature and carbon dioxide concentration, must be controlled.
bullets: **Temperature**: a lamp gives out heat, so use a water heat shield, an LED bulb, or a water bath; check with a thermometer.
**Carbon dioxide**: use the same volume and concentration of indicator or sodium hydrogencarbonate in every test.
**Background light**: carry out in a darkened room so the lamp is the only light source.
**Organism**: same number and size of algal balls, or same piece of pondweed.
**Lamp**: same bulb and power throughout.

head: Variable
Type
How it is controlled or changed
rows: Change lamp distance, measured with metre rule
Time to colour change, or bubbles per minute
Water heat shield or LED; check with thermometer
Same volume of indicator or NaHCO3 solution
Count the same number into each bottle

core.p: With the algal ball method you measure time, but you need a **rate**. Rate is inversely related to time: a shorter time means a faster rate.
bullets: Rate = 1 / time (units: per second, s^-1, or per minute).
For pondweed: rate = number of bubbles / time, e.g. bubbles per minute.
Calculate a mean for each distance, ignoring anomalous results.
Plot rate (y-axis) against distance or light intensity (x-axis) and draw a smooth curve of best fit.

callouts.p: If the indicator took 250 s to turn purple, rate = 1 / 250 = 0.004 s^-1. Shorter time = larger rate.

core.p: As the lamp moves closer, light intensity increases, so more light energy is available for photosynthesis and the rate increases. The indicator turns purple faster, or more bubbles are produced.
bullets: Rate decreases as distance increases.
The decrease is not linear because light intensity falls rapidly with distance (the inverse square law, covered in 6.6).
At very close distances the rate may level off because carbon dioxide concentration or temperature becomes limiting.
The foil-covered control should not turn purple; it may turn yellow because the algae respire without photosynthesising.

fig.cap: Typical results: rate of photosynthesis is highest when the lamp is closest and falls as distance increases, because light intensity decreases with distance.

core.p: Evaluating the method is a common exam question. Identify the error, explain its effect, and give a specific improvement.
bullets: **Judging colour change** is subjective: use a colour chart or a **colorimeter** to measure the colour objectively.
**Heat from the lamp** changes temperature: use an LED or water heat shield and monitor with a thermometer.
**Counting bubbles** is inaccurate because bubbles vary in size: collect gas in a gas syringe and measure volume.
**Background light** from windows: use a darkened room.
Algal balls of different sizes contain different amounts of algae: make them using a syringe of fixed size.
Repeat readings and calculate a mean to improve **repeatability**.

core.p: The practical is low risk, but some hazards need control.
bullets: Lamps get hot: do not touch the bulb, allow to cool before moving.
Water and electricity: keep water away from the lamp and plug.
Hydrogencarbonate indicator is low hazard but avoid contact with eyes; wash hands.
Take care in a darkened room to avoid trips.

callouts.t: Do not say the lamp adds energy as heat to the reaction
callouts.p: Heat from the lamp is an uncontrolled variable that can change enzyme activity; it is not the energy source for photosynthesis. Light is.

core.p: This practical shows light intensity acting as a **limiting factor**. Understanding the results requires the ideas from 6.3 and 6.4.
bullets: At large distances, light intensity is low and is the limiting factor, so moving the lamp closer increases the rate.
At small distances, the rate may stop increasing because carbon dioxide or temperature has become limiting.
Adding more sodium hydrogencarbonate would raise the plateau, showing carbon dioxide was limiting.
Respiration happens all the time; the indicator only turns purple when photosynthesis is faster than respiration.

analogy.p: Think of the algae as a phone charging from a small solar panel. Hold the panel right next to a lamp and the battery fills quickly; move it across the room and charging slows dramatically. Timing how long the battery takes to reach full is like timing how long the indicator takes to turn purple: the shorter the time, the faster the rate, which is why rate = 1 / time. Where it breaks down: the phone does not get slower if the room is cold or speed up with more carbon dioxide, but algae do, and the algae are also respiring and adding carbon dioxide back the whole time.

terms.d: A practical named in the Edexcel specification that can be examined in written papers.
The amount of light energy reaching a given area per second; increases as the lamp moves closer.
How fast photosynthesis takes place, measured as 1/time for colour change or oxygen produced per minute.
Small beads of algae immobilised in sodium alginate, used so the same amount of algae is in each test.
Indicator that changes colour with carbon dioxide concentration: yellow high, red atmospheric, purple low.
Compound added to water to supply carbon dioxide so it does not become limiting.
Beaker or tank of water placed between lamp and organism to absorb heat and keep temperature constant.
The variable that is changed, here light intensity (lamp distance).
The variable that is measured, here rate of photosynthesis.
A variable kept the same to make the test valid, such as temperature and carbon dioxide concentration.
An investigation that measures what it is supposed to, with only the independent variable affecting the result.
Results that are similar when the same person repeats the investigation with the same method.
A result that does not fit the pattern of the other results and is left out of the mean.
Instrument that measures colour or light absorbance of a solution objectively.
Light intensity is proportional to 1/distance squared (covered in spec point 6.6).

mistakes.w: The dependent variable is the distance of the lamp.
mistakes.r: Distance (light intensity) is the independent variable; rate of photosynthesis is the dependent variable.

mistakes.w: The indicator turns purple because oxygen is produced.
mistakes.r: It turns purple because carbon dioxide is removed by photosynthesis.

mistakes.w: Rate = time taken.
mistakes.r: Rate = 1 / time; a shorter time means a faster rate.

mistakes.w: Use a heat shield to make it warmer.
mistakes.r: A water heat shield absorbs heat from the lamp to keep the temperature constant.

mistakes.w: The bubbles are carbon dioxide.
mistakes.r: The bubbles are mainly oxygen produced by photosynthesis.

mistakes.w: Make it fair by doing it again.
mistakes.r: Repeating improves repeatability; controlling variables makes it a fair (valid) test.

mistakes.w: Counting bubbles is accurate.
mistakes.r: Bubbles vary in size; collecting gas in a gas syringe and measuring volume is more accurate.

mistakes.w: The foil-covered tube stays the same because nothing happens.
mistakes.r: The algae still respire, so carbon dioxide rises and the indicator may turn yellow.

exam.q: State the independent variable in this investigation.
model: light intensity / distance of lamp from algae
exam.tip: Distance is how light intensity is changed.

exam.q: Give two variables that should be controlled.
model: temperature
carbon dioxide concentration / number of algal balls / volume of indicator
exam.tip: Temperature and CO2 are the best answers because they are limiting factors.

exam.q: Explain why a beaker of water is placed between the lamp and the algal balls.
model: absorbs heat from the lamp
so temperature stays constant / temperature does not affect the rate
exam.tip: Link to controlling a limiting factor.

exam.q: Explain why the hydrogencarbonate indicator changes from red to purple.
model: algae photosynthesise and take in / remove carbon dioxide
lower carbon dioxide concentration turns indicator purple
exam.tip: It is CO2, not oxygen, that the indicator detects.

exam.q: The indicator took 400 s to turn purple. Calculate the rate of photosynthesis.
model: rate = 1 / 400
exam.tip: Always include units.

exam.q: Suggest why a tube of algal balls covered in foil was included.
model: as a control / to show light is needed for the colour change
no photosynthesis, only respiration, so indicator does not turn purple (may turn yellow)
exam.tip: Say what it shows, not just that it is a control.

exam.q: Describe how a student could improve the accuracy of judging the end point.
model: use a colour chart / standard colour to compare
or use a colorimeter to measure colour objectively
exam.tip: Name the specific piece of equipment.

exam.q: Explain why the rate of photosynthesis did not increase when the lamp was moved from 10 cm to 5 cm.
model: light was no longer the limiting factor
carbon dioxide concentration or temperature was limiting
exam.tip: Always name the other factor.

exam.q: Suggest one disadvantage of counting bubbles from pondweed and how to overcome it.
model: bubbles are different sizes / too fast to count
collect the gas in a gas syringe / measuring cylinder and measure volume
exam.tip: Give the problem and a matched improvement.

exam.q: Describe a method to investigate the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis using algal balls.
model: put equal numbers of algal balls in bottles with equal volume of hydrogencarbonate indicator
place lamp a measured distance away with metre rule
use water heat shield / keep temperature constant
time how long the indicator takes to change from red to purple
repeat at a range of distances, e.g. 10 to 50 cm
repeat each distance and calculate mean; calculate rate = 1/time
exam.tip: Cover equipment, IV, DV, controls, repeats and processing.

worked.q: Mean times for the indicator to turn purple were: 10 cm = 125 s, 20 cm = 250 s, 40 cm = 800 s. Calculate the rate at each distance.
steps: Rate = 1 / time.
worked.ans: 0.008 s^-1, 0.004 s^-1 and 0.00125 s^-1; rate falls as distance increases.

worked.q: A student counted bubbles from pondweed in three 1-minute repeats at 15 cm: 24, 26 and 41. Calculate the mean and explain your choice.
steps: 41 is much higher than the others, so it is anomalous.
Leave it out of the mean.
Mean = (24 + 26) / 2 = 25 bubbles per minute.
worked.ans: 25 bubbles per minute, excluding the anomalous 41.

worked.q: Model answer: Evaluate the algal ball method and suggest two improvements.
steps: Strength: algal balls give the same amount of algae in each tube, so the comparison is fair.
Weakness: deciding when the indicator is purple is subjective; use a colorimeter or colour chart.
Weakness: the lamp may heat the bottle; use an LED and a water heat shield and check temperature with a thermometer.
Repeat each distance three times and calculate a mean to check repeatability.
worked.ans: The method is valid if temperature and carbon dioxide are controlled; improve it with a colorimeter for the end point and an LED plus heat shield to control temperature.

bio_edx.5.3.summary: Light spreads out as it travels away from a lamp, so the same amount of light energy is shared over a bigger and bigger area. The **inverse square law** says light intensity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the source: light intensity is proportional to 1/d squared. Doubling the distance cuts the intensity to one quarter, and because light intensity is a limiting factor this changes the rate of photosynthesis, which is why it matters in the pondweed core practical (Higher tier).

core.p: Edexcel 1BI0 point 6.6H (Higher tier) asks you to **understand the relationship between light intensity and distance from a light source**, described by the inverse square law, and to use it to explain results from photosynthesis experiments where a lamp is moved closer to or further from a plant.
bullets: This is **Higher tier only** content in Topic 6.
You must be able to **state** the law, **use** it in calculations and **explain** why it happens.
It links directly to 6.3 (light as a limiting factor) and 6.5 (the light intensity core practical).
Typical exam skills: calculating relative light intensity, comparing intensities at two distances, explaining the shape of a rate against distance graph.

callouts.p: Questions on the inverse square law only appear on the Higher paper, often as 2 or 3 mark calculations.

core.p: **Light intensity** is the amount of light energy arriving on a given area per second. A plant leaf only absorbs the light that actually lands on it, so what matters for photosynthesis is how concentrated the light is where the plant is, not how bright the bulb is overall.
bullets: Light intensity is measured with a **light meter**, in **lux**.
In school experiments we often do not measure intensity directly; we change the **distance** between the lamp and the plant instead.
A more intense light delivers **more energy per second** to the chloroplasts.
More energy for the light-dependent part of photosynthesis means a faster rate, as long as light is the **limiting factor**.

callouts.p: The amount of light energy reaching a unit area per unit time.

core.p: The inverse square law states that **light intensity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance** from the light source. 'Inverse' means as one goes up the other goes down; 'square' means the effect is distance multiplied by itself, so the fall in intensity is much faster than the increase in distance.
bullets: Written as: **light intensity is proportional to 1 / d squared**, where d is the distance from the light source.
To find **relative light intensity**: relative intensity = 1 / d squared.
Double the distance (x2): intensity becomes 1/4 (divide by 2 squared = 4).
Triple the distance (x3): intensity becomes 1/9.
Halve the distance: intensity becomes **4 times** greater.
Increase distance x10: intensity becomes 1/100.

callouts.p: Light intensity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the light source.

core.h: Why the law works: light spreads out
core.p: A lamp gives out light in all directions. At a distance d the light passes through a certain area. At distance 2d the same light has spread out so it covers an area **twice as wide and twice as tall**, which is **4 times** the area. The same energy is shared over 4 times the area, so each square receives only a quarter of it.
bullets: Total light leaving the lamp per second stays the same.
The area the light is spread over increases with the **square** of the distance (area depends on length x width).
So energy per unit area (intensity) decreases with the square of distance.
Think of a sphere around the lamp: its surface area is proportional to the radius squared.

callouts.p: For full marks say the light energy is spread over a larger area, so less light energy reaches each unit area of the leaf.

fig.cap: Light from a lamp spreads out. At twice the distance (2d) the same light covers 4 squares instead of 1, so the intensity on each square is only one quarter (I/4).

core.h: The shape of the intensity against distance graph
core.p: If you plot relative light intensity against distance, you do not get a straight line. You get a **curve that falls steeply at first and then levels off**, getting closer and closer to zero but never quite reaching it.
bullets: Close to the lamp, a small move gives a **big change** in intensity.
Far from the lamp, moving further makes **little difference** because intensity is already low.
This is why moving a lamp from 5 cm to 10 cm matters much more than moving it from 50 cm to 55 cm.
If you instead plot intensity against **1/d squared** you get a **straight line through the origin**, which shows direct proportion.

callouts.p: Doubling the distance does not halve the light intensity; it quarters it.

core.p: Most exam questions ask you to work out how many times greater or smaller the intensity is when the distance changes. You do not need real units; you compare two values of 1/d squared.
bullets: Step 1: square each distance.
Step 2: work out 1 / d squared for each (or just compare the squares).
Step 3: divide one by the other to get the factor of change.
Shortcut: **factor change in intensity = (old distance / new distance) squared**.
If you have a measured intensity (e.g. in lux) at one distance, multiply it by this factor to predict the intensity at the new distance.
Keep distances in the **same units** (both cm or both m) before squaring.

callouts.p: Relative intensities such as 1/400 = 0.0025 may be asked for in standard form: 2.5 x 10 to the power -3.

core.h: Link to the rate of photosynthesis
core.p: When **light is the limiting factor**, the rate of photosynthesis is directly proportional to light intensity. Because light intensity is proportional to 1/d squared, the **rate of photosynthesis is also proportional to 1/d squared** over this range.
bullets: Move the lamp closer: higher light intensity, more energy absorbed by **chlorophyll**, faster photosynthesis, more **oxygen bubbles** per minute.
Move the lamp further: intensity falls by the square of distance, so rate falls sharply.
Plotting rate against 1/d squared gives a straight line while light is limiting.
At high light intensity the line **levels off (plateau)** because another factor, such as **carbon dioxide concentration** or **temperature**, becomes limiting.
Photosynthesis is endothermic: it needs energy transferred from the environment as light.

callouts.p: Greater distance, lower light intensity (by 1/d squared), less light energy absorbed, slower rate of photosynthesis, fewer bubbles of oxygen.

core.h: Using the law in the core practical
core.p: In the pondweed (e.g. Elodea or Cabomba) core practical, the lamp is placed at different distances and the number of oxygen bubbles, or volume of gas, produced per minute is recorded. The inverse square law lets you convert each distance into a **relative light intensity** so you can see the true relationship between light and rate.
bullets: Independent variable: **distance** from lamp (which controls light intensity).
Dependent variable: rate of oxygen production (bubbles per minute or gas volume per minute).
Control variables: **temperature**, **carbon dioxide** concentration (add sodium hydrogencarbonate), same piece and species of pondweed, same lamp.
Use a **heat shield** (beaker or tank of water) or an **LED** so the lamp does not heat the water and change temperature.
Allow the plant to **acclimatise** for a few minutes at each new distance before counting.
Do the experiment in a darkened room so the lamp is the only light source.

callouts.p: A filament lamp moved closer also warms the water; without a heat shield, a faster rate could be caused by temperature, not light.

core.p: Because intensity depends on distance squared, a small error in measuring distance becomes a bigger error in calculated intensity. Accurate measurement is therefore important.
bullets: Measure from the **centre of the bulb (filament)** to the **centre of the plant**, using a metre rule.
Use the same reference points every time.
A 1 cm error at 5 cm is a 20 percent error in distance and about a 44 percent error in intensity.
Repeat readings at each distance and calculate a **mean** to improve reliability.

callouts.p: If asked to improve the method, mention using a light meter to measure light intensity directly in lux at the plant.

core.p: The inverse square law works perfectly for a tiny **point source** of light spreading equally in all directions. Real lamps are not perfect point sources, so the law is an approximation.
bullets: Very close to a large lamp the law fits less well because the bulb has a size.
Reflectors, lamp shades or glass can focus or scatter light.
Background light from windows or other lamps adds extra light that does not follow the law from your lamp.
Water and glass absorb and reflect some light before it reaches the plant.
This is why results may not fit the predicted 1/d squared pattern exactly.

core.p: Growers use the same idea when positioning artificial lights. Light energy that does not reach the leaves is wasted money, so lamps are placed at a distance that gives high intensity without overheating or scorching plants.
bullets: Moving lamps closer greatly increases intensity and so the rate of photosynthesis, giving faster growth and higher **yield**.
Beyond a certain intensity, extra light gives **no further increase** because CO2 or temperature limits the rate, so extra lighting costs more than it earns.
Farmers balance the cost of electricity against the value of extra crop.
LEDs are used because they give light with little heat.

callouts.p: Once light is no longer the limiting factor, increasing light intensity further will not increase the rate of photosynthesis and wastes energy.

core.h: Interpreting data and graphs in exams
core.p: You may be given a table of distance and bubble counts and asked to describe, explain or calculate. Use precise language and quote data.
bullets: Describe: 'As distance increases, the number of bubbles per minute decreases.'
Explain using the law: 'Light intensity is inversely proportional to distance squared, so less light energy reaches the plant.'
Use numbers: 'Moving from 10 cm to 20 cm reduced the rate from 40 to about 10 bubbles per minute, a quarter, as predicted.'
If the rate does not change at the closest distances, say another factor is **limiting**.
Anomalous results should be identified and left out of the mean.

callouts.p: Just saying 'further away means less light' is usually worth only 1 mark; the square relationship earns the higher mark.

analogy.p: Imagine a fixed lump of butter (the light energy from the lamp each second). Spread it on one slice and it is thick; spread it over a slice twice as long and twice as wide (4 times the area) and every bit is only a quarter as thick. The thickness is like light intensity: same total butter, bigger area, thinner layer. Where it breaks down: butter can run out or be spread unevenly, while light keeps spreading forever in all directions and in three dimensions, and real light can also be absorbed or reflected on the way.

terms.d: The amount of light energy reaching a unit area per unit time.
Light intensity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the light source.
As one quantity increases, the other decreases by the same factor (e.g. one doubles, the other halves).
A value without units used to compare light intensities, calculated as 1 / distance squared.
A light source so small that its light spreads out equally in all directions from a single point.
The unit of light intensity measured by a light meter.
An instrument that measures light intensity, usually in lux.
The factor in shortest supply that stops the rate of a process, such as photosynthesis, increasing.
How fast glucose and oxygen are produced, often measured as volume of oxygen or bubbles per minute.
The green pigment in chloroplasts that absorbs light energy for photosynthesis.
A clear container of water placed between lamp and plant to absorb heat so temperature stays constant.
The variable that is changed in an investigation; here, distance from the lamp.
The variable that is measured; here, the rate of oxygen production.
A variable kept the same so it does not affect the results, e.g. temperature or CO2 concentration.
A reaction that takes in energy from the surroundings; photosynthesis takes in light energy.

mistakes.w: Doubling the distance halves the light intensity.
mistakes.r: Doubling the distance reduces light intensity to one quarter, because intensity is proportional to 1/d squared.

mistakes.w: Light intensity is inversely proportional to distance.
mistakes.r: Light intensity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance.

mistakes.w: Relative intensity at 20 cm is 1/20.
mistakes.r: Relative intensity is 1/20 squared = 1/400 = 0.0025.

mistakes.w: Moving the lamp closer gives more light so the plant gets hotter, which is the same thing.
mistakes.r: Light intensity and temperature are separate factors; a heat shield or LED keeps temperature constant so only light intensity changes.

mistakes.w: The further away, the less light because the light gets weaker or runs out.
mistakes.r: The same light energy is spread over a larger area, so less light energy reaches each unit area of the leaf.

mistakes.w: Moving the lamp closer will always increase the rate of photosynthesis.
mistakes.r: Only while light is the limiting factor; at high intensity CO2 concentration or temperature becomes limiting and the rate levels off.

mistakes.w: Measured distance from the edge of the lamp shade to the beaker.
mistakes.r: Measure from the light source (bulb) to the plant itself, the same way every time.

mistakes.w: Light intensity is measured in watts or with a thermometer.
mistakes.r: Light intensity is measured with a light meter in lux.

exam.q: State the inverse square law for light intensity.
model: Light intensity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the light source (intensity proportional to 1/d squared).
exam.tip: Must include 'square' for the mark.

exam.q: A lamp is moved from 10 cm to 20 cm from a plant. By what factor does the light intensity change?
model: Distance doubled so intensity changes by 1/2 squared.
Intensity decreases to one quarter (divided by 4).
exam.tip: Show the squaring step to secure the method mark.

exam.q: Calculate the relative light intensity at a distance of 25 cm. Give your answer in standard form.
model: = 0.0016 = 1.6 x 10 to the power -3.
exam.tip: Square first, then take the reciprocal.

exam.q: Explain why light intensity decreases as distance from a lamp increases.
model: Light spreads out from the source.
The same light energy is spread over a larger area so less energy reaches each unit area.
exam.tip: Refer to area for the second mark.

exam.q: The light intensity 10 cm from a lamp is 1200 lux. Calculate the light intensity at 30 cm.
model: Distance tripled so intensity divided by 3 squared = 9.
exam.tip: Use the factor (old/new) squared.

exam.q: Suggest why a student placed a beaker of water between the lamp and the pondweed.
model: To absorb heat from the lamp / act as a heat shield.
So that temperature stays constant and only light intensity affects the rate.
exam.tip: Link it to temperature as a control variable.

exam.q: Explain why the rate of photosynthesis decreases as the lamp is moved further away from the pondweed.
model: Light intensity decreases.
Inversely proportional to distance squared / doubling distance gives 1/4 intensity.
Less light energy absorbed by chlorophyll.
Light is the limiting factor so less photosynthesis / fewer oxygen bubbles produced.
exam.tip: Build a chain: distance, intensity, energy absorbed, rate.

exam.q: A student found that moving the lamp from 5 cm to 10 cm did not change the rate of photosynthesis, but moving it from 10 cm to 20 cm did. Explain these results.
model: Between 5 cm and 10 cm light is not the limiting factor.
Another factor such as CO2 concentration or temperature is limiting.
Beyond 10 cm intensity is low enough that light becomes the limiting factor, so rate falls.
exam.tip: Name the other limiting factor.

exam.q: Describe the shape of a graph of relative light intensity against distance from a lamp.
model: Intensity decreases steeply at short distances then more gradually.
Curve levels off approaching zero / is not a straight line.
exam.tip: Avoid 'decreases' alone: say how.

exam.q: Devise a method to investigate how distance from a light source affects the rate of photosynthesis in pondweed, and explain how you would use the inverse square law to analyse your results.
model: Place pondweed in a boiling tube of water with sodium hydrogencarbonate in a darkened room.
Place lamp at a set distance measured with a metre rule, e.g. 10 cm.
Leave to acclimatise, then count oxygen bubbles (or collect gas in a syringe or measuring cylinder) for a set time, e.g. 1 minute.
Repeat at other distances, e.g. 20, 30, 40 cm, with repeats and calculate means.
Control temperature with a heat shield or LED, same pondweed, same CO2.
Convert each distance to relative light intensity using 1/d squared and plot rate against 1/d squared; a straight line shows rate proportional to light intensity while light is limiting.
exam.tip: Six-mark answers need a logical sequence plus controls and analysis.

worked.q: A lamp is placed 15 cm from a plant and then moved to 5 cm. How many times greater is the light intensity at 5 cm?
steps: Relative intensity at 15 cm = 1 / 15 squared = 1/225.
Relative intensity at 5 cm = 1 / 5 squared = 1/25.
Check with shortcut: distance divided by 3, so intensity x 3 squared = x 9.
worked.ans: The light intensity is 9 times greater at 5 cm.

worked.q: A light meter reads 800 lux at 10 cm from a lamp. Predict the reading at 40 cm and at 20 cm.
steps: 40 cm is 4 times the distance, so intensity is divided by 4 squared = 16.
20 cm is 2 times the distance, so intensity is divided by 2 squared = 4.
worked.ans: About 50 lux at 40 cm and 200 lux at 20 cm (assuming a point source and no background light).

worked.q: Pondweed produced 48 bubbles per minute at 10 cm. Assuming light is the only limiting factor, predict the bubbles per minute at 20 cm, and explain why the real result was 14 bubbles per minute.
steps: Doubling distance reduces light intensity to 1/4.
If rate is proportional to light intensity, predicted rate = 48 / 4 = 12 bubbles per minute.
Real result is 14, slightly higher than predicted.
Possible reasons: background light in the room adds intensity, the lamp is not a perfect point source, or bubbles vary in size so counting is imprecise.
worked.ans: Predicted 12 bubbles per minute; the difference is due to experimental limitations such as background light and bubble size.

bio_edx.5.4.summary: Plants take in almost all their water and mineral ions through **root hair cells**, specialised cells on the surface of young roots. Each one has a long thin projection that gives a huge **surface area**, a thin wall and membrane for a short path, a concentrated vacuole so water enters by **osmosis**, and many **mitochondria** to release energy for the **active transport** of mineral ions against their concentration gradient. Understanding each adaptation and the process it helps is what the 6.7 questions test.

core.p: Edexcel 1BI0 point 6.7 asks you to **explain how the structure of the root hair cells is adapted to absorb water and mineral ions**. Every adaptation you name must be linked to the job it does and the transport process it supports.
bullets: Know the **structure**: projection (hair), thin cell wall, cell membrane, large permanent vacuole, many mitochondria, no chloroplasts.
Know the **processes**: water by **osmosis**; mineral ions by **active transport**.
Explain the **why**: each feature speeds up absorption.
This is a specialised cell (link to Topic 1 cell specialisation) and the start of water transport to the **xylem** (6.8, 6.9).

callouts.p: Marks come in pairs: name the feature, then say how it helps (e.g. many mitochondria, so more respiration releases energy for active transport).

core.h: Where root hair cells are found
core.p: Root hair cells are found in the **epidermis** (outer layer) of the young roots, just behind the growing tip. Thousands of them grow out between the soil particles, in direct contact with the thin film of **soil water** around each particle.
bullets: They are a type of epidermal cell with a long extension.
Each root hair is a **single cell**, not a multicellular hair.
Root hairs are short-lived and are constantly replaced as the root grows.
Together they massively increase the absorbing surface of the root system.

callouts.p: A root hair is part of one cell. It is not a small root and has no cells inside it.

fig.cap: A root hair cell. The long root hair projection pokes between soil particles. Note the thin cell wall, large vacuole of cell sap, nucleus and many mitochondria, and the absence of chloroplasts.

core.p: The long thin **root hair** projection gives the cell a **large surface area to volume ratio**. More membrane is in contact with soil water, so more water and mineral ions can be absorbed per second.
bullets: Rate of osmosis and active transport both increase with surface area of membrane.
Many root hairs across the whole root multiply this effect.
The hairs grow into tiny spaces between soil particles, reaching water a smooth root could not.
Damage to root hairs (e.g. when transplanting) slows water uptake and causes wilting.

callouts.p: The amount of surface compared with the volume inside; a high ratio means faster exchange with the surroundings.

core.h: Adaptation 2: thin cell wall and membrane
core.p: The cell wall of a root hair cell is **thin** and made of permeable cellulose, and the cell membrane beneath it is **partially permeable**. This gives a **short diffusion distance** for water to move into the cell.
bullets: A shorter distance means faster movement of water.
The cellulose wall is fully permeable, so water and ions pass through easily.
The **partially permeable** cell membrane controls what enters: water molecules pass, and carrier proteins move specific ions.
Root hair cells have **no waxy cuticle**, unlike leaf epidermis cells, so nothing blocks water entry.

core.p: The large permanent vacuole is filled with **cell sap**, a concentrated solution of sugars and salts. This keeps the cytoplasm and vacuole at a **lower water potential** (more concentrated) than the dilute soil water, so there is a steep concentration gradient for osmosis.
bullets: Soil water is a **dilute** solution (high concentration of water molecules).
Cell sap is **concentrated** (lower concentration of water molecules).
Net movement of water is **into** the cell by osmosis.
Mineral ions actively pumped in also make the cell contents more concentrated, which helps draw in more water.
Water entering makes the cell turgid.

callouts.p: Water moves by osmosis from the dilute soil water into the more concentrated cell sap of the root hair cell.

core.p: Water enters root hair cells by **osmosis**: the net movement of water molecules from a dilute solution to a more concentrated solution across a partially permeable membrane. It is a **passive** process, needing no energy from respiration.
bullets: Direction: from soil water (dilute) into the root hair cell (concentrated).
Through: the partially permeable cell membrane.
Energy: none needed; water moves down its concentration gradient.
If the soil water becomes more concentrated than the cell (e.g. after adding too much fertiliser or in salty soil), water leaves the cell by osmosis and the plant **wilts**.

callouts.p: The diffusion of water molecules from a dilute solution to a more concentrated solution across a partially permeable membrane.

fig.cap: Across the root hair cell membrane, water moves into the cell by osmosis (from dilute soil water to concentrated cell sap) while mineral ions are moved in by active transport, from low to high concentration.

core.h: Mineral ion uptake by active transport
core.p: The concentration of mineral ions in soil water is usually **lower** than inside the root hair cell. Ions therefore cannot be absorbed by diffusion, which would move them out. Instead they are absorbed by **active transport**, which moves substances **against a concentration gradient** using **energy from respiration**.
bullets: Direction: from low concentration (soil) to high concentration (cell).
Uses **carrier proteins** in the cell membrane that pick up specific ions.
Requires energy released by **respiration** (in mitochondria).
Examples of mineral ions: **nitrate** ions (to make amino acids and proteins), **magnesium** ions (to make chlorophyll), phosphate and potassium ions.
Active transport lets the plant take up ions even when they are scarce in the soil.

callouts.p: The movement of substances against a concentration gradient (from low to high concentration), requiring energy from respiration.

core.p: Root hair cells contain **many mitochondria**. Mitochondria are the site of **aerobic respiration**, which releases the energy needed for active transport of mineral ions.
bullets: More mitochondria, more respiration, more energy available, faster active transport.
Aerobic respiration needs **oxygen**, which root hair cells get from air spaces in the soil.
Waterlogged soil has little oxygen, so respiration and ion uptake fall and plants grow poorly.
Respiratory poisons (e.g. cyanide) stop active uptake of ions but not osmosis.

callouts.p: Write 'many mitochondria to release energy by respiration for active transport' rather than 'mitochondria make energy' (energy is released, not made).

core.p: Root hair cells have **no chloroplasts**. They are underground in the dark, so they cannot photosynthesise. Leaving out chloroplasts means more room inside the cell for the vacuole and mitochondria.
bullets: Root hair cells rely on **sucrose** transported to them in the **phloem** for respiration.
This is a common comparison question: palisade cells have many chloroplasts, root hair cells have none.
Do not say root hair cells photosynthesise.

core.p: Use this table to revise each feature with its function. In the exam, always give the feature and its explanation.
bullets: Features that help **water** uptake: large surface area, thin wall, concentrated vacuole.
Features that help **mineral ion** uptake: large surface area, many mitochondria, carrier proteins in membrane.

head: Feature
How it helps
Process helped
rows: Short distance for water to travel
Partially permeable membrane with carrier proteins
Controls entry; carriers move specific ions
Large permanent vacuole of concentrated sap
Keeps a concentration gradient for water entry
No light underground; space for other organelles

core.p: After entering the root hair cell, water moves across the **cortex** of the root from cell to cell by osmosis, because each cell further in is slightly more concentrated. It reaches the **xylem** in the centre of the root and is carried up to the stem and leaves.
bullets: Water is pulled up the xylem by **transpiration** from the leaves (transpiration stream).
Mineral ions dissolved in the water are carried up the xylem too.
Root hair uptake is the **first step** of the transpiration stream.
Faster transpiration means faster water uptake by root hairs.

fig.cap: Cross-section of a root. Water enters through root hairs, crosses the cortex cells by osmosis and reaches the xylem in the centre, which carries water and mineral ions up the plant.

core.p: Exam questions often ask you to compare how water and ions are taken up. Learn the differences precisely.
bullets: Both happen across the **cell membrane** of the root hair cell.
Both are faster with a **larger surface area**.
Only active transport needs **energy from respiration** and carrier proteins.

head: Osmosis (water)
Active transport (mineral ions)
rows: Dilute to concentrated solution (down water gradient)
Low to high ion concentration (against gradient)

callouts.p: Mineral ions are not taken up by osmosis. Osmosis is only for water.

analogy.p: A root hair cell is like a long thin sponge pushed into wet soil: its huge surface soaks up water passively because it is 'thirstier' (more concentrated) inside than the soil. Fitted into the sponge are tiny powered pumps (carrier proteins) run by batteries (mitochondria) that pull in scarce minerals even when the sponge already holds more than the soil. Where it breaks down: a real sponge soaks up water by capillary action, not osmosis through a membrane, and the pumps are selective proteins, not machines; the energy comes from respiration, which needs oxygen.

terms.d: A specialised epidermal cell of a young root with a long projection that absorbs water and mineral ions from the soil.
The diffusion of water molecules from a dilute solution to a more concentrated solution across a partially permeable membrane.
The movement of substances against a concentration gradient, from low to high concentration, requiring energy from respiration.
The difference in concentration between two areas.
A membrane that allows some molecules (such as water) through but not others.
Charged particles dissolved in soil water, such as nitrate and magnesium, that plants need for healthy growth.
Mineral ions used by plants to make amino acids and therefore proteins.
Mineral ions needed by plants to make chlorophyll.
Organelles where aerobic respiration takes place, releasing energy.
A protein in the cell membrane that transports specific molecules or ions across it during active transport.
The solution of sugars and salts stored in the permanent vacuole of a plant cell.
The surface area of an object divided by its volume; a higher ratio allows faster exchange.
Tissue made of dead hollow cells that transports water and mineral ions from roots to leaves.
The outer layer of cells of a root, stem or leaf.
Describes a plant cell that is swollen and firm because it has taken in water by osmosis.

mistakes.w: Root hair cells absorb mineral ions by osmosis.
mistakes.r: Mineral ions are absorbed by active transport; only water moves by osmosis.

mistakes.w: Root hair cells absorb mineral ions by diffusion because they move to where they are needed.
mistakes.r: Ion concentration is lower in the soil than in the cell, so ions must be moved against the gradient by active transport.

mistakes.w: Mitochondria make energy for active transport.
mistakes.r: Mitochondria are the site of respiration, which releases energy for active transport.

mistakes.w: Root hair cells have chloroplasts to make food.
mistakes.r: Root hair cells have no chloroplasts because they are underground with no light.

mistakes.w: The root hair is made of lots of cells.
mistakes.r: Each root hair is an extension of a single root hair cell.

mistakes.w: Water moves from a high concentration solution in the soil to a low concentration in the cell.
mistakes.r: Water moves from a dilute solution (soil water) to a more concentrated solution (cell sap) by osmosis.

mistakes.w: The root hair gives a big surface area so water can diffuse.
mistakes.r: Large surface area increases the rate of osmosis of water and active transport of ions.

mistakes.w: Active transport moves ions from high to low concentration using energy.
mistakes.r: Active transport moves ions from low to high concentration, against the concentration gradient.

exam.q: Name the process by which root hair cells absorb water.
model: Osmosis.
exam.tip: One word, but spell it correctly.

exam.q: Name the process by which root hair cells absorb mineral ions.
model: Active transport.
exam.tip: Diffusion is wrong here.

exam.q: Explain why root hair cells contain many mitochondria.
model: To carry out (aerobic) respiration to release energy.
Energy needed for active transport of mineral ions.
exam.tip: Mention both respiration and active transport.

exam.q: Explain how the shape of a root hair cell is adapted for its function.
model: Long thin projection gives a large surface area.
So more water and mineral ions can be absorbed (faster).
exam.tip: Feature then function.

exam.q: Give one difference between osmosis and active transport.
model: Active transport requires energy from respiration but osmosis does not (or active transport moves substances against a concentration gradient, osmosis is down a gradient; or osmosis is only water).
exam.tip: Make the comparison explicit using 'but' or 'whereas'.

exam.q: Explain why mineral ions cannot be absorbed by diffusion into root hair cells.
model: Concentration of mineral ions is lower in the soil than in the root hair cell.
Diffusion would move ions out, so they must be moved against the concentration gradient.
exam.tip: Refer to which side is more concentrated.

exam.q: Root hair cells do not contain chloroplasts. Explain why.
model: Roots are underground / in the dark.
So no light for photosynthesis, so chloroplasts would not be useful.
exam.tip: Link absence of light to absence of photosynthesis.

exam.q: A farmer's field becomes waterlogged. Explain why the crop shows signs of mineral deficiency.
model: Water fills air spaces so there is less oxygen in the soil.
Less aerobic respiration in root hair cells so less energy released.
Less active transport so fewer mineral ions absorbed.
exam.tip: Build a chain from oxygen to respiration to active transport.

exam.q: Explain why adding too much fertiliser to soil can cause a plant to wilt.
model: Soil water becomes more concentrated than the cell sap of root hair cells.
Water leaves the root hair cells by osmosis (or less water enters).
Less water reaches leaves so cells lose turgor and the plant wilts.
exam.tip: Describe the direction of osmosis.

exam.q: Explain how the structure of root hair cells is adapted for the uptake of water and mineral ions.
model: Long hair-like projection gives large surface area for absorption.
Thin cell wall gives short distance for water to move.
Partially permeable membrane allows water in by osmosis.
Large vacuole of concentrated cell sap maintains a concentration gradient so water enters by osmosis from dilute soil water.
Many mitochondria release energy by respiration for active transport.
Carrier proteins in membrane move mineral ions such as nitrate against their concentration gradient.
exam.tip: Cover both water and ions, and link every feature to a process.

worked.q: Model answer: compare a root hair cell with a palisade mesophyll cell in a leaf.
steps: Both are plant cells with a cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus and large permanent vacuole.
Root hair cell has a long projection for a large surface area for absorbing water and ions; palisade cell is column shaped and tightly packed.
Root hair cell has no chloroplasts because it is underground; palisade cell has many chloroplasts to absorb light for photosynthesis.
Root hair cell has many mitochondria for active transport of mineral ions.
worked.ans: Both are specialised plant cells, but the root hair cell is adapted for absorption (large surface area, many mitochondria, no chloroplasts) while the palisade cell is adapted for photosynthesis (many chloroplasts).

worked.q: Applied example: a scientist treated roots with a chemical that stops respiration. Uptake of nitrate ions fell by 95 percent but water uptake fell by only 10 percent. Explain these results.
steps: Nitrate ions are absorbed by active transport, which needs energy from respiration.
With respiration stopped, no energy is released, so active transport almost stops: nitrate uptake falls by 95 percent.
Water is absorbed by osmosis, which is passive and needs no energy, so water uptake continues.
The small drop in water uptake may be because fewer ions are pumped in, so the cell sap becomes less concentrated and the gradient for osmosis is less steep.
worked.ans: Active transport of ions depends on respiration so it almost stops; osmosis does not need energy so water uptake barely changes.

worked.q: Calculation: the concentration of nitrate ions is 0.2 mmol per dm3 in soil water and 5.0 mmol per dm3 in a root hair cell. How many times more concentrated is the cell, and what does this tell you about uptake?
steps: The cell contains 25 times the nitrate concentration of the soil.
Nitrate must move from low (soil) to high (cell) concentration, against the concentration gradient.
This requires active transport using energy from respiration.
worked.ans: 25 times more concentrated, so nitrate is taken up by active transport.

bio_edx.5.5.summary: Plants have two transport tissues. **Xylem** is made of dead, hollow cells joined end to end with no end walls and walls strengthened by **lignin**, forming continuous tubes that carry **water and mineral ions** up from the roots in one direction. **Phloem** is made of living **sieve tube elements** with perforated **sieve plates**, supported by **companion cells** full of mitochondria, and it carries dissolved **sucrose** up and down the plant by translocation. For 6.8 you must link each structural feature to the function it allows.

core.p: Edexcel 1BI0 point 6.8 asks you to **explain how the structure of xylem and phloem are adapted to their functions in the plant**. You need the key features of each tissue and the reason each feature helps.
bullets: **Xylem**: transports water and dissolved mineral ions from roots to stems and leaves.
**Phloem**: transports dissolved food (mainly **sucrose**) around the plant.
Xylem and phloem are found together in **vascular bundles** in roots, stems and leaves.
Related points: transpiration (6.9) is the movement of water through xylem; translocation (6.10) is the movement of sucrose through phloem.

callouts.p: For every feature, add 'so that' and give the function, for example: no end walls so that water flows in a continuous column.

core.p: Xylem carries **water and mineral ions** from the roots up through the stem to the leaves. It also gives the plant **support**. Movement is in **one direction only: upwards**.
bullets: Water is pulled up by **transpiration** (evaporation of water from leaves).
Water is needed in leaves for photosynthesis, for cooling and to keep cells turgid.
Mineral ions such as nitrate and magnesium are carried dissolved in the water.
Movement through xylem is **passive**: it does not need energy from the xylem cells.

core.p: Xylem vessels develop from cells that line up end to end. As they mature, the cells **die**, their **end walls break down** and their walls become thickened with **lignin**. The result is a long, hollow, strong tube.
bullets: **Dead cells with no cytoplasm or organelles**: nothing blocks the flow of water; the lumen is completely hollow.
**No end walls**: cells join into a **continuous tube**, so water moves in an unbroken column from root to leaf.
**Lignin** thickening in the walls: makes the walls strong and rigid so vessels do not collapse under the tension of the transpiration pull; also **waterproof**; gives the plant support.
**Pits** (gaps in the lignin): let water and mineral ions move sideways into neighbouring vessels and cells.
**Narrow tubes**: help water move up as a continuous column.

callouts.p: A strong, waterproof substance deposited in the cell walls of xylem vessels that strengthens them.

fig.cap: Longitudinal section of a xylem vessel. Dead cells with no end walls form a hollow tube; lignin thickens and strengthens the walls; pits allow sideways movement of water. Water and mineral ions move upwards only.

core.p: Transpiration from the leaves pulls water up the xylem. This puts the water column **under tension** (it is being pulled, not pushed). Without strong walls, the vessels would collapse inwards like a soft straw when you suck hard.
bullets: Lignin gives the vessel walls **mechanical strength**.
Lignified xylem forms the **wood** of trees and supports tall stems.
Lignin is waterproof, so water stays in the vessel until it reaches a pit.
Lignin is often laid down in **rings or spirals** in young xylem so the stem can still grow longer.

callouts.p: Mention both strength (stops vessels collapsing, supports the plant) and waterproofing for full credit.

core.p: Phloem carries **dissolved food**, mainly **sucrose** and also amino acids, from where it is made or stored (the **source**, e.g. leaves) to where it is needed (the **sink**, e.g. roots, growing tips, fruits and storage organs). This is called **translocation**.
bullets: Movement can be **up or down** the plant (in both directions).
Translocation needs **energy**: sucrose is actively loaded into the phloem.
Sucrose is used for **respiration**, for growth and is converted to **starch** for storage.
Glucose made in photosynthesis is converted to sucrose for transport because sucrose is soluble but less reactive.

callouts.p: The movement of dissolved sucrose (and other food molecules) through the phloem from source to sink.

core.p: Phloem is made of columns of **living cells** called **sieve tube elements** joined end to end. Their structure is reduced so dissolved sugars can flow through easily.
bullets: **Sieve plates**: the end walls are perforated with holes, so the cell sap containing sucrose can flow from one cell to the next.
**No nucleus** and very **little cytoplasm**: more space for the flow of sucrose solution.
Cells are **living** with a cell membrane, unlike xylem.
Walls are **not lignified**.

callouts.p: The perforated end wall between two sieve tube elements that lets phloem sap flow through.

fig.cap: Phloem tissue. Living sieve tube elements are joined by perforated sieve plates and have no nucleus. Each has a companion cell with a nucleus and many mitochondria. Sucrose moves both up and down.

core.p: Each sieve tube element has a **companion cell** next to it, connected by small pores. Because the sieve tube element has no nucleus and few organelles, the companion cell keeps it alive and supplies the energy needed for translocation.
bullets: Companion cells have a **nucleus** and dense cytoplasm.
They contain **many mitochondria**, which carry out **respiration** to release energy.
This energy is used for **active transport** of sucrose into (and out of) the sieve tubes.
Companion cells carry out the life processes for the sieve tube elements.

callouts.p: Translocation needs energy from respiration in the mitochondria of companion cells.

core.p: Comparison questions are very common. Use a table and always compare like with like.
bullets: Remember: **xylem = water, up, dead, lignin**; **phloem = food, both ways, living, sieve plates**.
Both are long tubes of cells joined end to end, found in vascular bundles.

callouts.p: Xylem carries water; phloem carries food. A memory aid: phloem carries food (both start with an 'f' sound).

core.h: Where xylem and phloem are found
core.p: Xylem and phloem are grouped together in **vascular bundles**. Their arrangement differs between organs but they always run together through the plant.
bullets: In a **stem**, vascular bundles are arranged in a **ring** near the outside, with phloem towards the outside and xylem towards the inside. This helps support the stem against bending.
In a **root**, xylem is in the **centre**, which helps the root resist pulling forces.
In a **leaf**, the vascular bundles form the **veins**; xylem brings water to leaf cells and phloem removes sucrose.
