core.h: Linking structure to the whole plant
core.p: The two tissues work together: xylem supplies the leaves with water and mineral ions for photosynthesis, and phloem carries the sugars made by photosynthesis to every other part of the plant.
bullets: Root hair cells take in water by osmosis and ions by active transport, which then enter the **xylem**.
Leaves use water and CO2 to make glucose; it is converted to **sucrose** and loaded into the **phloem**.
Phloem delivers sucrose to roots, which cannot photosynthesise, so root cells can respire and carry out active transport.
Mineral ions carried by xylem (e.g. nitrate) are used to make amino acids, which can then be transported in phloem.

core.p: Exam questions sometimes use experiments or real situations to test understanding of xylem and phloem.
bullets: **Ringing** (removing a ring of bark): bark contains phloem, so sucrose cannot reach the roots; sugars build up above the ring and the swelling forms there. Xylem, deeper in the wood, still carries water so leaves do not wilt at first.
**Coloured dye**: a celery stalk placed in coloured water shows dye in the xylem only, showing water moves up through xylem.
**Aphids** feed by inserting their mouthparts into phloem to get sugary sap.
Woody stems are strong because of lignified xylem.

callouts.p: Explain that the phloem was removed, so translocation of sucrose to the roots stopped; the roots eventually die because they cannot respire.

analogy.t: Water pipes and a delivery train
analogy.p: Xylem is like an empty metal drainpipe running up a building: dead, hollow, rigid (lignin is the metal) and with no blockages, so water can be pulled up through it with no energy from the pipe itself. Phloem is like a goods train line between stations: the carriages (sieve tube elements) have open doors between them (sieve plates) and are emptied of furniture (no nucleus) to make room for cargo, while engines alongside (companion cells with mitochondria) supply the energy to load the sucrose, and trains can run in either direction. Where it breaks down: real drainpipes carry water down by gravity, whereas xylem pulls water up by transpiration; and phloem sap flows as a liquid, not as separate parcels.

terms.d: Plant tissue made of dead, hollow, lignified cells that transports water and mineral ions upwards from roots to leaves.
Plant tissue made of living sieve tube elements and companion cells that transports dissolved sucrose around the plant.
A strong, waterproof substance in xylem cell walls that strengthens them and supports the plant.
The hollow space inside a tube such as a xylem vessel.
A thin, non-lignified area in a xylem wall that allows water to pass sideways.
A living phloem cell with no nucleus and little cytoplasm, joined end to end with others via sieve plates.
A perforated end wall between sieve tube elements that lets phloem sap flow through.
A cell next to a sieve tube element with a nucleus and many mitochondria, providing energy for translocation.
The movement of dissolved sucrose through the phloem from source to sink, requiring energy.
The movement of water from roots, through xylem, to the leaves where it evaporates.
A part of the plant where sucrose is made or released, such as a leaf.
A part of the plant where sucrose is used or stored, such as roots, growing tips or fruits.
A group of xylem and phloem tissues running together through roots, stems and leaves.
A soluble sugar made from glucose; the form in which carbohydrate is transported in phloem.
Dissolved ions such as nitrate and magnesium taken up from the soil and carried in xylem.

mistakes.w: Xylem transports food and phloem transports water.
mistakes.r: Xylem transports water and mineral ions; phloem transports dissolved sucrose.

mistakes.w: Xylem cells are living and have no nucleus.
mistakes.r: Xylem cells are dead, with no cytoplasm; it is phloem sieve tube elements that are living with no nucleus.

mistakes.w: Lignin makes the xylem flexible so it can bend.
mistakes.r: Lignin strengthens and waterproofs xylem walls so vessels do not collapse and the plant is supported.

mistakes.w: Phloem only transports sugar down to the roots.
mistakes.r: Phloem transports sucrose both up and down, from source to sink.

mistakes.w: Phloem transports glucose.
mistakes.r: Phloem transports sucrose (glucose is converted to sucrose for transport).

mistakes.w: Sieve plates filter the sap.
mistakes.r: Sieve plates are perforated end walls that allow sap to flow from one sieve tube element to the next.

mistakes.w: Companion cells make energy.
mistakes.r: Companion cells have many mitochondria that release energy by respiration for active transport of sucrose.

mistakes.w: Xylem needs energy from the plant to move water.
mistakes.r: Water moves through xylem passively, pulled by transpiration; no energy is used by the xylem cells.

exam.q: Name the tissue that transports sucrose in a plant.
model: Phloem.
exam.tip: Spelling 'phloem' correctly matters.

exam.q: State two substances transported in the xylem.
model: Water.
Mineral ions (e.g. nitrate or magnesium ions).
exam.tip: Not sugar or glucose.

exam.q: Explain how the lack of end walls in xylem vessels helps their function.
model: Forms a continuous hollow tube.
So water can flow without obstruction / as a continuous column from roots to leaves.
exam.tip: Feature then benefit.

exam.q: Explain why xylem vessels contain lignin.
model: Lignin strengthens the walls / makes them rigid and waterproof.
So vessels do not collapse under the tension of transpiration / supports the plant.
exam.tip: Give a reason, not just 'for strength'.

exam.q: Explain the role of companion cells in phloem.
model: Companion cells have many mitochondria.
Release energy by respiration.
Energy used for active transport of sucrose into the sieve tubes / translocation.
exam.tip: Link mitochondria to energy for translocation.

exam.q: Give two ways the structure of a sieve tube element is adapted for transport.
model: Sieve plates / perforated end walls allow sap to flow between cells.
No nucleus / little cytoplasm so more space for flow of sucrose solution.
exam.tip: Two different features for two marks.

exam.q: Compare the structure of xylem and phloem.
model: Xylem cells are dead but phloem cells are living.
Xylem has no end walls whereas phloem has sieve plates.
Xylem walls contain lignin, phloem walls do not.
Phloem has companion cells; xylem does not.
exam.tip: Each mark needs a direct comparison with 'whereas' or 'but'.

exam.q: A ring of bark (containing phloem) is removed from a tree trunk. Explain why the roots eventually die.
model: Phloem is removed so sucrose cannot be translocated to the roots.
Root cells cannot photosynthesise so receive no sugar.
No glucose for respiration so no energy and cells die.
exam.tip: Remember xylem is still intact so water still reaches the leaves.

exam.q: Explain why movement in phloem is described as an active process but movement in xylem is passive.
model: Translocation requires energy from respiration in companion cells.
For active transport / loading of sucrose.
Water in xylem moves due to transpiration / evaporation from leaves so no energy used by xylem.
exam.tip: Name the processes: translocation and transpiration.

exam.q: Explain how the structures of xylem and phloem are adapted to their functions.
model: Xylem: dead cells, no cytoplasm, hollow lumen so no obstruction to water flow.
Xylem: no end walls so continuous tube for water and mineral ions from roots to leaves.
Xylem: lignin strengthens walls, prevents collapse and supports the plant, waterproof.
Phloem: living sieve tube elements joined by sieve plates allowing sap to flow between cells.
Phloem: little cytoplasm and no nucleus so more room for sucrose solution.
Phloem: companion cells with many mitochondria release energy for active transport / translocation of sucrose in both directions.
exam.tip: Balance the answer: about three points for each tissue.

worked.q: Model answer (4 marks): describe the functions of xylem and phloem.
steps: Xylem transports water from the roots to the leaves.
Xylem also transports dissolved mineral ions, in one direction (upwards).
Phloem transports dissolved sucrose (and amino acids) from sources such as leaves.
Phloem carries it to sinks such as roots, growing regions and storage organs, in both directions.
worked.ans: Xylem: water and mineral ions, upwards only. Phloem: sucrose, from source to sink, up and down.

worked.q: Applied example: a celery stalk was placed in red dye for 2 hours. When cut across, only small dots near the outside of the stalk were stained. Identify the tissue and explain the result.
steps: Water moves up the stalk through the xylem in the transpiration stream.
The dye is dissolved in the water, so it travels in the xylem.
Xylem is found in vascular bundles, which appear as dots arranged near the outside of the stalk.
Other cells are not stained because water enters them in smaller amounts and the dye stays mostly in the vessels.
worked.ans: The stained dots are xylem in vascular bundles, showing water travels upwards through xylem.

worked.q: Calculation: dye moved 9.6 cm up a xylem vessel in 12 minutes. Calculate the rate in cm per hour.
steps: Rate = distance / time = 9.6 / 12 = 0.8 cm per minute.
Convert to per hour: 0.8 x 60 = 48 cm per hour.
worked.ans: 48 cm per hour.

bio_edx.5.6.summary: **Transpiration** is the loss of water vapour from the leaves of a plant, mainly through the **stomata**. Water evaporating from the leaf pulls a continuous column of water up the **xylem** from the roots, so transpiration is what moves water and dissolved **mineral ions** from the soil to every part of the plant. Stomata are pores controlled by pairs of **guard cells**, which open the pore in the light so carbon dioxide can diffuse in for photosynthesis and close it to cut water loss, so a plant always has to balance gas exchange against drying out.

core.p: Transpiration is the **loss of water vapour from the parts of a plant above ground, mainly from the leaves**. Water inside the leaf **evaporates** from the surfaces of mesophyll cells into the air spaces, and the water vapour then **diffuses** out of the leaf through the **stomata** into the air outside, where there is less water vapour.
bullets: It is two processes in a row: **evaporation** (liquid water to water vapour inside the leaf) then **diffusion** (water vapour moves out down a concentration gradient).
Most transpiration (about 90%) happens through the stomata; a little is lost through the **waxy cuticle**.
It is a **passive** process: the energy comes from the Sun heating the leaf, not from the plant's respiration.
Transpiration is a side effect of having stomata open for **gas exchange**: a leaf cannot let carbon dioxide in without also letting water vapour out.
The **transpiration stream** is the continuous movement of water from the roots, up the xylem and out of the leaves.

callouts.p: The loss of water vapour from the leaves (and other aerial parts) of a plant by evaporation and diffusion, mainly through the stomata.
The continuous flow of water (with dissolved mineral ions) from the roots, through the xylem, to the leaves, where it is lost by transpiration.

core.p: Water first has to get into the plant. Soil water is a very dilute solution, while the cytoplasm and cell sap of **root hair cells** are more concentrated, so water moves into root hair cells **by osmosis** (from a dilute solution to a more concentrated solution across a partially permeable membrane). Mineral ions such as nitrate are taken in by **active transport**, because their concentration is usually higher inside the root than in the soil.
bullets: Root hair cells have a **large surface area** so more water enters by osmosis per second (covered fully in 6.7).
Water then passes from cell to cell across the **root cortex** towards the centre of the root, again by osmosis.
Water then enters the **xylem vessels** in the root.
Mineral ions dissolved in the water are carried up with it: this is how ions reach the leaves.
Active transport of mineral ions needs **energy from respiration** in the root cells, so roots need oxygen.

callouts.p: Do not say mineral ions enter by osmosis. Water enters by osmosis; mineral ions enter by active transport.

core.h: Step 2: water moves up the xylem
core.p: Xylem vessels are long, hollow tubes made of **dead cells** joined end to end with **no end walls** and walls strengthened with **lignin**. Water moves up them as an unbroken column, from the roots, through the stem and into the veins of every leaf.
bullets: No end walls and no cytoplasm means there is nothing to block the flow, so water moves quickly.
**Lignin** makes the walls strong and waterproof, so the vessels do not collapse inwards when water is pulled up under tension.
Flow in xylem is **one way only: upwards**, from roots to leaves (unlike phloem, which can go both ways).
Movement up the xylem does not need energy from the plant: it is driven by water evaporating from the leaves.
The xylem carries **water and dissolved mineral ions**, not sugars.

fig.cap: The transpiration stream in a whole plant. Water enters root hair cells by osmosis, rises in the xylem as an unbroken column, moves into the leaves, evaporates inside them and diffuses out of the stomata as water vapour.

core.h: Why water rises: the transpiration pull
core.p: When water evaporates from the leaf and diffuses out of the stomata, the leaf cells replace it by drawing water from the xylem in the leaf veins. Because **water molecules are attracted to each other (cohesion)**, the column of water in the xylem behaves like a chain: pulling water out at the top pulls the whole column up from the roots. This is the **transpiration pull**.
bullets: Loss of water at the top creates a **pull (tension)** on the water column in the xylem.
The column is **continuous** from root to leaf, so water is pulled up the whole height of the plant.
The faster water evaporates from the leaves, the faster water is drawn up the xylem and the faster water is taken in at the roots.
This is why the rate of water **uptake** is used as a measure of the rate of transpiration in a potometer (see 6.12-6.13).
If the column is broken by an air bubble, water cannot be pulled up that vessel: this is why shoots for a potometer are cut under water.

callouts.p: Evaporation from leaf cells, then diffusion out of the stomata, then water drawn out of the xylem, then the whole water column pulled up, then more water enters the roots by osmosis.

core.p: In the leaf, water leaves the xylem in the veins and moves into the **mesophyll cells** by osmosis. A thin film of water covers the walls of the **spongy mesophyll** cells. This water **evaporates** into the **air spaces**, so the air spaces become very humid. Water vapour then **diffuses out through the stomata** because there is a higher concentration of water vapour inside the leaf than in the air outside.
bullets: The many **air spaces** in the spongy mesophyll give a huge internal surface area for evaporation.
The concentration gradient of water vapour is from **inside the leaf (high)** to **outside air (lower)**.
Anything that keeps this gradient steep (wind blowing vapour away, dry air) speeds up transpiration.
Most stomata are on the **lower surface** of the leaf, which is shaded and cooler, so less water evaporates than if they were on top.
The upper surface has a thicker **waxy cuticle**, which is waterproof and reduces evaporation.

core.h: Structure of stomata and guard cells
core.p: A **stoma** (plural stomata) is a tiny pore in the epidermis of a leaf. Each stoma is surrounded by **two guard cells**, which change shape to open and close the pore. Guard cells have special features that let them do this.
bullets: Guard cells are **sausage or kidney shaped** and found in pairs, one each side of the pore.
The cell wall on the **inner side (next to the pore) is thicker and less stretchy** than the outer wall.
Guard cells contain **chloroplasts**, unlike the other cells of the lower epidermis.
They have a large vacuole, so they can take in or lose a lot of water and change volume.
Stomata are found mostly on the **lower epidermis** of leaves (floating leaves such as water lilies have them on top instead).
The epidermis around the stomata is covered in a **waxy cuticle**, so the stomata are the main route for gases in and out.

callouts.p: A pore in the epidermis of a leaf, surrounded by two guard cells, which allows carbon dioxide and oxygen to diffuse into and out of the leaf and water vapour to diffuse out.

core.h: How guard cells open and close the stoma
core.p: Opening and closing depends on how much water the guard cells contain. When guard cells **take in water by osmosis they become turgid**. Because the inner wall is thicker and less flexible than the outer wall, the swelling cells **bend (curve) away from each other**, and the pore between them **opens**. When guard cells **lose water they become flaccid**, they straighten, and the pore **closes**.
bullets: **Turgid** guard cells = **stoma open**.
**Flaccid** guard cells = **stoma closed**.
The uneven thickness of the wall is the key: if both walls stretched equally, the cells would just get fatter, not bend apart.
Stomata usually **open in the light** (when carbon dioxide is needed for photosynthesis) and **close in the dark** (when it is not, saving water).
Stomata also **close when the plant is short of water** (for example on a hot, dry day), because guard cells lose water and become flaccid. This reduces water loss and helps stop the plant wilting.
Closing has a cost: less carbon dioxide can enter, so the rate of photosynthesis falls.

Guard cells

rows: CO2 enters for photosynthesis; water vapour lost

core.h: Why the guard cells contain chloroplasts
core.p: Guard cells are the only cells in the lower epidermis with chloroplasts. This is linked to them opening in the light: in light the guard cells can photosynthesise and make sugars, which helps them take in water by osmosis and become turgid.
bullets: This means stomata tend to open **when light is available**, exactly when the leaf needs carbon dioxide for photosynthesis.
In exams, the mark is usually for linking open stomata with light and gas exchange, and closed stomata with dark or water shortage.
Other epidermis cells lack chloroplasts so light can pass straight through to the palisade mesophyll below.

callouts.p: You do not need detailed ion movements in guard cells for Edexcel GCSE. Turgid means open, flaccid means closed, and the thick inner wall is why they bend.

core.h: The role of stomata in gas exchange
core.p: Stomata exist because the leaf must exchange gases with the air. In the light, the leaf uses **carbon dioxide** for photosynthesis and produces **oxygen**; both move by **diffusion** through the stomata. Water vapour diffuses out through the same pores.
bullets: **Carbon dioxide diffuses in** through open stomata, into the air spaces and then into mesophyll cells.
**Oxygen diffuses out** (made in photosynthesis faster than it is used in respiration in the light).
In the dark, respiration still happens: oxygen is needed and carbon dioxide is produced, but stomata are mostly closed so exchange is slow.
**Water vapour diffuses out** whenever stomata are open: this is transpiration.
The air spaces in the spongy mesophyll connect to the stomata, so gases reach every cell quickly.

head: Substance
Direction through stomata (in light)
Why
rows: Used in photosynthesis, so concentration inside is low
Made in photosynthesis, so concentration inside is high
Evaporates into air spaces, so concentration inside is high

core.h: Why transpiration matters to the plant
core.p: Transpiration is not just water being wasted: the stream it creates does several useful jobs. But too much transpiration can make the plant lose water faster than it takes it in, causing it to **wilt**.
bullets: **Transports water** from roots to leaves, where water is a raw material for **photosynthesis**.
**Transports mineral ions** dissolved in the water, such as **nitrates** (for making proteins) and **magnesium** (for making chlorophyll).
**Keeps cells turgid**, which supports the leaves and soft stems so leaves are held out to the light.
**Cools the leaf**: evaporation of water takes heat energy from the leaf, like sweating.
Downside: if water is lost faster than it is replaced, cells become **flaccid** and the plant **wilts**. Closing stomata reduces this risk.

core.h: Balancing gas exchange and water loss
core.p: A leaf faces a trade-off: it needs open stomata to get carbon dioxide for photosynthesis, but every open stoma also lets water vapour escape. Plants balance this with several features.
bullets: **Stomata close** in the dark and when water is short, so water is only lost when the benefit (photosynthesis) is possible.
**Waxy cuticle** on the leaf surface stops water evaporating through the epidermis.
**Most stomata on the lower surface**, out of direct sunlight, so it is cooler and less water evaporates.
Plants in dry places have extra adaptations such as fewer stomata or stomata sunk in pits (covered in 6.14B).
Grade 9 point: link each feature to **reducing evaporation or reducing diffusion** of water vapour, and say what the cost is (less carbon dioxide uptake).

callouts.p: Open stomata: more CO2 for photosynthesis but more water lost. Closed stomata: water saved but photosynthesis limited by CO2.

core.h: Linking transpiration to the whole plant
core.p: Exam questions often test whether you can join up root, xylem, leaf and stomata into one story. Practise writing the whole route in order with the correct process at each stage.
bullets: Soil to root hair cell: **osmosis** (water) and **active transport** (mineral ions).
Across root to xylem: osmosis from cell to cell.
Up the xylem: **transpiration pull**, water column held together by cohesion.
Xylem to mesophyll cells: osmosis.
Mesophyll cell surface to air spaces: **evaporation**.
Air spaces to outside: **diffusion** of water vapour through the **stomata**.

analogy.t: Drinking through a very long straw
analogy.p: The xylem is like a long straw with its bottom in a glass of water (the soil). The leaves are like your mouth: when water vapour escapes from the leaves (you suck), the whole column of water in the straw is pulled up, because the water sticks together. The stomata are like your lips: open them and drinking (and water loss) happens; close them and the flow stops. The guard cells are the muscles of the lips. Where it breaks down: when you drink through a straw you use your own energy, but a plant spends none of its own energy pulling water up; the energy comes from the Sun evaporating the water. Also, in a straw the liquid ends up in you, but in a plant most of the water is lost to the air as vapour.

terms.d: The loss of water vapour from the leaves of a plant by evaporation and diffusion, mainly through the stomata.
The continuous movement of water and dissolved mineral ions from the roots, up the xylem and out of the leaves.
The pulling force on the water column in the xylem caused by water evaporating from the leaves.
A small pore in the leaf epidermis, surrounded by two guard cells, through which gases diffuse in and out.
A pair of cells around each stoma that change shape to open and close it; they have a thick inner wall and contain chloroplasts.
Describes a plant cell that is full of water and firm, with its contents pushing against the cell wall.
Describes a plant cell that has lost water and become soft and limp.
Tissue of dead, hollow cells with lignified walls and no end walls that carries water and mineral ions up from the roots to the leaves.
A strong, waterproof substance in the walls of xylem vessels that stops them collapsing.
The change of liquid water into water vapour, here from the surfaces of mesophyll cells into the air spaces.
The net movement of particles from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration.
The diffusion of water molecules from a dilute solution to a more concentrated solution across a partially permeable membrane.
Movement of substances against a concentration gradient using energy from respiration; how root hair cells take in mineral ions.
A waterproof waxy layer covering the leaf epidermis that reduces water loss by evaporation.
Drooping of a plant when cells lose water faster than it is replaced and become flaccid.
The attraction between water molecules that keeps the water column in the xylem unbroken.

mistakes.w: Transpiration is the loss of water from the plant.
mistakes.r: Transpiration is the loss of water VAPOUR, by evaporation and diffusion, mainly through the stomata of the leaves.

mistakes.w: Water moves up the xylem by osmosis.
mistakes.r: Water is pulled up the xylem by the transpiration pull caused by evaporation from the leaves; osmosis is only for movement into and between cells.

mistakes.w: Mineral ions enter the root hair cells by osmosis.
mistakes.r: Water enters by osmosis; mineral ions enter by active transport, using energy from respiration.

mistakes.w: Guard cells open when they lose water.
mistakes.r: Guard cells take in water and become turgid, which opens the stoma; flaccid guard cells close it.

mistakes.w: The guard cells get bigger so the hole gets bigger.
mistakes.r: The thicker, less flexible inner wall makes turgid guard cells curve/bend apart, opening the pore.

mistakes.w: Stomata let oxygen in for photosynthesis.
mistakes.r: Carbon dioxide diffuses in for photosynthesis; oxygen diffuses out.

mistakes.w: Water evaporates out of the stomata.
mistakes.r: Water evaporates inside the leaf from mesophyll cell surfaces into the air spaces, then the water vapour diffuses out of the stomata.

mistakes.w: Xylem carries water and sugar.
mistakes.r: Xylem carries water and mineral ions upwards only; sugars (sucrose) are carried in the phloem.

mistakes.w: Stomata close at night to stop oxygen escaping.
mistakes.r: Stomata close in the dark to reduce water loss, because no carbon dioxide is needed for photosynthesis.

exam.q: Define the term transpiration.
model: Loss of water vapour from the leaves/plant (by evaporation), through the stomata
exam.tip: Say water vapour, not just water, and mention leaves or stomata.

exam.q: Name the tissue that carries water from the roots to the leaves.
model: Xylem
exam.tip: Spell it correctly; phloem would get no mark.

exam.q: State two substances that diffuse through the stomata of a leaf in the light, and the direction each moves.
model: Carbon dioxide diffuses into the leaf
Oxygen / water vapour diffuses out of the leaf
exam.tip: You need both the substance and the direction for each mark.

exam.q: Give two functions of the transpiration stream.
model: Transports water to the leaves for photosynthesis
Transports mineral ions (e.g. nitrates/magnesium)
Keeps cells turgid / supports the plant
Cools the leaves by evaporation
exam.tip: Any two; be specific about what water or ions are used for.

exam.q: Explain why most stomata are found on the lower surface of a leaf.
model: Lower surface is shaded / cooler / out of direct sunlight
So less water is lost by evaporation / transpiration
exam.tip: State the condition, then link it to reduced water loss.

exam.q: Explain how guard cells cause a stoma to open.
model: Guard cells take in water by osmosis
They become turgid
Thicker (inner) wall means the cells bend/curve apart, opening the pore
exam.tip: The thick inner wall is the mark most students miss.

exam.q: Explain why stomata close when a plant is short of water, and the disadvantage of this to the plant.
model: Guard cells lose water / become flaccid so stomata close
Reduces water loss by transpiration / prevents wilting
Less carbon dioxide can diffuse in, so rate of photosynthesis decreases
exam.tip: A 'disadvantage' mark almost always means linking to carbon dioxide and photosynthesis.

exam.q: Describe how water moves from the xylem in a leaf into the atmosphere.
model: Water moves from xylem into mesophyll cells by osmosis
Water evaporates from mesophyll cell surfaces into the air spaces
Water vapour diffuses out through the stomata (down a concentration gradient)
exam.tip: Use the three process words in order: osmosis, evaporation, diffusion.

exam.q: Explain how the structure of xylem vessels is adapted to transport water.
model: Dead cells / no cytoplasm so no obstruction to flow
No end walls so form a continuous hollow tube
Walls strengthened with lignin
So vessels do not collapse under tension / are waterproof
exam.tip: Pair every feature with how it helps.

exam.q: A gardener notices that a plant's leaves wilt on a hot, sunny afternoon but recover in the evening. Explain these observations.
model: Hot/sunny: high rate of transpiration / evaporation
Water lost faster than taken up by the roots
Cells lose water and become flaccid, so leaves droop
In the evening transpiration falls / stomata close, so water uptake replaces losses and cells become turgid again
exam.tip: Compare rate of loss with rate of uptake: that is the key idea.

exam.q: Explain how water and mineral ions are transported from the soil to the leaves of a plant.
model: Water enters root hair cells by osmosis
From a dilute soil solution to more concentrated cell sap
Mineral ions taken up by active transport, using energy from respiration
Water moves across the root into the xylem
Water evaporates from the leaves and diffuses out through stomata (transpiration)
This pulls a continuous column of water up the xylem (transpiration pull)
Mineral ions are carried dissolved in the water in the xylem
Xylem has no end walls / is lignified, allowing a continuous flow
exam.tip: Level-marked: give a logical sequence from soil to leaf, naming the process at each step.

worked.q: Model answer: Explain why a plant needs stomata, even though they cause water loss.
steps: State the main purpose: stomata allow carbon dioxide to diffuse into the leaf for photosynthesis.
Add the second gas: oxygen produced in photosynthesis diffuses out.
Link to water: when stomata are open, water vapour also diffuses out, which is transpiration.
Explain the benefit of transpiration: it pulls water and mineral ions up the xylem to the leaves.
Explain control: guard cells close stomata in the dark or when water is short, to reduce water loss.
worked.ans: Stomata are needed for gas exchange (CO2 in, O2 out) for photosynthesis; the water loss they cause drives the transpiration stream that supplies water and ions, and guard cells close them when water would otherwise be wasted.

worked.q: Applied example: A student coats the lower surface of leaf A and the upper surface of leaf B with petroleum jelly (which is waterproof). After two days leaf B has lost far more mass than leaf A. Explain this result.
steps: Petroleum jelly blocks the stomata on the surface it covers, so water vapour cannot diffuse out there.
Most stomata are on the lower surface of a leaf.
Leaf A has its lower surface covered, so most stomata are blocked and little transpiration happens.
Leaf B has only the upper surface covered (few stomata, already has a waxy cuticle), so most stomata are still open.
Leaf B therefore loses more water vapour by transpiration, so it loses more mass.
worked.ans: Leaf B loses more mass because its lower surface, which has most of the stomata, was left uncovered, so water vapour could still diffuse out.

worked.q: Applied example: In a hedge, the leaves facing the sun at midday sometimes have closed stomata. Explain why, and predict the effect on the rate of photosynthesis.
steps: High temperature and strong light increase evaporation, so transpiration is fast.
If water is lost faster than it is taken up, the guard cells lose water and become flaccid.
Flaccid guard cells close the stomata, reducing further water loss.
With stomata closed, carbon dioxide cannot diffuse into the leaf.
Carbon dioxide becomes the limiting factor, so photosynthesis slows even though light is plentiful.
worked.ans: Stomata close because the guard cells become flaccid as the plant loses water; this saves water but reduces carbon dioxide uptake, so the rate of photosynthesis falls.

bio_edx.5.7.summary: **Translocation** is the transport of dissolved sugars, mainly **sucrose**, through the **phloem** from where they are made or released (the **source**, usually the leaves) to where they are used or stored (the **sinks**, such as growing tips, roots, fruits and storage organs). Unlike water moving in the xylem, translocation happens in **living cells**, can go **both up and down** the plant, and **needs energy**, which is supplied by the many mitochondria in the **companion cells** next to the sieve tubes.

core.p: Leaves make glucose by photosynthesis, but every living cell in the plant needs sugar for respiration and growth, including cells in the roots that never see light. The plant converts glucose into **sucrose** and moves it in solution through the **phloem** to wherever it is needed. This movement is called **translocation**.
bullets: Translocation moves **sucrose** (and other dissolved food molecules such as amino acids) in the **phloem**.
The sucrose is dissolved in water to form a sugary solution often called **phloem sap**.
It moves from a **source** (where sugar is made or released) to a **sink** (where sugar is used or stored).
It can go **up or down** the stem, depending on where the sources and sinks are.
It is an **active process** that needs **energy** from respiration.

callouts.p: The movement of sucrose (dissolved food molecules) through the phloem from the leaves to other parts of the plant, for respiration, growth and storage.

core.p: Glucose made in photosynthesis is converted to **sucrose** before it is transported. Sucrose is a sugar made of two sugar units joined together, and it is the main form in which carbohydrate is moved around a plant.
bullets: Sucrose is **soluble**, so it can be carried dissolved in the phloem sap.
Sucrose is **less reactive** than glucose, so it is not used up by cells along the way in respiration as it travels.
At the sink, sucrose is converted back into glucose (and fructose) to be used.
Do not confuse sucrose with **starch**: starch is **insoluble**, so it is used for storage, not transport.

callouts.p: The substance carried in translocation is sucrose. Starch cannot be transported because it is insoluble.

core.p: Phloem tissue is made of columns of living cells called **sieve tube elements** (sieve tubes), each with a smaller **companion cell** beside it. The end walls between sieve tube elements are not removed completely like in xylem; instead they form **sieve plates** full of pores.
bullets: **Sieve tube elements** are living cells joined end to end to form long tubes.
They have **very little cytoplasm** and **no nucleus**, leaving more space for the sap to flow.
**Sieve plates** are end walls with **pores** (holes), so the sap can pass from one cell to the next.
Each sieve tube element has a **companion cell** next to it, which has a nucleus and lots of **mitochondria**.
The companion cell keeps the sieve tube element alive and provides it with energy.
Phloem is found with xylem in the **vascular bundles** in roots, stems and leaf veins.

core.p: Translocation needs energy, mainly to **load sucrose into the sieve tubes** at the source, often against a concentration gradient. This energy comes from **respiration**, and that is why companion cells are packed with **mitochondria**, the site of aerobic respiration.
bullets: Mitochondria carry out **aerobic respiration**, releasing energy.
The energy is used by the companion cells to **actively transport sucrose** into the sieve tubes.
Sieve tube elements have lost most of their organelles, so they **depend on their companion cells** for energy.
If respiration is stopped (for example with a poison, low oxygen or low temperature), translocation slows or stops.
This is a key difference from xylem, where transport is passive and the cells are dead.

callouts.p: Translocation requires energy; companion cells contain many mitochondria, which release this energy by respiration.

core.p: A **source** is any part of the plant that releases sucrose into the phloem. A **sink** is any part that takes sucrose out of the phloem to use or store it. Sucrose always moves from source to sink, so the direction of flow depends on where these are at the time.
bullets: Main **source**: **photosynthesising leaves**.
**Storage organs** (such as potato tubers, carrot roots or bulbs) can be a **source in spring**, when stored starch is turned into sucrose to fuel new growth before leaves are open.
**Sinks**: growing tips of shoots (buds), **roots**, developing **fruits and seeds**, and storage organs being filled in summer.
Because sinks can be above (shoot tips, fruits) or below (roots) the source, sucrose moves **both upwards and downwards**.
A storage organ can switch from sink (summer, filling up) to source (spring, emptying).

head: Part of plant
Source or sink?
Why
rows: Makes glucose in photosynthesis, converted to sucrose
Growing: needs sugar for respiration and new cell walls
Cannot photosynthesise; needs sugar for respiration (e.g. active transport of ions)
Converting sucrose to starch for storage
Starch converted back to sucrose for new shoots

core.p: You can describe translocation as a sequence from the moment the sugar is made to when it is used.
bullets: 1. In the leaf, **glucose** is made by photosynthesis in the mesophyll cells.
2. Glucose is converted to **sucrose**.
3. Sucrose is **loaded into the sieve tubes** at the source using **energy** provided by the companion cells (active transport).
4. Water follows the sucrose into the phloem, and the sap **flows along the sieve tubes**, passing through the pores in the **sieve plates**.
5. At the sink, sucrose is **removed from the phloem** into the cells that need it.
6. The sucrose is converted back to glucose and used for respiration, or converted into starch, cellulose, proteins and other substances.

callouts.p: For long answers go: made where, converted to what, loaded how (energy, companion cells), carried where (phloem, sieve plates, both directions), used for what at the sink.

core.h: What happens to sucrose at the sink
core.p: Once sucrose reaches a sink it is turned back into glucose and used in many ways. This is why translocation matters: it supplies the raw material for almost everything the plant builds.
bullets: **Respiration**: releasing energy for processes such as active transport, cell division and growth.
**Starch**: an insoluble store, for example in potatoes, seeds and roots.
**Cellulose**: to build cell walls in growing regions.
**Amino acids and proteins**: glucose combined with **nitrate ions** absorbed from the soil.
**Lipids (fats and oils)**: stored in seeds.
**Sucrose** stored in fruits to make them sweet (attracting animals to spread seeds).

core.p: Edexcel often asks you to compare the two transport systems in a plant. The key is to remember that the **xylem** moves **water and mineral ions** upwards by the **transpiration stream**, while the **phloem** moves **sucrose** both ways by **translocation**.
bullets: Xylem cells are **dead**; phloem cells are **living**.
Xylem has **no end walls**; phloem has **sieve plates** with pores.
Xylem walls are thickened with **lignin**; phloem walls are not.
Transport in xylem is **passive** (driven by evaporation from the leaves); translocation **needs energy**.
Xylem flow is **upwards only**; phloem flow is **up and down**.

core.p: Scientists have collected evidence that sugars travel in the phloem. You may be given data from experiments like these and asked to interpret it.
bullets: **Aphids** feed by pushing their mouthparts into the phloem. If the aphid is cut off, the mouthparts keep oozing sap, and the sap contains **sucrose**.

**Ringing experiments**: removing a ring of bark (which contains the phloem but not the xylem) from a tree trunk causes the bark **above the ring to swell**, because sugar coming down from the leaves builds up there and cannot reach the roots.
In a ringed tree, leaves above stay healthy at first (xylem is intact, so they still get water), but the roots eventually die from lack of sugar.
**Radioactive carbon dioxide** given to a leaf is built into sugars, and the radioactivity is later found in the phloem and in sinks both above and below the leaf, showing two-way movement.

callouts.p: Swelling above the ring means sugar was moving down in the phloem. Leaves not wilting means water still moves up in the xylem, which was not removed.

core.p: Because translocation depends on living cells and respiration, anything that affects respiration in the phloem affects translocation. This lets you explain unfamiliar data at grade 9.
bullets: **Low temperature** slows enzyme-controlled respiration, so less energy is released and translocation slows.
**Lack of oxygen** reduces aerobic respiration in companion cells, so loading of sucrose slows.
**Respiratory poisons** stop translocation, but do not stop water moving in the xylem.
**Less light** means less photosynthesis, so less sucrose is available at the source to be transported.
**Damage to phloem** (ringing, aphids, disease) reduces how much sucrose reaches the sinks, so growth of roots and fruits suffers.

core.h: Why translocation matters to the whole plant
core.p: Without translocation, only the green parts of a plant would get sugar. Every non-photosynthetic tissue depends on the phloem.
bullets: **Roots** need sugar for respiration, which provides the energy for **active transport of mineral ions** from the soil.
Growing regions need sugar to make **cellulose** for new cell walls.
Seeds and fruits need stored food so the next generation can grow.
Storage organs let the plant survive winter and **regrow quickly in spring** using stored food.
So translocation links photosynthesis in the leaves to growth everywhere else.

analogy.p: Think of the phloem as a delivery network: the leaves are factories (sources) that make the product (sucrose), and the roots, shoot tips and fruits are shops (sinks) that use or store it. The sieve tubes are the roads, the sieve plates are toll gates with several lanes (pores), and the companion cells are the depots with fuel tanks (mitochondria) that supply the energy to load the lorries. Lorries can drive both up and down the roads, depending on where the shops are. Where it breaks down: real delivery lorries carry separate packages and use their own fuel all the way, whereas in the phloem the sucrose flows as a dissolved solution, and energy is mainly used to load it, not to push each molecule along. Also, a factory never becomes a shop, but a potato tuber switches from sink to source.

terms.d: The movement of sucrose (dissolved food molecules) through the phloem from sources to sinks.
Living tissue made of sieve tube elements and companion cells that transports sucrose and other dissolved food around the plant.
A soluble sugar made from glucose in the leaves; the main form in which sugar is transported in the phloem.
A living phloem cell with little cytoplasm and no nucleus, joined end to end with others to form a sieve tube.
The end wall between sieve tube elements, containing pores that let the sap flow from cell to cell.
A cell next to each sieve tube element, with a nucleus and many mitochondria, that supplies the energy for translocation.
Organelles where aerobic respiration happens, releasing energy; abundant in companion cells.
Part of a plant where sucrose is made or released into the phloem, such as a photosynthesising leaf.
Part of a plant where sucrose is used or stored, such as roots, growing tips, fruits and storage organs.
The solution of sucrose and other dissolved substances in water that flows in the sieve tubes.
Movement of substances against a concentration gradient using energy from respiration; used to load sucrose into sieve tubes.
An insoluble storage carbohydrate made from glucose; stored at sinks but not transported.
A part of the plant, such as a tuber or bulb, that stores food; a sink in summer and a source in spring.
A group of xylem and phloem tissues found together in roots, stems and leaf veins.
Removing a ring of bark (and so phloem) from a stem, used as evidence that sugars travel down in the phloem.

mistakes.w: The phloem carries glucose.
mistakes.r: The phloem carries sucrose; glucose is converted to sucrose before transport.

mistakes.w: Translocation moves water and minerals up the plant.
mistakes.r: That is the transpiration stream in the xylem; translocation moves sucrose in the phloem.

mistakes.w: Phloem only carries sugar downwards from the leaves to the roots.
mistakes.r: Phloem carries sucrose both up and down, from sources to sinks (e.g. up to shoot tips and fruits, down to roots).

mistakes.w: Phloem cells are dead like xylem.
mistakes.r: Phloem is made of living cells: sieve tube elements and companion cells.

mistakes.w: Companion cells have mitochondria to make sugar.
mistakes.r: Mitochondria carry out respiration to release energy for translocation (loading sucrose); sugar is made by photosynthesis in chloroplasts.

mistakes.w: Translocation does not need energy because it flows like water in the xylem.
mistakes.r: Translocation is an active process that requires energy from respiration.

mistakes.w: Sieve plates block the phloem.
mistakes.r: Sieve plates contain pores which allow the sap to pass from one sieve tube element to the next.

mistakes.w: The roots are a source because they store food.
mistakes.r: Roots are usually a sink; a storage organ is only a source when it releases stored sugar, e.g. in spring.

exam.q: Name the process by which sucrose is transported around a plant.
model: Translocation
exam.tip: Do not write transpiration: they are easy to mix up.

exam.q: Name the tissue that transports sucrose.
model: Phloem
exam.tip: One word answer; spell it correctly.

exam.q: Give two parts of a plant that act as sinks for sucrose.
model: Roots
Growing tips / buds / shoots
Fruits / seeds
Storage organs (e.g. tubers) in summer
exam.tip: Any two sensible sinks.

exam.q: Explain why companion cells contain many mitochondria.
model: To carry out (aerobic) respiration to release energy
Energy needed for translocation / to load sucrose into the sieve tubes (active transport)
exam.tip: Link mitochondria to respiration and then to translocation.

exam.q: Explain why sucrose in the phloem can move both up and down the stem.
model: Sucrose moves from source to sink
Sinks can be above (shoot tips, fruits) or below (roots) the source / leaves
exam.tip: Always use the words source and sink.

exam.q: Describe how the structure of phloem is adapted for translocation.
model: Sieve tube elements have little cytoplasm / no nucleus, so more room for flow
Sieve plates have pores so sap can pass between cells
Companion cells have many mitochondria to provide energy
exam.tip: Give each feature and say how it helps.

exam.q: Give three differences between transport in the xylem and transport in the phloem.
model: Xylem carries water and mineral ions; phloem carries sucrose
Xylem one direction (up); phloem both directions
Xylem passive / no energy; phloem needs energy
Xylem dead cells; phloem living cells
exam.tip: Write each difference as a matched pair: xylem ... whereas phloem ...

exam.q: A ring of bark containing the phloem was removed from a tree trunk. After some weeks the bark just above the ring had swollen. Explain this observation.
model: Phloem removed so sucrose cannot pass the ring
Sucrose is translocated down from the leaves
So sucrose builds up above the ring, causing swelling (more growth/storage)
exam.tip: Say what was removed, which way sugar flows, and why it builds up.

exam.q: In spring, a potato tuber acts as a source, but in summer it acts as a sink. Explain this.
model: In spring, stored starch is converted to sucrose
Sucrose is transported to new shoots/leaves for growth (source)
In summer, sucrose from leaves is transported to the tuber and stored as starch (sink)
exam.tip: Source = releases sucrose; sink = receives and uses or stores it.

exam.q: A respiratory poison was added to the roots of a plant. Predict and explain the effect on translocation to the roots.
model: Translocation would slow / stop
Less respiration so less energy to move/unload sucrose (translocation needs energy)
exam.tip: Respiration links to energy which links to translocation.

exam.q: Explain how sugars made in the leaves of a plant reach the roots and are used there.
model: Glucose made by photosynthesis in leaf (mesophyll) cells
Glucose converted to sucrose (soluble) for transport
Sucrose loaded into phloem / sieve tubes at the source using energy
Energy from respiration in mitochondria of companion cells
Sucrose solution flows through sieve tubes, through pores in sieve plates, down to roots (sink)
This is translocation
In the roots sucrose is converted back to glucose for respiration
Energy used for active transport of mineral ions / or stored as starch
exam.tip: Level-marked: follow the sugar from leaf to root in order, using correct terms throughout.

worked.q: Model answer: Explain why translocation requires energy but the movement of water in the xylem does not.
steps: State that translocation is the active movement of sucrose in living phloem cells.
Explain that sucrose is loaded into the sieve tubes by active transport, which needs energy.
Link energy to respiration in the many mitochondria of the companion cells.
Contrast with xylem: water is pulled up by the transpiration pull, caused by evaporation from the leaves.
The energy for evaporation comes from the Sun, and xylem cells are dead, so no respiration is involved.
worked.ans: Translocation needs energy from respiration in companion cells to load sucrose into living sieve tubes, whereas water in dead xylem is pulled up passively by evaporation from the leaves.

worked.q: Applied example: Radioactive carbon dioxide (containing carbon-14) was supplied to one leaf halfway up a bean plant. After 3 hours radioactivity was found in the shoot tip, the developing pods and the roots, but not in the other mature leaves. Explain these results.
steps: The leaf used the carbon dioxide in photosynthesis, so the carbon-14 ended up in glucose and then sucrose.
The sucrose was translocated in the phloem away from the leaf (the source).
Radioactivity appeared above the leaf (shoot tip, pods) and below it (roots), so translocation went both up and down.
Shoot tip, pods and roots are sinks: they use sucrose for growth, respiration or storage.
Other mature leaves are sources themselves (they make their own sugar), so they do not take in sucrose.
worked.ans: Sucrose containing carbon-14 was translocated in the phloem in both directions from the source leaf to the sinks (shoot tip, pods, roots); mature leaves are sources, so they received none.

worked.q: Applied example: An aphid feeding on a stem is anaesthetised and its body cut away, leaving its mouthparts in the stem. Sap drips from the mouthparts. Suggest what this shows and what the sap would contain.
steps: Aphids feed from the phloem, so the mouthparts are inserted into a sieve tube.
Sap continues to flow out, showing the contents of the sieve tubes are moving under pressure.
Analysis of the sap would show it contains sucrose dissolved in water (plus amino acids).
This is evidence that sucrose is transported in the phloem.
worked.ans: It shows that phloem sieve tubes contain a flowing solution; the sap contains dissolved sucrose (and amino acids), evidence that sucrose is translocated in the phloem.

bio_edx.5.8.summary: A leaf is an organ built for two linked jobs: **absorbing light for photosynthesis** and **exchanging gases** (carbon dioxide in, oxygen and water vapour out). Every layer has a feature that helps: a **transparent waxy cuticle and epidermis** let light through, the **palisade mesophyll** is packed with **chloroplasts** near the top surface, the **spongy mesophyll** has **air spaces** for diffusion, **stomata** controlled by **guard cells** let gases in and out, and **xylem and phloem** in the veins bring water and take away sugar. Being **broad, flat and thin** gives a large surface area and a short diffusion distance.

core.p: A leaf is a **plant organ**: a group of different **tissues** working together. Its main function is **photosynthesis**, which needs light, carbon dioxide and water, and makes glucose and oxygen. This means the leaf also has to be good at **gas exchange**. Edexcel expects you to explain how each part of the leaf's structure helps with these jobs.
bullets: Word equation: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen (light energy absorbed by chlorophyll).
Raw materials reach the leaf in two ways: **carbon dioxide** from the air by diffusion through stomata; **water** from the roots via the xylem.
Products leave in two ways: **oxygen** by diffusion out of the stomata; **glucose** converted to sucrose and carried away in the phloem.
The tissues, from top to bottom: waxy cuticle, upper epidermis, palisade mesophyll, spongy mesophyll (with vascular bundles), lower epidermis with stomata, waxy cuticle.

callouts.p: For every feature give: the feature, what it does, and how that increases the rate of photosynthesis or gas exchange.

fig.cap: Cross-section of a leaf. From top to bottom: waxy cuticle, upper epidermis, palisade mesophyll packed with chloroplasts, spongy mesophyll with air spaces and a vascular bundle (xylem above, phloem below), and the lower epidermis with a stoma between two guard cells.

core.p: The overall shape of a leaf is the first adaptation. A **broad, flat** shape gives a **large surface area** to absorb light and to exchange gases. Being **thin** means a **short diffusion distance**, so carbon dioxide does not have far to travel from the stomata to the cells that photosynthesise.
bullets: **Large surface area** exposed to light, so more light is absorbed and the rate of photosynthesis is higher.
**Large surface area** for gas exchange, so more carbon dioxide can diffuse in.
**Thin**: most cells are close to the surface and to an air space, so diffusion is fast.
Leaves are often arranged on the stem so they **do not shade each other** (a mosaic pattern).
The **petiole** (leaf stalk) and stem can turn the blade to face the light.

core.p: The **waxy cuticle** is a thin, non-living layer of wax on the outside of the epidermis. It is **waterproof** and **transparent**.
bullets: **Waterproof**: reduces water loss by evaporation from the leaf surface, so the leaf does not dry out.
**Transparent**: lets light pass straight through to the photosynthesising cells below.
It is usually **thicker on the upper surface**, which gets more direct sunlight and heat.
Because the cuticle is almost gas-tight, gases must enter and leave mainly through the **stomata**.

callouts.t: Do not say it stops photosynthesis gases
callouts.p: The cuticle reduces water loss; it does not take part in gas exchange. That is the job of the stomata.

core.p: The **upper epidermis** is a single layer of tightly packed cells that covers and protects the top of the leaf. Its cells are **transparent** and have **no chloroplasts**.
bullets: **No chloroplasts and transparent**, so light passes through to the palisade layer without being absorbed.
**Single layer** of cells, so it is thin and light does not have far to travel.
Tightly packed cells and the cuticle form a **protective barrier** against pathogens and water loss.
The upper epidermis has **few or no stomata** in most plants, which reduces water loss from the sunny side.

core.p: The **palisade mesophyll** is the main site of photosynthesis. Its cells are tall, column-shaped and packed with **chloroplasts**, which contain **chlorophyll** to absorb light.
bullets: **Near the upper surface**, so the cells receive the most light.
**Many chloroplasts** in each cell, so more light is absorbed and the rate of photosynthesis is high.
**Tall, thin, column shape** and **tightly packed** side by side: many cells fit under each area of leaf surface, so as much light as possible is captured.
Chloroplasts are often near the edges of the cells, with a large **vacuole** in the middle pushing them out towards the light.
Narrow gaps between the cells connect to the air spaces, so carbon dioxide can reach them.

fig.cap: A palisade mesophyll cell. It is tall and column shaped, packed with chloroplasts for absorbing light, with a cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus and a large central vacuole that keeps the chloroplasts near the edge of the cell.

core.p: Below the palisade layer is the **spongy mesophyll**, made of loosely packed, irregular cells with large **air spaces** between them. It is the main site of **gas exchange** inside the leaf.
bullets: **Air spaces** let carbon dioxide **diffuse** from the stomata to all the mesophyll cells quickly.
Air spaces give a **very large internal surface area** for gases to dissolve into and out of the cells.
Cell surfaces are **moist**, so gases dissolve before diffusing into the cells.
Spongy mesophyll cells contain **some chloroplasts** (fewer than palisade cells), so they also photosynthesise.
Water also evaporates from these cell surfaces into the air spaces, which is the first step of transpiration.

callouts.p: The net movement of particles from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration.

core.h: Lower epidermis, stomata and guard cells
core.p: The **lower epidermis** contains most of the **stomata**. Each stoma is a pore surrounded by two **guard cells**, which control its size. Gases enter and leave the leaf mainly through these pores.
bullets: **Stomata allow carbon dioxide to diffuse in** for photosynthesis, and **oxygen and water vapour to diffuse out**.
**Guard cells** become **turgid** (take in water) and curve apart to **open** the stoma, and become **flaccid** to **close** it.
Stomata **open in the light** when carbon dioxide is needed, and **close in the dark** or when water is short, reducing water loss.
Most stomata are on the **lower surface**, which is shaded and cooler, so less water is lost by evaporation.
Many stomata are spread over the lower surface so no cell is far from a source of carbon dioxide.
Guard cells are the only epidermis cells with **chloroplasts**.

core.p: Gas exchange is driven by **diffusion down concentration gradients** that photosynthesis and respiration create. In the light, photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide faster than respiration makes it, so carbon dioxide concentration inside the leaf is **lower** than outside and it diffuses **in**. Oxygen is made faster than it is used, so it diffuses **out**.
bullets: Path of carbon dioxide: air outside → **stoma** → **air spaces** → dissolves on moist surfaces of **mesophyll cells** → chloroplasts.
Path of oxygen: chloroplasts → mesophyll cell → air spaces → stoma → air.
Water vapour also diffuses out through the stomata (transpiration).
In the **dark**, only respiration happens: oxygen diffuses in and carbon dioxide diffuses out, but slowly because most stomata are closed.
Photosynthesis keeps the carbon dioxide concentration low inside, so a **steep concentration gradient** is maintained.

core.p: The **veins** are **vascular bundles** containing **xylem** and **phloem**. A dense network of veins runs through the leaf so no cell is far from a supply of water or a route for removing sugar.
bullets: **Xylem** brings **water** (a raw material for photosynthesis) and **mineral ions** such as magnesium (needed to make chlorophyll).
Water from the xylem also keeps the mesophyll cells **turgid**, which helps support the leaf so it is held out flat to the light.
**Phloem** carries the **sucrose** made from glucose away from the leaf to the rest of the plant (translocation).
Removing sugar stops it building up in the leaf cells.
The vascular bundles, especially the **midrib**, also give the leaf some **support**.

core.p: Use this table to revise: for each feature, learn the function and the reason it increases the rate of photosynthesis.
bullets: Light reaches the chloroplasts: transparent cuticle and epidermis, palisade near the top.
Light is absorbed: many chloroplasts containing chlorophyll, large surface area.
Carbon dioxide is supplied: stomata, air spaces, thin leaf.
Water is supplied and sugar removed: xylem and phloem in veins.

core.h: The compromise: gas exchange versus water loss
core.p: The features that make a leaf good at gas exchange (large surface area, many stomata, moist air spaces) also make it lose water. A grade 9 answer shows you understand this trade-off.
bullets: Open stomata let carbon dioxide in, but water vapour diffuses out at the same time.
The **waxy cuticle**, **stomata mostly on the lower surface** and the **ability to close stomata** reduce water loss.
When stomata close to save water, carbon dioxide uptake falls and **carbon dioxide can become a limiting factor** for photosynthesis.
Plants in dry habitats have extra features such as thicker cuticles, fewer stomata or smaller leaves (covered in 6.14B).

callouts.p: Describe = say what the feature is. Explain = say what it is AND how it increases photosynthesis or gas exchange. Most leaf questions say explain.

analogy.p: A leaf is like a flat, solar-powered factory. The glass roof (transparent cuticle and upper epidermis) lets sunlight in but keeps the rain out (waterproof). The top floor is packed with solar panels (chloroplasts in the palisade layer) where the light is brightest. Below is a ventilated warehouse with open corridors (spongy mesophyll and air spaces) so delivery of carbon dioxide reaches every worker. The loading-bay doors on the underside (stomata) open and close under the control of doormen (guard cells), letting carbon dioxide in and oxygen out. Pipes (xylem) bring in water and conveyor belts (phloem) carry the finished sugar away. Where it breaks down: a real factory decides what to make, but a leaf has no control centre; and factory doors do not leak water, whereas every open stoma loses water vapour, so the leaf must constantly balance gas exchange against drying out.

terms.d: A transparent, waterproof layer of wax covering the epidermis that reduces water loss.
A single layer of transparent cells with no chloroplasts that protects the top of the leaf and lets light through.
Layer of tall, tightly packed cells with many chloroplasts near the top of the leaf; the main site of photosynthesis.
Layer of loosely packed cells with air spaces between them, allowing gases to diffuse through the leaf.
Gaps between spongy mesophyll cells that give a large surface area and allow gases to diffuse quickly to and from cells.
Organelle containing chlorophyll where photosynthesis takes place.
Green pigment in chloroplasts that absorbs light energy for photosynthesis.
Pore in the leaf epidermis, mostly in the lower surface, through which carbon dioxide diffuses in and oxygen and water vapour diffuse out.
Pair of cells around each stoma that open it when turgid and close it when flaccid.
Single layer of cells on the underside of the leaf containing most of the stomata.
Group of xylem and phloem tissues that supplies the leaf with water and removes sugars.
Tissue that transports water and mineral ions from the roots to the leaves.
Tissue that transports sucrose from the leaves to other parts of the plant.
Movement of gases (carbon dioxide and oxygen) between the leaf and the air by diffusion.
How far molecules have to travel by diffusion; a thin leaf keeps this short, so diffusion is faster.
The total area of exposed surface; a large area allows more light to be absorbed and more gas exchange.

mistakes.w: The waxy cuticle helps photosynthesis by absorbing light.
mistakes.r: The cuticle is transparent, so light passes through it; it is waterproof and reduces water loss.

mistakes.w: The upper epidermis has lots of chloroplasts.
mistakes.r: The upper epidermis is transparent with no chloroplasts, so light passes through to the palisade mesophyll.

mistakes.w: The palisade layer is at the bottom of the leaf.
mistakes.r: Palisade mesophyll is near the upper surface, where it receives the most light.

mistakes.w: Air spaces store oxygen for the plant.
mistakes.r: Air spaces allow gases (carbon dioxide in, oxygen out) to diffuse quickly to and from the mesophyll cells and give a large surface area.

mistakes.w: Stomata let in oxygen for photosynthesis.
mistakes.r: Stomata let carbon dioxide diffuse in for photosynthesis; oxygen diffuses out.

mistakes.w: A thin leaf means it is light and easy to hold up.
mistakes.r: A thin leaf gives a short diffusion distance, so carbon dioxide reaches the mesophyll cells quickly.

mistakes.w: Leaves have a big surface area so they can make more glucose.
mistakes.r: A large surface area absorbs more light and allows more carbon dioxide to diffuse in, so the rate of photosynthesis increases.

mistakes.w: The xylem in the leaf carries glucose away.
mistakes.r: Xylem brings water and mineral ions into the leaf; phloem carries sucrose away.

mistakes.w: Most stomata are on the top so they get more light.
mistakes.r: Most stomata are on the lower surface, which is cooler and shaded, so less water is lost.

exam.q: Name the layer of a leaf where most photosynthesis takes place.
model: Palisade mesophyll
exam.tip: Write palisade mesophyll, not just mesophyll.

exam.q: State the function of the stomata.
model: Allow gases (carbon dioxide/oxygen/water vapour) to diffuse into and out of the leaf
exam.tip: Name a gas and its direction for a safe mark.

exam.q: Explain why the upper epidermis of a leaf is transparent.
model: Allows light to pass through
To reach the palisade mesophyll / chloroplasts for photosynthesis
exam.tip: Link transparency to light reaching chloroplasts.

exam.q: Explain how the palisade mesophyll cells are adapted for photosynthesis.
model: Contain many chloroplasts
To absorb more light
Near the upper surface / tightly packed / column shaped to receive most light
exam.tip: Feature then reason, twice or more.

exam.q: Explain how the spongy mesophyll is adapted for gas exchange.
model: Air spaces between cells
Allow carbon dioxide to diffuse quickly to cells / large surface area for gas exchange
exam.tip: Mention air spaces and diffusion.

exam.q: Explain how the waxy cuticle helps the leaf.
model: Waterproof, so reduces water loss / evaporation
Transparent so light can pass through
exam.tip: Two separate properties, two marks.

exam.q: Explain why leaves are broad and thin.
model: Broad: large surface area to absorb light / for gas exchange
Thin: short diffusion distance for carbon dioxide (to reach mesophyll cells)
exam.tip: One mark for each shape feature with its reason.

exam.q: Describe the route taken by a carbon dioxide molecule from the air to a chloroplast in a palisade cell.
model: Diffuses in through a stoma
Through the air spaces in the spongy mesophyll
Dissolves in moisture on the cell surface / diffuses into palisade cell to chloroplast
exam.tip: Name every structure in order and use the word diffuses.

exam.q: Explain why the concentration of carbon dioxide in the air spaces of a leaf is lower in the light than in the dark.
model: In the light, photosynthesis takes place
Carbon dioxide is used faster than respiration produces it
In the dark only respiration occurs, producing carbon dioxide
exam.tip: Compare photosynthesis and respiration rates.

exam.q: Explain why the veins of a leaf branch to form a dense network.
model: Xylem delivers water/mineral ions close to every cell for photosynthesis
Phloem removes sucrose from every cell / short distance for transport
exam.tip: Mention both xylem and phloem roles.

exam.q: Explain how the structure of a leaf is adapted for photosynthesis and gas exchange.
model: Broad / flat: large surface area to absorb light
Thin: short diffusion distance for gases
Transparent cuticle and epidermis let light through
Palisade mesophyll near top with many chloroplasts to absorb light
Spongy mesophyll with air spaces for diffusion of carbon dioxide / large surface area
Stomata allow carbon dioxide in and oxygen out
Guard cells open/close stomata to control gas exchange and water loss
Xylem supplies water; phloem removes sucrose
exam.tip: Level-marked: cover both photosynthesis (light) and gas exchange (diffusion) features, each with a reason.

worked.q: Model answer: Explain why most chloroplasts in a leaf are found in the palisade mesophyll rather than the spongy mesophyll.
steps: State where the palisade layer is: near the upper surface of the leaf.
Explain that light enters from above, through the transparent cuticle and upper epidermis.
So the palisade cells receive the most light, and having many chloroplasts there absorbs as much light as possible.
Spongy mesophyll is lower down, where much of the light has already been absorbed, so fewer chloroplasts are needed.
Spongy mesophyll is instead adapted for gas exchange, with air spaces.
worked.ans: Palisade cells are nearest the upper surface and receive the most light, so packing chloroplasts there maximises light absorption and the rate of photosynthesis; the spongy layer gets less light and is specialised for gas exchange instead.

worked.q: Applied example: A student counts stomata in the same area of leaf surface. Upper surface: 3 stomata per field of view. Lower surface: 45 stomata per field of view. Calculate the ratio of lower to upper stomata and explain the difference.
steps: Ratio lower : upper = 45 : 3.
Divide both by 3: 15 : 1.
So there are 15 times as many stomata on the lower surface.
The lower surface is shaded and cooler, so less water evaporates and diffuses out through stomata there.
Having stomata on the lower surface still allows carbon dioxide to diffuse in, but reduces water loss.
worked.ans: Ratio 15 : 1; the lower surface has more stomata because it is cooler and shaded, so gas exchange can happen with less water loss by transpiration.

worked.q: Applied example: Plant A has leaves 0.2 mm thick. Plant B has leaves 0.8 mm thick. Suggest which plant would have the faster supply of carbon dioxide to its mesophyll cells, and explain why.
steps: Carbon dioxide reaches the mesophyll cells by diffusion from the stomata.
The rate of diffusion is faster when the diffusion distance is shorter.
Leaf A is 4 times thinner (0.8 / 0.2 = 4), so the distance from stomata to cells is much shorter.
So carbon dioxide reaches cells in leaf A faster, supporting a higher rate of photosynthesis (if other factors are not limiting).
worked.ans: Plant A, because its thinner leaf gives a shorter diffusion distance, so carbon dioxide diffuses to the mesophyll cells faster.

bio_edx.5.9.summary: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from leaves through the stomata, and its rate is measured as the rate of water uptake using a potometer. Increasing light intensity, temperature and air movement all increase the rate, while higher humidity decreases it. You must explain each effect using stomata, kinetic energy and the concentration gradient, and calculate rates from bubble movement, tube volume and graph gradients.

core.p: You must be able to **explain how light intensity, air movement and temperature affect the rate of transpiration**, measured as the rate of water uptake, and you must be able to **calculate transpiration rate** from potometer readings and graphs.
bullets: The three named factors are **light intensity**, **air movement (wind)** and **temperature**.
**Humidity** is also a key factor and often appears in exam questions alongside the three named factors.
Rate calculations: rate = volume (or distance) of water taken up divided by time.
You may need to convert units, calculate volume from bubble movement in a capillary tube, or use a graph gradient.
Links back to 6.9: transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the leaves, mainly through the **stomata**.

callouts.p: The loss of water vapour from the leaves (and stems) of a plant by evaporation and diffusion, mainly through the stomata.

core.h: Why water uptake is used to measure transpiration
core.p: It is hard to measure water vapour leaving a leaf directly, so we measure how fast the shoot **takes up water** instead. Almost all water taken up replaces water lost by transpiration, so the two rates are very close.
bullets: Water lost from leaves pulls more water up the **xylem** in a continuous column (the **transpiration stream**).
So rate of water uptake is approximately equal to rate of transpiration.
It is not exactly equal: a small amount of water is used in **photosynthesis** and to keep cells **turgid**.
This is why a potometer measures **water uptake**, not transpiration directly.

callouts.p: In a 'evaluate' question, say a potometer measures water uptake; some water is used for photosynthesis and turgor, so it slightly overestimates water lost.

core.p: Water **evaporates** from the surfaces of mesophyll cells into the air spaces inside the leaf. Water vapour then **diffuses** out through open stomata, from a high concentration inside the leaf to a lower concentration in the air outside.
bullets: Two steps: **evaporation** (liquid to gas) then **diffusion** of water vapour.
The steeper the **concentration gradient** of water vapour between the air spaces and the outside air, the faster diffusion happens.
Stomata must be **open** for most water loss; guard cells control the size of the opening.
Any factor that speeds evaporation, steepens the gradient, or opens stomata increases transpiration rate.

core.p: As light intensity increases, **more stomata open** (and they open wider) so that more carbon dioxide can diffuse in for photosynthesis. Open stomata also let more water vapour diffuse out, so the rate of transpiration increases.
bullets: Brighter light means guard cells open the stomata so CO2 can enter for **photosynthesis**.
More or wider stomata gives a larger area for water vapour to **diffuse out**.
So transpiration rate **increases** with light intensity.
At high light intensity the rate **levels off** because all the stomata are already fully open; another factor now limits the rate.
In the dark, most stomata **close**, so transpiration is very slow.

callouts.p: More light, more stomata open, more water vapour diffuses out, faster transpiration, faster water uptake.

core.p: As temperature rises, water molecules gain **kinetic energy** and move faster. This increases the rate of **evaporation** from mesophyll cell surfaces and the rate of **diffusion** of water vapour out of the stomata.
bullets: Higher temperature means more **kinetic energy** for water molecules.
Water **evaporates** faster into the air spaces.
Water vapour **diffuses** out of the stomata faster.
Warm air can also hold more water vapour, which helps keep the concentration gradient steep.
So transpiration rate **increases** with temperature.
Very high temperatures can cause stomata to close to reduce water loss, if the plant starts to wilt.

callouts.p: Use the phrase 'water molecules have more kinetic energy' for the temperature mark. 'Water evaporates faster' alone often only gets one mark.

core.p: Moving air **blows away water vapour** that has just diffused out of the leaf. This keeps the concentration of water vapour just outside the stomata low, maintaining a **steep concentration gradient**, so diffusion is faster.
bullets: In still air, a layer of humid air builds up around the leaf.
This makes the concentration gradient **shallower**, so diffusion slows down.
Wind removes this humid layer, so the gradient stays **steep**.
So transpiration rate **increases** as air movement increases.
In the lab, air movement is changed using a **fan** at different distances or speeds.

callouts.p: Say wind removes water vapour from around the leaf, keeping a steep concentration gradient. Never say wind pulls or sucks water out.

core.p: Humidity is the amount of water vapour in the air. In **humid** air the concentration of water vapour outside the leaf is already high, so the concentration gradient is **shallow** and diffusion is slower.
bullets: Higher humidity gives a **lower** transpiration rate.
Dry air gives a steep gradient and a **higher** rate.
In the lab, humidity can be raised by putting a **clear plastic bag** over the shoot.
Humidity is the only common factor that **decreases** transpiration as it increases.

core.p: Learn the factor, the effect and the reason as a set; exam marks are usually one for the effect and one or two for the explanation.
bullets: Always state the **direction** of the change (increases or decreases).
Always give the **reason** linked to stomata, evaporation or the concentration gradient.

head: Factor increased
Effect on rate
Reason
rows: More stomata open, so more water vapour can diffuse out
Water molecules have more kinetic energy, so faster evaporation and diffusion
Water vapour blown away, keeping a steep concentration gradient
More water vapour in the air, so shallower concentration gradient

core.p: A **potometer** measures the rate of water uptake by a leafy shoot. As the shoot takes up water, an **air bubble** moves along a **capillary tube** against a scale. The distance moved in a set time gives the rate.
bullets: Cut the shoot **under water** and at a slant, so no air enters the xylem and blocks the water column.
Assemble the apparatus **under water** and make sure it is **airtight** (seal joints with petroleum jelly).
Dry the leaves gently, because wet leaves give a lower rate at first.
Introduce one air bubble by lifting the capillary end out of the water briefly.
Leave the shoot to **acclimatise** for a few minutes before taking readings.
Record the distance the bubble moves in a fixed time, for example 5 minutes.
Use the **reservoir and tap** to push the bubble back to the start between readings.
Repeat each condition and calculate a mean.

callouts.p: When testing one factor, keep the others the same: same shoot, same temperature, same light intensity, same air movement, same humidity, same time.

core.h: Changing each factor in a potometer experiment
core.p: Only one factor (the independent variable) is changed at a time; the distance the bubble moves per minute is the dependent variable.
bullets: **Light intensity**: move a lamp to different distances from the shoot; use a heat filter or water tank so temperature does not change.
**Temperature**: place the potometer in rooms or water baths at different temperatures, or use a heater; monitor with a thermometer.
**Air movement**: use a fan at different speed settings or distances.
**Humidity**: cover the shoot with a plastic bag, or spray water inside the bag.
Plot the rate against the factor on a line graph.
