core.p: Rate is always **amount divided by time**. For a potometer the amount can be the **distance** the bubble moves or the **volume** of water taken up.
bullets: **rate = distance moved by bubble / time** (units such as mm per min).
**rate = volume of water taken up / time** (units such as mm3 per min or cm3 per hour).
Volume taken up in a capillary tube = cross-sectional area x distance moved.
Cross-sectional area of a tube = pi x r squared (r = radius = diameter / 2).
Convert units first: 1 cm = 10 mm; 1 cm3 = 1000 mm3; 1 hour = 60 minutes.
To compare shoots of different size, divide by leaf **surface area** (rate per cm2 of leaf).
Percentage change = (new - original) / original x 100.

callouts.p: rate = distance / time; volume = pi x r squared x length; rate = volume / time.

core.p: If a graph shows total volume of water taken up against time, the **rate is the gradient** of the line.
bullets: Gradient = change in y / change in x.
For a straight line, pick two points far apart for accuracy.
For a curve, draw a **tangent** at the time asked and find its gradient (Higher).
A steeper line means a faster rate of water uptake.
A line that flattens means the rate is slowing, for example as stomata close at night.

callouts.p: Check whether the graph shows total volume (use the gradient) or rate (read the value directly).

core.h: Evaluating results and sources of error
core.p: Grade 9 answers can explain why potometer results may be inaccurate and how to improve them.
bullets: Air leaks or air in the xylem give falsely low or no readings, so cut under water and seal joints.
Not all water taken up is transpired; some is used in photosynthesis and for turgor.
Changing light with a lamp also changes temperature unless a heat shield is used.
Different shoots have different leaf areas and numbers of stomata, so use the same shoot or work out rate per unit leaf area.
Repeat readings, remove anomalies and calculate a mean to improve **reliability**.

analogy.p: Leaves lose water like wet washing drying. On a warm day (temperature) the water evaporates faster; on a windy day the damp air is blown away so it dries faster; on a humid day the air is already damp so it dries slowly. Light is like unpegging the washing so more of it is exposed, as light opens more stomata. Where it breaks down: washing loses water from its whole surface, but a leaf loses most water through stomata it can open and close, and the plant replaces the lost water from the xylem.

terms.d: Loss of water vapour from a plant's leaves by evaporation and diffusion, mainly through the stomata.
The continuous movement of water from the roots, up the xylem, to the leaves, where it is lost by transpiration.
Pores, mainly on the underside of leaves, that allow gas exchange and water vapour loss.
Pairs of cells that surround each stoma and change shape to open or close it.
Apparatus used to measure the rate of water uptake by a leafy shoot.
A narrow tube in a potometer along which the air bubble moves as water is taken up.
The change of liquid water into water vapour, here from the surfaces of mesophyll cells.
Net movement of particles from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration.
The difference in concentration between two areas; a steeper gradient gives faster diffusion.
The amount of water vapour in the air.
Energy of movement; molecules move faster when they have more.
The amount of light energy reaching a given area; affects how many stomata are open.
How much of something happens per unit time, such as mm of bubble movement per minute.
Change in y divided by change in x on a graph; gives the rate when y is total volume and x is time.
Area of the circular end of a tube, equal to pi x r squared.
Tissue of dead, hollow, lignified cells that carries water and mineral ions from roots to leaves.

mistakes.w: Light makes the plant photosynthesise more so it uses more water, so transpiration increases.
mistakes.r: More light causes more stomata to open, so more water vapour diffuses out of the leaf.

mistakes.w: Wind sucks the water out of the leaves.
mistakes.r: Wind removes water vapour from around the leaf, maintaining a steep concentration gradient, so water vapour diffuses out faster.

mistakes.w: Heat makes the water evaporate.
mistakes.r: Water molecules gain more kinetic energy, so evaporation and diffusion of water vapour are faster.

mistakes.w: Humidity increases transpiration.
mistakes.r: Higher humidity decreases transpiration because the concentration gradient of water vapour is shallower.

mistakes.w: A potometer measures transpiration exactly.
mistakes.r: A potometer measures water uptake; some water is used in photosynthesis and to keep cells turgid.

mistakes.w: Rate = time / distance.
mistakes.r: Rate = distance (or volume) / time.

mistakes.w: Using diameter instead of radius in pi r squared.
mistakes.r: Halve the diameter to get the radius before squaring.

mistakes.w: Water leaves the leaf through the xylem.
mistakes.r: Water vapour leaves through the stomata; xylem carries water up to the leaf.

mistakes.w: Forgetting units or mixing mm and cm in calculations.
mistakes.r: Convert all values to the same units first and give units with the answer, e.g. mm3 per min.

exam.q: State what is meant by transpiration.
model: Loss of water vapour from leaves / through stomata (by evaporation and diffusion).
exam.tip: Say water vapour, not just water.

exam.q: Name the apparatus used to measure the rate of water uptake by a plant shoot.
model: Potometer.
exam.tip: Spell it correctly; it is a common one mark question.

exam.q: Explain why a potometer measures water uptake rather than the rate of transpiration.
model: Some water taken up is used by the plant / not all water is lost.
For photosynthesis / to keep cells turgid.
exam.tip: Two marks: the idea of water being used, plus a named use.

exam.q: Explain how an increase in temperature affects the rate of transpiration.
model: Rate of transpiration increases.
Water molecules have more kinetic energy.
Faster evaporation from cells / faster diffusion of water vapour out of stomata.
exam.tip: State the effect first, then the kinetic energy reason.

exam.q: Explain why the rate of transpiration increases when a fan is switched on near a plant.
model: Water vapour is removed from around the leaf / stomata.
Maintains a steep concentration gradient so faster diffusion of water vapour.
exam.tip: Use the phrase 'concentration gradient'.

exam.q: Explain why the rate of water uptake by a plant is lower at night than during the day.
model: Less or no light at night.
Stomata close.
Less water vapour diffuses out, so less water drawn up the xylem.
Also lower temperature so slower evaporation.
exam.tip: Any three points; link stomata closing to less water loss.

exam.q: In a potometer, the bubble moved 36 mm in 4 minutes. Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm per minute.
model: = 9 mm per min.
exam.tip: Show the working for the method mark.

exam.q: The capillary tube has a radius of 0.5 mm. The bubble moves 40 mm in 10 minutes. Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm3 per minute. Use pi = 3.14.
model: Rate = 31.4 / 10 = 3.14 mm3 per min.
exam.tip: Area first, then volume, then divide by time.

exam.q: Suggest two precautions when setting up a potometer to obtain valid results.
model: Cut the shoot under water / assemble under water.
Make apparatus airtight / seal joints with petroleum jelly.
Dry leaves / allow time to acclimatise / keep other variables constant.
exam.tip: Any two; each needs to be a clear practical action.

exam.q: Describe how a potometer could be used to investigate the effect of light intensity on the rate of water uptake.
model: Cut shoot under water and fit into potometer under water; make airtight.
Introduce an air bubble into the capillary tube.
Place a lamp at a set distance, e.g. 10 cm, and allow plant to acclimatise.
Measure distance bubble moves in a set time, e.g. 5 minutes.
Reset bubble using the reservoir and repeat at different distances, e.g. 20, 30, 40, 50 cm.
Control temperature (heat filter or water tank), air movement and humidity; use the same shoot.
Repeat at each distance and calculate a mean rate (distance / time).
exam.tip: Six mark method: independent, dependent and control variables, plus repeats and how you calculate rate.

exam.q: A student found the rate of water uptake increased as light intensity increased but then stayed the same at high light intensities. Explain these results.
model: As light intensity increases more stomata open.
More water vapour diffuses out, so more water taken up.
At high light intensity all stomata are fully open.
Another factor, e.g. temperature or air movement, now limits the rate.
exam.tip: Explain both parts of the graph: the rise and the plateau.

worked.q: A potometer bubble moves 2.4 cm in 6 minutes. Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm per minute.
steps: Convert to mm: 2.4 cm x 10 = 24 mm.
Rate = distance / time = 24 / 6.
Rate = 4 mm per min.
worked.ans: 4 mm per min

worked.q: A capillary tube has a diameter of 1 mm. The bubble moves 15 mm in 5 minutes. Calculate the volume of water taken up per hour in mm3. Use pi = 3.14.
steps: Radius = diameter / 2 = 0.5 mm.
Area = pi x r squared = 3.14 x 0.5 x 0.5 = 0.785 mm2.
Volume in 5 min = 0.785 x 15 = 11.775 mm3.
Rate per minute = 11.775 / 5 = 2.355 mm3 per min.
Rate per hour = 2.355 x 60 = 141.3 mm3 per hour.
worked.ans: 141.3 mm3 per hour (about 141 mm3 per hour)

worked.q: Rate of water uptake was 3.2 mm per min in still air and 5.6 mm per min with a fan. Calculate the percentage increase and explain it.
steps: Change = 5.6 - 3.2 = 2.4 mm per min.
Percentage increase = 2.4 / 3.2 x 100 = 75%.
Explanation: the fan blows water vapour away from the leaf surface, keeping a steep concentration gradient, so water vapour diffuses out of the stomata faster and more water is drawn up.
worked.ans: 75% increase, because air movement maintains a steep water vapour concentration gradient.

bio_edx.5.12.summary: Plant hormones control growth, so farmers and growers use them as tools. **Auxins** are used as **selective weedkillers** and in **rooting powders** for cuttings; **gibberellins** are used to end **seed dormancy** (germination), make plants **flower** and produce **bigger and seedless fruit**; **ethene** gas is used to **control fruit ripening** so fruit can be picked unripe, transported without damage and ripened just before sale. For a grade 9 answer you must link each use to what the hormone does inside the plant and to the commercial benefit.

core.h: What plant hormones are and why they are useful commercially
core.p: Plant hormones are chemicals made in small amounts in one part of the plant that move to other parts and control growth and development. Because they control things like cell elongation, root growth, germination, flowering and ripening, humans can make synthetic versions or apply natural ones to control crops. This lets growers raise yields, cut costs and time their harvests to match demand.
bullets: Edexcel names three hormone groups for this point: **auxins**, **gibberellins** and **ethene**.
Auxins mainly control **cell elongation** in shoots and growth of roots.
Gibberellins control **germination**, **stem elongation**, **flowering** and **fruit development**.
Ethene is a **gas** that controls **fruit ripening** (and leaf fall).
Commercial use relies on applying the hormone at a **controlled concentration** at the **right time**.
Benefits are usually about **higher yield**, **less waste**, **faster production** or **meeting consumer demand**.

callouts.p: A chemical produced by a plant that coordinates and controls growth and responses to the environment.
Auxins: weedkillers and rooting powders. Gibberellins: germination, fruit and flower formation, seedless fruit. Ethene: fruit ripening.

core.p: Synthetic auxins are sprayed on fields of cereal crops such as wheat. **Broad-leaved weeds** (dicots, such as dandelions and daisies) absorb much more of the auxin than the **narrow-leaved crop** (grasses such as wheat). The weed receives a very high auxin dose, which makes its cells elongate and grow **too rapidly and uncontrollably**; the weed cannot support this growth, its stem twists and its transport tissues are disrupted, so it **dies**. The crop is barely affected.
bullets: They are called **selective** because they kill only some plant types (broad-leaved) and leave the crop (narrow-leaved).
Broad leaves have a **larger surface area**, so more spray lands on them and is absorbed.
Narrow, upright cereal leaves absorb **much less** auxin.
Fewer weeds means **less competition** for light, water, mineral ions and space.
So the crop gets more resources, photosynthesises more and gives a **higher yield**.
Lawns are treated in the same way: grass survives, daisies and dandelions die.

callouts.p: Auxin weedkillers do not poison the weed; they kill it by causing uncontrolled, too-rapid growth.
Always name both the effect on the weed (grows too fast and dies) and the benefit (less competition, higher crop yield).

core.p: A **cutting** is a small piece of stem with leaves cut from a parent plant. If the cut end is dipped in **rooting powder** (or gel) containing auxin, the cutting grows **roots quickly**. It can then be planted in compost and grows into a new plant.
bullets: Auxin at the right concentration **stimulates root growth** at the cut end.
Roots form **faster** and **more reliably** than without hormone.
Each new plant is a **clone**: genetically identical to the parent, so it keeps desirable features (for example flower colour or disease resistance).
Growers can produce **large numbers of plants quickly and cheaply** from one good parent.
Used for many garden and crop plants that are slow or hard to grow from seed.
Downside: clones have **no genetic variation**, so one disease could affect them all.

callouts.p: Rooting powder contains auxins and makes cuttings develop roots rapidly, giving many identical plants.

core.p: Auxins have different effects at different concentrations, and shoots and roots respond differently. Commercial products are therefore made up at carefully chosen concentrations: a low dose that encourages roots in rooting powder, and a high dose that causes damaging overgrowth in weedkiller.
bullets: Rooting powder: auxin concentration chosen to **promote** root formation.
Weedkiller: high concentration that causes **uncontrolled** growth in broad-leaved weeds.
Too much hormone can harm the plant you want to help, so instructions must be followed.
This is why hormones are applied in **measured doses**, not just poured on.

callouts.p: The same hormone can be a growth promoter or a killer depending on dose and plant type: a good grade 9 point.

core.p: Many seeds have a period of **dormancy** when they will not germinate even in good conditions. Gibberellins **break seed dormancy** and start germination. In the seed, gibberellins switch on the production of enzymes such as **amylase**, which break down stored starch into sugars that the embryo uses for respiration and growth.
bullets: Applying gibberellins makes seeds germinate **even when they otherwise would not** (for example without a cold period).
Gives **faster, more uniform germination**, so a whole crop grows at the same rate.
Used in **brewing**: barley seeds are treated with gibberellin to germinate (malting); amylase converts starch to **maltose**, a sugar used to make beer.
Saves time for growers and brewers.

callouts.p: A state in which a seed does not germinate even when conditions are suitable.

core.p: Gibberellins can make plants **flower** earlier, or flower when they would not normally do so (for example outside their normal season, or without the usual day length or cold trigger). Growers use this to produce flowers to sell at a time of high demand.
bullets: Plants can be made to flower **at any time of year**, not just in their natural season.
Can make plants flower **without** the normal environmental trigger.
Useful for flower growers selling for events (for example Valentine's Day or Mother's Day).
Can also be used to make plants **bigger** by stimulating **stem elongation**.

core.p: Gibberellins promote **fruit growth**. Sprayed on fruit crops they increase fruit **size**. Grapes are a common example: gibberellin makes the grapes larger and also lengthens the stalks so bunches are less tightly packed, which reduces fungal disease.
bullets: Bigger fruit gives a **higher yield and market value**.
Longer stalks in grape bunches: more air flow, fewer moulds.
Fruit growth can be stimulated even **without fertilisation** (see seedless fruit).

core.p: Normally fruit only develops after a flower is **fertilised**, and the fruit contains seeds. If gibberellins are applied to flowers, fruit can develop **without fertilisation**, so the fruit contains **no seeds**. Seedless grapes and seedless citrus fruit are produced this way.
bullets: No fertilisation, so **no seeds** develop, but the fruit still grows.
Consumers **prefer** seedless fruit, so it sells for more.
Also removes reliance on **pollination** (useful if pollinating insects are scarce).

callouts.p: Gibberellins can make fruit form without fertilisation, giving seedless fruit.
Seedless fruit is made with gibberellins in this spec, not with ethene. Ethene only ripens fruit.

core.p: **Ethene** is a plant hormone that is a **gas**. It is produced by ripening fruit and **speeds up ripening**: it triggers changes such as starch turning to sugar (sweeter), the fruit softening, and colour change (for example green to yellow in bananas).
bullets: Fruit such as bananas is **picked unripe** while it is firm and green.
Unripe fruit is **hard**, so it is **less easily bruised or damaged** during transport.
It is transported and stored at **low temperature** and low ethene (sometimes with ethene absorbers or extra CO2) to **slow ripening**.
Near the shop, fruit is exposed to **ethene gas** in ripening rooms so it ripens **just in time** for sale.
Result: **less waste**, longer shelf life, fruit available all year round, ripe when the customer buys it.
Because ethene is a gas, one ripe fruit can speed up ripening of others nearby (one bad apple...).

callouts.p: A gaseous plant hormone that controls fruit ripening.
Give the full sequence: picked unripe, transported (less damage), ethene added, ripens ready for sale.

core.p: This table pulls together every use the spec names. Learn it as hormone, use, how it works, and benefit.
bullets: Each use links a **biological effect** to a **commercial benefit**.
Exam answers that give both parts score full marks.

head: Hormone
Commercial use
How it works
Benefit
rows: Broad-leaved weeds absorb more, grow too fast, die
Many cloned plants quickly and cheaply
Breaks seed dormancy, switches on amylase
Fast, even germination; malting for brewing
Flowers at times of high demand
Pick unripe, less damage and waste, ripe for sale

core.h: Advantages and disadvantages of using plant hormones
core.p: Evaluating hormone use is a common 6 mark style task. Weigh the benefits for food production against possible problems.
bullets: Advantage: **higher yields** and more efficient food production to feed a growing population.
Advantage: **less food waste** (ethene control) and products available **all year**.
Advantage: weedkillers reduce need for weeding by hand, saving **labour and cost**.
Disadvantage: weedkillers can **reduce biodiversity** by killing wild flowers that insects feed on.
Disadvantage: spray can **drift** onto other plants or wash into habitats.
Disadvantage: cuttings give **clones**, so low genetic variation and vulnerability to disease.
Disadvantage: hormones and their application **cost money**, and wrong doses can damage crops.

callouts.p: For evaluate questions give at least one advantage and one disadvantage, then a conclusion.

analogy.t: Plant hormones as a building site foreman
analogy.p: Think of a plant as a building site and hormones as the foreman's instructions. Auxin rooting powder is the foreman shouting 'build foundations here now' at the cut stem, so roots go in fast. Auxin weedkiller is giving the weed such an extreme 'build faster!' order that the workers throw up walls with no support and the whole structure collapses. Gibberellin is the 'start work today' order that ends the waiting period (dormancy) or opens the flower shop early. Ethene is the 'finish and decorate' signal sent just before opening day so the fruit is ready on time. Where it breaks down: a foreman thinks and decides, but hormones are just chemicals whose effect depends on concentration and on which cells respond to them; nothing is planned.

terms.d: A chemical produced by plants that controls growth and responses.
A plant hormone that controls cell elongation in shoots and affects root growth.
A plant hormone that promotes germination, stem elongation, flowering and fruit growth.
A gaseous plant hormone that speeds up fruit ripening.
A herbicide that kills some types of plant (broad-leaved weeds) but not others (narrow-leaved crops).
A weed with wide leaves (a dicot) that absorbs more auxin spray than grasses.
A powder containing auxin that makes cuttings grow roots quickly.
A piece of stem with leaves taken from a parent plant to grow a new, genetically identical plant.
An organism genetically identical to its parent.
The start of growth of a seed into a seedling.
A resting state in which a seed does not germinate even in suitable conditions.
Fruit that develops without fertilisation, produced using gibberellins.
Fusion of male and female gametes; normally needed for seeds and fruit to form.
Changes in fruit such as softening, sweetening and colour change, controlled by ethene.
The amount of useful crop produced per area.
When organisms need the same limited resources, such as light, water and mineral ions.

mistakes.w: Auxin weedkillers poison the weeds.
mistakes.r: They cause broad-leaved weeds to grow too rapidly or uncontrollably, so they die.

mistakes.w: Weedkillers kill all plants.
mistakes.r: They are selective: they kill broad-leaved weeds but not narrow-leaved crops such as wheat.

mistakes.w: Weedkillers help the crop grow because auxin makes it grow.
mistakes.r: The crop benefits because there is less competition from weeds for light, water and mineral ions, increasing yield.

mistakes.w: Rooting powder contains gibberellins.
mistakes.r: Rooting powder contains auxins.

mistakes.w: Ethene is used to make seedless fruit.
mistakes.r: Gibberellins produce seedless fruit; ethene ripens fruit.

mistakes.w: Ethene is a liquid sprayed on fruit.
mistakes.r: Ethene is a gas that the fruit is exposed to in ripening rooms.

mistakes.w: Fruit is picked unripe so it ripens on the plant.
mistakes.r: Fruit is picked unripe because it is firm and less likely to be damaged in transport; it is ripened later with ethene.

mistakes.w: Gibberellins make seeds dormant.
mistakes.r: Gibberellins break dormancy and start germination.

mistakes.w: Plants from cuttings are genetically different from the parent.
mistakes.r: They are clones, genetically identical to the parent plant.

exam.q: Name the plant hormone used in rooting powder.
model: Auxin
exam.tip: One word answer; spell it auxin.

exam.q: Name the plant hormone that is a gas and causes fruit to ripen.
model: Ethene
exam.tip: Accept ethylene, but ethene is the spec term.

exam.q: State one commercial use of gibberellins.
model: Any one: ending seed dormancy / promoting germination; making plants flower; increasing fruit size; producing seedless fruit
exam.tip: Name a use, not just 'growth'.

exam.q: Explain why fruit growers spray gibberellins on grape flowers.
model: Fruit develops without fertilisation
So seedless grapes are produced, which consumers prefer / larger fruit
exam.tip: Link the effect to the commercial benefit.

exam.q: Explain how rooting powder helps a gardener produce many plants of a prize variety.
model: Auxin in powder stimulates rapid root growth on cuttings
New plants are clones, so have the same desirable features as the parent
exam.tip: Mention clones to explain why the variety stays the same.

exam.q: Bananas are picked green and exposed to ethene before sale. Explain the advantages of this.
model: Unripe fruit is firm so less damaged/bruised during transport
Ethene ripens fruit at a controlled time
So fruit is ripe when it reaches shops, reducing waste / longer shelf life
exam.tip: Give the sequence and a benefit at each stage.

exam.q: Explain how a selective weedkiller containing auxin increases the yield of a wheat crop.
model: Broad-leaved weeds absorb more auxin than narrow-leaved wheat
Weeds grow too rapidly/uncontrollably and die
Wheat is unaffected
Less competition for light, water, mineral ions, so wheat grows more and yield increases
exam.tip: Four marks need effect on weed, effect on crop and the competition link.

exam.q: Explain why maltsters treat barley seeds with gibberellins.
model: Gibberellins break dormancy so seeds germinate quickly and together
Amylase produced breaks starch into sugar (maltose) used for brewing
exam.tip: Link to enzymes breaking down stored starch.

exam.q: Suggest one disadvantage of using auxin weedkillers on farmland.
model: Kills wild flowers so reduces biodiversity / food for insects; or spray drift harms other plants
exam.tip: Think about the environment beyond the crop.

exam.q: Evaluate the use of plant hormones in commercial food production.
model: Auxin weedkillers kill broad-leaved weeds by causing too-rapid growth
Reducing competition so crop yields increase
Auxin rooting powder gives many identical plants quickly but clones lack variation so vulnerable to disease
Gibberellins give seedless/larger fruit and control germination/flowering to meet demand
Ethene allows unripe fruit to be transported with less damage and ripened for sale, reducing waste
Disadvantages: weedkillers reduce biodiversity, cost, wrong doses damage crops; conclusion that benefits for food supply generally outweigh costs if used carefully
exam.tip: Balance advantages and disadvantages across all three hormones and finish with a justified conclusion.

worked.q: A farmer sprays one field of wheat with auxin weedkiller and leaves a second field unsprayed. The sprayed field yields 8.4 tonnes per hectare and the unsprayed field 7.0 tonnes per hectare. Calculate the percentage increase in yield and explain it.
steps: Increase = 8.4 - 7.0 = 1.4 tonnes per hectare
Percentage increase = (1.4 / 7.0) x 100 = 20%
Explanation: auxin is absorbed mostly by broad-leaved weeds, which grow too fast and die
Wheat now has less competition for light, water and mineral ions, so it photosynthesises and grows more
worked.ans: Yield rises by 20% because removing weeds reduces competition for resources.

worked.q: A supermarket chain imports bananas from the Caribbean by ship, taking about two weeks. Describe and explain how plant hormones are used so that the bananas arrive in good condition and are ripe in the shop.
steps: Bananas are picked unripe while green and firm
Firm fruit is less easily bruised during the long journey
They are kept cool with low ethene levels to slow ripening
On arrival they are put in ripening rooms and exposed to ethene gas
Ethene speeds ripening so the bananas become yellow, soft and sweet just before sale
worked.ans: Picking unripe and ripening with ethene at the destination reduces damage and waste and gives ripe fruit on time.

worked.q: A grower has one rose bush with an unusual flower colour and wants 200 identical bushes quickly. Explain the best method.
steps: Take many stem cuttings from the parent rose
Dip the cut ends in rooting powder containing auxin
Auxin stimulates rapid root growth
Plant cuttings in compost; they grow into new plants
All are clones so have the same flower colour; this is faster than growing from seed, which would give variation
worked.ans: Use cuttings with auxin rooting powder to produce many genetically identical roses quickly.
